THE WARRIOR'S A warrior rode upon a quest For deeds to crown a noble name. And give to her whom he loved best Not only love, but fame. Where'er the storm of war might drift, Its din to him was music rare; Nor e'er did smoke of battle lift But he was there. Of him the lands afar had heard; His prowess lived in many a song; His name became a household word— The Righter of the Wrong. The years like moments sped away, While onward still some vision lured, And calm within his bosom lay His love assured. Bat the sweet lady for whose sake The warrior rode upon his quest Found the years long to watch and wake For tidings east or west; And of t she sat within her bower Silent and sad as day grew dim, And oft she climbed the lofty tower To watch for him. "0 love," she sighed, "since life is sweet, Since life is brief, why seek so long For gifts to lay before my feet? Thou doest lovea wrong. I cannot ride from east to west To meet thee in the battle's fray, But I must bear an aching breast From day to day." Homeward at length the warrior turned, Sated with victory, and full fain To tell the love that once more burned Into a cherished pain. His glorious steed with trappings gay Bore him right proudly, and his train Of gallant knights far stretched that day Across the plain. But as they neared the castle walls Where dwelt the lady of his love, What sight upon their joyance falls. What sound their fear doth move? .9. funeral train from out the gate To tolling bells is slowly led : Olsry and love have come too late— They greet the dead. —Ha; per's 31agazine.

"Will you join me in a cup of tea, Mr. Simpkins?"—Mr Simpkins: "Alt, thank you; but wouldn't it be rather crowded ?" " Why," exclaimed a tourist, " a donkey couldn't climb that hill," ard then he added, "you may rest assured I'm not going to try it." Big girl (to five-year-old Fannie on a boarding-school stair) : "Oh, Fannie, give me a kiss." Fannie: " Can't ; I've only one left, and I want that for seed." A counsel, being questioned by a Judge to know "for whom he was concerned," replied, "I am concerned, my lord, for the plaintiff, but I am employed by the defendant." A POSI,R.—MoIIy (regarding a bust on a pedestal): "Oh, what a dear little boy !" Grandnapa : "That was me when I was your age, Molly." Molly : "And who is it now, grandpapa ?" A seedy man was recently bewailing the fact that he had on a worn-out pair of shoes. "Never mind," said a friend sympathetically, "there is many an honest heart beats be- neath a pair of old shoes" Mrs. Demming asked Matilda, the house eervant, a few nights ago: "What dreadful scratching is that out in the kitchen ? It must be the dog trying to get in. I never heard anything like it in my life." "Dat's no dog scratchin' de doahe Dat'e de cook writin' a lub letter to her honeysuckle, who works down in de Austin ice factory." Some years since a letter directed to "Zramfridavi," was I received at the London Post-office. Unable to find such a person, it was referred to the savans, who found out at last that it was intended for Sir Humphry Davy, the great chemist. A. commercial traveller passing through Weston, near Bridgewater, seeing a sign over the door with this one word, " Agoraqrdere," he called to the woman to inquire what she sold, when she said that she did not sell anything, but that "Aquas were cured here." Two little bright thoughts of Dr. Oliver Wendell Holmes's are now going the round of the New York papers. A young physician was breakfasting with the doctor, and asked him for a suitable motto. "Small favours gratefully received," was the witty response. At another time he was complaining to a lady of the minute portion of honey that was put before him at an hotel at tea--" A mere trifle; the work of a very young bee in an idle half-hour " Did they give you no comb, doctor ?" she laughingly inquired. "Possibly one tooth, madam !" A story is told of a great French satirist which finely illustrates his knowledge of human nature. He was travel- ling in Germany, in entire ignorance of its language and currency. Having obtained some small change for some of his French coins, he used to pay coachmen and others in the following manner. Taking a handful of the numia- matical specimens from his pocket, he counted them one by-one, into the creditor's hands, keeping his eyes fixed all the time on the receiver's face. A soon as he perceived the least twinkle of a smile, he took back the last coin de- posited in the hand, and returned it, with the remainder, to his pocket. He afterwards found that, in pursuing this method, he had not overpaid for anything. CRICKET AND ITS Foannuerarmas.—Now, as far as we can ascertain, cricket seems to have been evolved out of stool-ball, and tip-cat, or as it was called, cat and dog. From stool-ball was borrowed the primitive wicket—a stool, or cricket—which (perhaps) gave its name to the pastime. From stool-ball, too, we have the custom of tossing or bowl- irg the ball to the striker. From cat and dog we borrow that part of the game which consists in running between two fixed points while the ball (at cat and dog the cat, or piece of wood) is being fielded or returned, by the other side. Cat and dog is in one sense a classical game. Bunyan tells us that he was playing at it, and just about to strike the cat, when he beard a supernatural voice bidding him fcrbear. I remember reading this passage in childhood, and fancying that Banyan was torturing a poor puss, and that bia heart was suddenly wrung by a sense of his own cruelty. Ben Bunyan was merely affected by a consciousness of the wickedness of primitive cricket. It seems that in some districts, cat and dog was less like knur and spell, or trap, bat, and ball, than I have supposed. The cat was not hit up and then knocked away by the player, as in tip-cat, but was thrown or bowled to him, as at cricket. —English Illustrated Magazine. Meoloeuarate MARDlS.—During the last few months everyone has been speaking of the Nelda but comparatively few, it is safe to say, have connected any precise idea with the title assumed by Sheikh Mohammed of Dongola, or have had before their minds in using that title the remark- able passages in the past history of Islam which the name of Diandl calls up to the Oriental student. And, singularly enough, uncertainty as to the true meaning of a word which Is far from uncommon in Arabic authors has not been con- fined to persons ignorant of Arabic. For as the name of the Matadi is written in ordinary Arabic books, that is without the points marking the vowels, it is possible to read and explain it in more than one way. A writer in The Times, who may be safely identified with an Arabic scholar of most distinguished eminence, has recently proposed to speak, not of the Mandi, but of the Multda and interprets the word as meaning " the guide," the spiritual and inspired guide that Is, of the followers of Islam. It is well, therefore, to observe at the outset that it can be shown conclusively that this view, though supported by an eminent scholar, is certainly wrong. Without going into questions of grammar, it is enough to say that the decision between the current pro- nunciation and that proposed in The Times can be made at once, if the word is found in verse, by the simple process of scansion. Now there are abundance of verses in which the Mallen is spoken of, and they prove that the current pro- nunciation is correct. They prove also that the word is the passive participle of a verb meaning to guide, and the Mandi therefore is not the guide of the faithful, but he who is himself guided by divine grace and inspiration.—Professor W. Robertson Smith, in Good Words. A MEMORABLE PASSAGE in the life of the late Rev. Dr. S. H. Cox was his entrance into Exeter Hall, as a delegate _

I;o—tn. the American Bible Society. "Dr. Cox," says-the narrator, "arrived in Exeter Hall after the meeting was be- gun, and a tirade sgainst America greeted him as he en- tered. As the speaker sat down Dr. Cox was announced as the delegate from the American society. The terrible de. nunciation just delivered had excited the indignation of the audience, and Dr. Cox was received with respectful cold- ness ; but his splendid figure, his gallant, courteous, com- manding presence, his irresistible smile, lightened instantly the gloom of the hall and conciliated tits audience. He be. ban—' My Lord,' addressing the nobleman who presided over the vast assembly, 'twenty days ago I was taken by the tug Hercules from the quay in New York to the good ship Samson lying in the stream, thus, my Lord, going from strength to strength. By the good hand of the Lord I was brought to your shores just in time to reach this house, and to enter in the midst of the burning denunciations of my beloved country that have fallen from the lips of the gentle- man who ha just sat down. He ha reproached that country for the existence of slavery, which I abhor as much as he. But be did not tell you, my lord, that when we re- volted from your Government one of the reasons alleged was the fat that your King had forced that institution upon US in spite of our remonstrances, and that the original sin rests with you and your fathers. And now, my lord, instead of indulging in mutual reproaches, I propose that the gentleman shall be Shem and I will be Japhetb, and taking the mantle of charity, we will walk backward, and we will cover the nakedness of our common father." "The effect," said Dr. Wm. Adams, who witnessed the scene, "was instantaneous and overwhelming. The day was won, and a more popular orator than Dr. Cox was not heard during the anniversaries." THRIFT.—The latest official ret.7rns of Provident Societies in England and Wales show a membership of six millions and funds amounting to thirty-eight millions of pounds. The ROYAL CLOTBING CLUB, of 57. South John-street, Liver- yool, is one of the Institution, for the encouragement of thrift, whereby Clothing may be obtalne I by easy payments of Is and 23 per week. Th:s club has he n an enormous success in bone- fitting the middle and working c'asses, the economical system upon wh!ch it is conducted enabling it to supply clothing of exceptional quality at moderate prices. The public should send Sr prcspectus and join at once, as nothing is to be gained by de:ay in matters of thriftiness.—.Adrt.

R ASK. FARM FRIZZ 01 4e 4rt —it connection with the county meeting of :ts ss fst the ear 1885, to be held at Preston in July,) • s s ta tie value of £395 are offered by the Preston Loca. J n nittee, the Right Hon. the Earl of Derby, 13. G , Mrs. 'Mitt)", of Lytham Hall, and the society, for different descriptions of farms, as dairy, arable, or stock-breeding. The competition applies to an unusually wide area, and the seven classes are so ar- ranged as to include nearly every variety of agricultural holding. In Class 1 the sum of £5O is offered for the beet. managed arable farm of 100 acres and upwards in extent, with at least two-thirds of its area under rotation of crop- ping; and £25 for the second beat. The next section is for arable farms above 30 and under 100 acres, under the same conditions, £3O being set aside for the best, and £l5 for the second in merit. Class 3 has a prize of £5O for the beat- managed dairy farm of 100 acres and upwards, where the management and cultivation are most anccesafally directed to the production of milk7butter, or cheese; with a second prize of £25. In the fourth class there are premiums of £3O for the best, and £l5 for the second best, dairy farm above 30 and under 100 acres. The next division includes stock- breeding farms of 100 acres or upwards, where the manage- ment is principally and most successfully directed to the breeding and rearing of farm stock, cattle, sheep, horses, or pigs; and here there are prizes of £5O and £25 respectively. Similar farms of smaller extent, between 30 and 100 acres, may compete in the sixth class, first prize £3O, second £l5 In the remaining class three prizes, £2O, £lO, and £5, are offered for farms of not more than 40 acres, where the prin- cipal part of the labour is contributed by the farmer's own family. We may add that the first four classes (for arable and dairy farms) are open to farms situate within so much of the district of the Royal Manchester, Liverpool, and North Lancashire Agricultural Society as is included in the Royal Agricultural Society's district G (Cheshire, Lanca- shire, and North Wales) ; and that the other three classes are limited to farms in the same district which are situate north of the Ribble, and within the Hundreds of Blackburn and Leyland. The custom of offering these prizes, which annually results in revealing many Interesting features of the farming of the particular district to which the camps• tition is confined, originated in 1870, and is regarded as an extremely valuable addition to the society's other opera- tions. The object of the prizes is, of course, to encourage good and profitable farming as a business, and therefore it has been found necessary to restrict the competitions to tenant farmers paying a bond fide rent for at least three. fourths of the land which they cultivate, thus excluding so- called "model firms" which are held as an amusement at a great expense by wealthy men. The judges will be in- structed especially to consider general management with a view to profit; productiveness of crops; quality and suita- bility of live stock ; management of grass land ; state of gates, fences, roads, and general neatness ; mode of book. keeping followed (if any) ; and, in the case of .dairy farme, management of the dairy and dairy produce. The judges will be authorised to recommend to the council of the society the award of medals or certificates to any really deserving persons engaged on any of the competing farms for distinguished merit in the discharge of their duties ; these recommendations to be accompanied by a certificate of good character and length of service from the competing farmer.

div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING.

ONIONS —The dry weather has arrested the growth of these, so that many are now ready for storing; and to leave them in the soil after reaching this stage, is to invite them to make secondary growth, which they will assuredly do, and this is most undesirable to onions that are intended to keep. We would therefore advise that they should be ex- amined, and all showing signs of maturity secured, and any that have mouldy patches at the point where the roots emerge from should be laid by themselves to be used first, for they will only keep a short time. Onions with thick necks should have a twist at that part, and the top bent down. This operation checks the flow of sap to the top, and confines it to the bulb, which on that account is calculated to increase in size. Bat apart from that, they mature so much earlier, and are also more likely to keep. A dry airy position is the place for the onion after it is taken up, and if some contrivance could be made so that they may be moved into the sun a few hours daily for the first three or four days, it would help to dry them more effectually. THE STRAWBERRY Ben.—Now that planting is supposed to be completed, all the runners should be trimmed either by running a knife round each plant or by chopping with the spade, and, as many of the runners will have firmly rooted in the spaces between the permanent plants, the hoe will be required to remove them, and the rake will do the remainder. After all is cleared the beds should have a slight forking, just sufficient to break the surface which has been hardened by the continuous traffic in gathering the fruit. This is a good time to apply a covering of manure to the surface, because now all is cleared away. The roots of the permanent plants are more exposed, and the mulching which was placed round them to preserve the fruit clean, has naturally drawn them nearer the surface than they would be if no such surface dressing had been applied. If the manure is of good quality the autumn rains will wash all the fertilising properties out of it into the soil, to be taken up by the roots for the benefit of next year's crop. THE FRONT GARDEN.—Some plants have faced the pact dry period with the greatest indifference. For instance, the Sunflowers were never so fine as this season. Thanks fora much dwarfer race in place of the huge disc on a 71t. or Bft stem. Helianthus rigidus is a perennial 3ft. high, with flower 3in. across, which appear in numbers. We have, also, some that are annuals, of recent introduction. Rudbeckia Newmani is a perennial that might be taken for a miniature sunflower, which also has been most floriferous and maintained its green foliage to the very last. The same may be said of the Chrysanthemum Leucanthemum, the number of its white and yellow flowers being produced with undeviating regularity. The erratic Gladioli has been uncommonly fine and some that were accidentally left in the ground daring the winter have done as well as any. Anemore Japonica, the pink and white, showed a most de- termined effort to produce successive flowers. On the other hand there was a paucity of flower on the Dahlias that were not artificially watered. The same may be said of Sweet Peas, and it may be noted of these that they continue to flower more freely and for a greater length of time if the pods are remcved as soon as they form; for nothing tasks the energy of a plant more than forming its seeds, and this is specially manifest amongst the Leguminose, the class to which the Sweet Pea belongs. The flowers on some of the older plants of herbaceous nbloxes were completely with- ered the last fortnight of the drought. These are such strong rooting plants that they suck all moisture out of the soil even in ordinary seasons, and for this reason they al- ways enjoy a good mulching as soon as their flowers are about to expand. _ _

THE WINDOl9.—Some of the earliest pruned Pelar- goniums will be broken sufficiently so as to be ready for potting, when nearly all the soil must be shaken away from them, and the plants placed in pots a size less than those they have occupied. The pots must be washed, especially inside, and perfectly dry when used, or it will be found most difficult to turn the plants out if it is necessary to in- troduce them into a larger pot in the spring. A quantity of clean crocks should be got in readiness for the purpose of draining the pots; also soil, which should consist of par- tially decayed turfy loam chopped or pulled into pieces, but not sifted, as is the custom with some; for it is highly im- portant that all fibre should be retained in the soil. A quantity of leaf mould will also be required, but this may be passed through a half•inch sieve, and the rougher por- tion reserved to place on the drainage to prevent the smaller particles of soil mingling with the crocks. The proportions of loam and leaf mould are regulated by the nature of the first. If heavy more leaf mould is added, and if sandy less; but, as a rule, three of loam and one of leaf soil, with an eighth of sand, makes a good compost.

LIJITACY.—In 1882 there were 1,142 lunatics, from whose estates £20,479 was drawn, while £22 687 was expended upon them. From 1873 to 1882 the total number of such lunatics was 10,220, from whose estates £lB3OOl had been drawn, while there had been expended upon the lunatics £218,639, leaving a total excess of expenditure over receipts amounting to £34 648. _

A UOI:113AN fieuerr.—Excepting southern Italy, there is no country which can compare with Greece in beauty and interest to the intelligent traveller. It is not a land for creature comforts, though the climate is splendid, and though the hotels in Athens are as good as those in any European town. It is not a land for sunny,' though the society at Athens is excellent, and far easier of access than that of most European capitals. But if a man is fond of the large effects of natural scenery, he will find, in the Southern Alps and fiords of Greece, a variety and a richness of colour which no other part of Europe affords. If he is fond of the details of natural scenery, flowers, shrubs, and trees, he will find the wild flowers, and flowering trees of Greece more splendid than anything he has yet Been. If he desires to study national character, and peculiar manners and customs, he will find in the hardy mountaineers of Greece one of the most unreformed societies, hardly yet affected by the great tide of sameness which is invading all Europe, in dress, fabrics, and usages. And yet, in spite of the folly still talked in England about brigands, he will find that without troops, or police, or patrols, or any of those melancholy safegualds which are now SO obtrusive in England and Ireland, life and property are as safe as they ever were in our most civilised homes. Let him not know a word of history, or of art, and he will yet be rewarded by all this natural enjoyment; perhaps also, if he be a politi- cian, he may study the results of a constitution made to order, and planted in a nation of no political training, but of high intelligence.—English Illustrated Magazine. THE MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY.

PREPARATION FOR SHOWS. Some time ago a correspondent asked for some informa- tion as to the preparation of birds for exhibition, but we thought it better to postpone replying to the question until the show season, for at the time it was asked no exhibitions were being held. Shows are now becoming more and more plentiful, and as the question of condition will be given more and more weight as the season advances, it is very im- portant indeed that the birds be made to look their best. We do not mean by this that any unfair methods should be resorted to in order to improve the fowls, and make them seem what they are not, for trimming or faking in any or every form we most strongly denounce, but simply that the birds shall show themselves in the best way they can. What is known by condition is simply having fowls or animals in the pink of health and bloom. Condition is, or I ought to be, healthiness, for anything in perfect health has a beauty which can never be supplied in any other way. This is one of the so-called secrets of success in exhibiting. And the exhibitor who can send his specimens in the best condition stands a much better chance of winning than if he neglected this matter. Many a worse bird has beaten a better one, simply because it was well shown. The good appearance brought out the merits of the fowl, whereas in the other case, the bad condition, rough plumage, dull ap- pearance, and listless manner, so detracted from the other good points that the judge could not place it as high as it would otherwise have been. It is perfectly right that this should be so, and the exhibitor who sends an ill-conditioned specimen to a show deserves to be pat low down. Granting, then, to condition this important position, the question naturally comes how to obtain it. If condition be health, then to de this the birds most be kept healthy. It is true that many exhibition birds are far from healthy, and that brilliant plumage is a matter of breeding, and of artificial feeding But birds so bred and fed do not last long. Feeding up on rich foods may succeed for a time, but soon the natural result follows, and the birds lose that which gave them their prominence. sooner or later this forcing system of feeding is found to be a failure. And the experience of all exhibitors teaches that the most natural system pays best in the bog ran. For the early chicken shows birds are of ten forced unnaturally, bat very seldom is a winner at such eh° ws of any use at the winter exhibi- tions. By that time the forcing has brought its natural result, and the fowl is unable to bear the strain. Those that are allowed to grow naturally, to mature slowly, to develop properly, stand the best, and ultimately ate the best birds. Fowls intended to be killed early may be forced with advantage, but those designed as breeders or for exhibition ought not to be fed up in this way. The plan we have always adopted has been to al'o v birds we wish to show as much liberty as possible up to within a week of the time of exhibition. The &sire: of this is to allow them to strengthen and mature. They are then each, or in pairs, put into a large pen or o .ge, some- thing like the pens used at shows, but larger, say, for large birds four feet by two and a half feet, and for small birds two and a half feet square. This cage is indoors and about three feet from the ground. One object in this is to make the birds familiar with confinement in a pen, wish the pass- ing to and fro before the pen, and with the stirring up pro- cess so common at shows. The owner should, therefore, train the birds in this way whilst they are in the pen, for many a first-class specimen has lost a prize because it was so wild. When anyone comes near a pen containing a fowl of this kind it rushes about, jumping up and down en- deavouring to escape, and neither the judge or anyone else can really see what it is like. All this cl 2 be prevented in the way we have stated, and some fowls, Bantameespecially, get nearly as much drilling as a regiment of raw recruits. They thus get to understand the whole business, knowing what is expected of them, and show themselves off to the best advantage. There is no need for as much training as is generally given to Bantams for ordinary fowls, but as much as can be done in a week will take from them the fear of being looked at and of being kept in a small pen. It is useful also to handle them once or twice each day. Judges often require to get a bird out of the pen to examine it, and if it submits to the process willingly it has a better chance of success than if it violently struggled against it. We do not believe in feeding up birds for show upon an artificial and forcing diet. The reasons for this have been already stated. But it is quite allowable that slightly richer food should be given, so long as this is not overdone. Oar plan has been to give a little aromatic compound in the soft food—Spratt's we have found to be the best meal for the morning meal,—and twice or thrice during the week of preparation we mix a little linseed in the soft food. This is best prepared as follows :—To a pint of water a fourth of a pint of whole linseed will be needed. Let the water boil, and whilst still on the fire throw in the seed. The sudden application of the heat causes the send to hurst, and if the water is allowed to gently boil for 10 or 15 minutes the lin- seed will be found to have absorbed all the water, and the whole be a jelly. This whilst hot should be mixed with the meal, and there will be sufficient moisture to take up enough for a feed for half a dozen or eight birds. Every day it is a good plan to take each fowl out of the pen, stand it on a box or hamper, and smooth down the feathers the right way with both hands. This is very effec- tive in obtaining an evenness of feather and preventing roughness in plumage; and before they are sent off to the show the faces, combs, wattles, legs, and feet should be well washed, if the whole body is not entirely cleansed with water. Bat this question of washing we must leave over to another week, when we shall tally describe the process.

SEA.SON&BLE BIN FS. Sometimes at this season of the year hens are troubled with a complaint that is known by the name "Down be- hind." This is generally caused by over-feeding or too stimulating food, though it may also be due to weakness in the egg organs. It is distinguished by a portion of the intestines coming down at the vent, and unless the hen is relieved she will soon die. The remedy is to gently return the part whenever it protrudes, afterwards injecting a little cold water, in which some alum has been dissolved. This treatment must be accompanied by a low diet, and the ab- sence of stimulating food. But it is also necessary to ob- serve th tt fowls with a tendency to this complaint should be cartfully and somewhat sparingly fed at all times.

CHANGE OF PLUMAGE IN 'ME WILD DUCK.—The Drake leaves his mate directly she commences to hatch her eggs, and then undergoes, in common with many other male birds of the Duck family, one of the strangest transformations known to naturalists. The plumage of the Drake is, up to this time, exceedingly handsome. The bill is yellowish. green ; the. irides hazel; the head and upper part of the neck a rich glossy green, with a ring of white; the lower part of the neck and bock a greyish chestnut-brown; the rump and upper tail-coverts bluish-black; the middle tail- feathers velvet black, and curled upwards; front and sides of the neck rich dark chestnut; breast, belly, vent, greyish white; under tall•corers velvet-black ; legs orange-yellow. As already mentioned, a wonderful change takes place in the appearance of the Drake at the time of breeding. First, the back and breast chauge colour, then the curled feathers are lost, the splendid plumage of the head and neck becomes dull and grey, and about the first week in July all the hand- some markings have disappeared, and the bird has assumed the dull brown colour of the female. This extraordinary change, however, lasts only for a couple of months, and by the first week in October the Drake has discarded his sad- coloured garb, and once more appears in all the beauty of his original plumage.—Frocu "Familiar Wild Birds" for September. _ _

LIFE IN A MANITOBA LOG HonsE.—My next door neighbour, four miles away, is not near enough to encourage morning calla. And for pearly four months last winter I was not well enough to go out, and consequently did not see a woman. This was not such a loss as it appears. The population round us chiefly consists of half-breeds and Indians, with a sprinkling of English settlers. They are most hospitable, but extremely rough, dirty, and uncivilised. Our post office is four miles away, and we can send oft and also fetch letters once a week. Let me describe the interior of the post-office, one day last winter when I had occasion to call there. The postmaster is a very rough Canadian ; his wife is a half-breed, a tall, handsome woman. When we drove up she was out of doors in the snow, chopping' firewood. Her lord and master was sitting in his only downstairs room, with his feet on the stove, and a pipe in his month. In the same room, which was bare of carpet or curtain, and contained the family bed, were three little children—a boy, aged seven, swearing lustily; a girl, about five, sucking her fingers, who began to howl as soon as I spoke; and a baby of two years, seated in frying-pan on the floor, engaged in carefully wrapping up its bare feet in a dishcloth. Their mother followed us into the house, and promptly seizing the handle of the pan, proceeded to eject the baby, and to wipe out the pan with the aforementioned cloth. Next she broke about a dozen eggs into the pan, fried them, and having made tea and produced her solitary teaspoon, she invited my husband and myself to partake, or, as she phrased it, to "sit in" with the family. It is needless to add that, after what I had just witnessed, I declined the hospitality as graciously as I knew how. This is my nearest female neighbour. Another interesting house is the home of a Justice of the Peace for the province, who is a settler near us He is a Scotchman, and can quote Alison's "History of Europe." His household comprises himself and his wife —a half-breed woman—a married daughter, her husband, and their two children; two other grown-up daughters, a son of fifteen, another of ten, and two young men lodgers. The house is a log cabin, and consists simply of one fair- sized room. It is scarcely a cause for surprise that the whole of this family suffered from scarlet fever last spring. The only wonder is that they all recovered. In such a thinly settled country it is naturally very difficult to get any sort of female help. Even in Winnipeg servants are hard to find, and when found are of such temper and quality that I consider the lady most fortunate who can do without one. A friend of mine there paid £36 a year to a very in- ferior servant, whose husband (an artisan) was besides allowed to live with her in the house. And I have known this man smoke a cigar in the hall with his hat on. When his wife left, at two days' notice, he explained that he was sorry to inconvenience my friend, as she suited his wife very well; but that she (his wife) was "leaving to better her- self." From £3O to £4O is an ordinary salary for a domes- tic servant in Winnipeg. An hotel cook expects from £6O to £lOO, or more still if the hotel be large. Under these circumstances, it is hopeless to think of a servant on the prairie, so I do the work myself, with occasional masculine aid. I have to make even the bread and the butter, and prepare everything that is eaten. If I drive 12 miles with linen, and again the same distance to fetch it home, I can, by dint of great persuasion and prelty speeches, occasionally induce a half-breed woman to wash it. She charges me four shillings a dozen, and sends it back clean, certainly, but neither ironed nor even folded. So I generally manage, by the help of patience and a washing-machine, to do every- thing for myself.—All the rear Rouryt.

Rain fell all through the afternoon, but in spite of the weather the number of visitors were large. Nearly 12,000 people paid ,at the turnstiles in the course of the day. Apparently it needs a dood deal of rain to disturb those whose business and inclination take them to cattle shows. The money drawn at the gates on Saturday amounted to £5BO, and in addition to this sum the grand stand yielded £55. The financial results of the show are fairly satisfactory, though they are not equal to those of the two previous years. TRACTION ENGINE COMPETITION.—Tho point of the pro- ceedings on Saturday was the award of the judges who for three days have been testing the merits of the traction engines. The Society offered a gold medal "for the best traction engine suitable for roads, farm, and field work, of not loss than six and not more than ten horse power," a pre- ference to be given to one on springs. A large number of m tkers entered, and tie competition proved extremely inter- estinp.e The judges have thought it well not to give a 'silent" award. "The judges bag to report,' they say, "that they have now completed the trials, which extended into three days, of traction engines en road and field. There were 14 entries in all for competition, and of these 12 were presented for trial and were tested The trials made were mainly devoted to performance, that is to say, to ascertain the distance each engine would haul a given load for a given quantity of fuel. Observations were made as to design, workmanship, steadiness in running, and otherwise. The trials were made in two series —the first to determine (a) the time taken to get up steam to 100. b pressure from atmospheric temperature; (b) steadi- ness in running on a hard macadam road, steering and the like; (c) the distance each engine could haul a load on a grass field for a given quantity of weighed fuel supplied. The second series differed from the first in ha-inae the fires drawn and fuel supplied to relight when the steam pressure fell to 100 lb. Having regard to the merits generally of the engines tested, both those for general agricultural purposes and for heavy haulage, the time obtainable during the show of maleing tests and the narrow margins in efficiency be- tween some of the engines the judges might have hesitated in awarding the medal without more exhaustive trials. But giving due weight to fitness and performance, and consider- ing the subject all round, they hereby award the gold medal to Messrs Aveling and Porter, of Rochester. They feel, however, that other three of the exhibitors have engines which approach so closely in efficiency and merit that they recommend that to each of them there should be awarded the society's silver medal. These are Messrs J and H NPLaren, Leeds; Mr Edwin Foden, Sandbach ; and Messrs John Fowler and Co, Leeds." The judges in this competi- tion were Mr J T King, Liverpool, Mr W Scotson, Aigburth, and Mr J Whalley, Warrington. The engine for which the gold medal is given is described as a " patent eight-horse power agricultural locomotive engine for hauling and thresh- ing." It is fitted with spring wheels. The only other prizes awarded on Saturday were for leap- ing and driving. Although these competitions were for "con- solation " purposes they were of an interesting charac- tear, and held the attention of a large crowd for a couple of hours.

div.head: TECHNICAL EDUCATION AT THE
div.p: TECHNICAL EDUCATION AT THE
HEALTHERIES.

That there should be any connection between technical education and that increasingly-popular exhibition known as " The Healtheries," may at the outset seem somewhat incongruous ' • but on well-balanced reflection it will be found that after all, in an indirect way perhaps, there is a something which links them. For instance, manual la- bour properly directed is, without question, conducive to health, aye, and to happiness ; but, on the other hand, is it not but too painfully apparent, ever and over again, that from ignorance and a lack of technical knowledge, toil that ehould be light and agreeable becomes a drudgery, and that that which should be only mere healthy exercise requires for its accomplishment a 'strain mental and bodily far greater in proportion to the result achieved ? Moreover, this is not an ago when men cmn afford to waste either time or labour. The time was when English manufactures stood prominent, and for that matter, so far as quality goes—un- less manufactured on the shoddy principle—they do so now. But whereas in old days we had things pretty much in our own hands, now we have to compete with the foreigner ha almost every branch of industry. It is not that the foreigner's goods are better, for they are not,—they are nearly always inferior; but then they are cheap, or rather low priced, and that is an irresistible attraction to the great mass of the public. Why is it that the foreigner is thus able to compete with us in our own markets? It must be admitted that to some extent it is due to the fact that he lives cheaper and works for less money than the English- man ; but, nevertheless, it is no use shutting one's eyes to the fact that it is in great measure due to his superior know- ledge. Without question, our friends across the channel have been far more alive to the importance of technical education than we have. On the Continent technical education in some form or other enters largely into the ordinary course of instruction for the young, and the importance attached to it is shown by the fact that the members of the Royal House of Prussia all learn some trade. In England, however, until late years, technical education has been very much neg- lected, and though it is now becoming more general, it is not imparted at all as it should be.. It is only quite re- cently that it has had that official recognition it demands and deserves. If we as a notion are to continue to hold our own, technical education must form part of ordinary in- struction of the young. Every large town should have its technical school, such as are to be found on the Continent ; and it would be an incalculable boon if a workshop were attached to every school. To the children of the classes who live by manual labour the value of instruction such as could be given there will be obvious; but beyond that, we contend that the knowledge there gained would be found useful and profitable, afford a means of enjoyment, and at the some time be conducive to health in the case of those whose daily avocations lie in another direction. Such as them, if they had but the necessary knowledge—say, how I to handle a chisel and plane, or to work at the lathe—would find relaxation and pleasurable exercise by executing in propria persona those numerous odd jobs which always want doing in a house, and if only on this ground technical education is not out of place with such an exhibition as "The Healtheries," not the least interesting department in which is the "City Guilds Workshops." They are rather difficult to find, being stowed away in the east arcade, and approached by a flight of stairs from the Ranges department, but when found they are worth noting. As we said previously, of late years more attention has has been given to techaical instruction, and indeed some of our larger schools have workshops attached to them. 1 All this has tended to increase the number of amateur me- chanics, to an extent, perhaps far greater than would be supposed. A more convincing proof of this could hardly be found than that supplied by the exhibition made, in connexion with the City Guilds Institute, by the "Britan- nia Company" engineers, lathe and tool makers, of Col- chester. Not only does the display made by this company, —who, by the bye, are also exhibiting at the Crystal Palace International Show—point to the steady ad'vance of techni- cal knowledge amongst the mosses, but it tells a tale of spirit and enterprise and pluck which is worth recording.

In the year 1867, the Britannia Company started as makers of sewing machines on the Wheeler and Wilson and other systems; and they still continue to manufacture machines of this sort, though of recent years they have con- fined themselves to those of the Singer type. The manu- facture of these various forms of sowin machines, in order to their production speedily and profitably, necessitated the introduction of a considerable number of special tools and appliances, which either had to be imported or made for the purpose in England. Under these circumstances the firm thought it wise to extend the sphere of their opera- tions, and the result was that in a few years they had gained a wide-spread reputation as makers of lathes, special , engineers' tools, such as milling machines, slide .rests, drill- ing machines, planing and shaping machines, fret cutting appliances, eccentric, geometric and other chucks, dro. As makers of lathes their reputation was such that they secured contracts from the Government for special machines and appliances of this sort adapted for the use of the Royal Navy, and they generally have work on hand for that de- portment. Thorough business tact has from the first char- ac erisecl the management of this company, and wherever an opening appeared the Britannia Company ac-ailed them- selves of it, and their manufactures have become known far and wide. They have been extensive exhibitors at various International Exhibitions, and at those of New Zealand, Amsterdam, Calcutta, and Lendon they have been awarded honours and medals. As their name became spread so their works at Colchester increased until their are now a sight worth seeing. Anyone interested in mechanics might do WOrge than take a holiday in paying the works a visit. The managers are very ready to allow visitors to inspect the premises only stipulating that conversations are not entered into with the workmen ; while Colchester is a tine old town, of itself fully deserving the tourist's consideration, amongst other attrac- tions there are the fine ruins of the castle, many Roman

buildings, and there is an excellent museum. The Britan- nia Works are very conveniently situated near the railway station, and the extensive warehouse ' for castings extends under the very platform. The workshops, separated by a road from the warehouse, are full of labour-saving machi- nery of most ingenious construction, and in fact without its aid the company would hardly be able to finish and turn out the large numbers of different parts of uniform sizes and 'shapes as they do. Some of the machines in use here are capable of doing the work of twenty skilled mechanics. The sight of a number of parts of machines in every stage of manufacture, passing systematically from hand to hand until they reach the finisher, is both novel and interesting, though perhaps it is a matter of wonderment to the visitor how it is done. An idea as to the extent and variety of the manufactures produced may be gathered from the fact that the company turn out no less than 160 different kinds of lathes, besides all sorts of drillingmachines for engineers, and amateurs fratsaws and special appliances required in different trades.

The manufacture of mechanical appliances for amateurs is a branch to which the Brittannia Company de- vote special attention. It is a large and growing depart- ment, but a somewhat troublesome one, for ama- teurs often have little "fads " and fancies which are unknown to the practical mechanic. This de- partment, however, is under the charge of a man well ex- perienced in the wants and requirements of the amateur who will find all that he can possibly need. Special at- tention is also given to the manufacture of lathes and ap- pliances for technical schools and colleges. That these two last-named departments should be made specialities is another strong proof of the extent to which technical edu- cation is spreading, and of the increasing number of ama- teurs, who, in their leisure moments, find recreation and ex- ercise in m,mhanical employment. For these reasons, therefore, the City Guilds Institute Workshops, and the productions of the Brittania Company, on view there are well placed in " The Healtheries," and a visit to this par- ticular quarter will prove as deeply interesting, in every sense of the word, as it must be instructive, and to the masses who daily pass through the turnstiles of the Ken- sington grounds. In the same workshop may also be seen a splendid dis- play of lathes, and of specimens of turning Of the lathes the world cannot produce such an array as may be seen in the exhibits of Evans and Holtzaptfell. The lathes exhibi- ted by these firms are of the highest finish, they are, there- fore, too expensive for the technical school or the ordinary amateur. No visitor, interested in mechanics, should fail to visit this section, as such a collntion may never be seen again. •

div.head: SIIoCKING CANNIBALISM AT SEA.— CHARGE OF MURDEE, AGAINST THE
div.p: SIIoCKING CANNIBALISM AT SEA.— CHARGE OF MURDEE, AGAINST THE
SURVIVORS.

A Plymouth correspondent writes :—The brigantine Montezuma, of Hamburg, which arrived at Falmouth on Saturday, r(p)rted having on board three men named Thos. Dudley, of Colchester ' • Edwin Stephens, of Southampton ; and Edward Brooks, of Brightlingsea, who had been rescued after having experienced frightful sufferings at sea. These men, with a man named Richard Parker, of Southampton, were engaged to take out the yacht Mignonette to a gentle- man at Sydney, New South Wales. They left Southampton on 19th May, and had a fine voyage up to the time of their crossing the line on the 17th June. From this date their , troubles commenced. Dirty weather set in, and for several days a succession of heavy gales was experienced. On the 3rd of July a frightful storm was met with, and a huge- sea , swept over the yacht with such force as to lay her right open. The captain, seeing that the yacht was rapidly foundering, , ordered the boat to be got out. This was done, but with the exception of two small tins of preserved turnips they were without either food or water. The turnips lasted but four or five days, and their sufferings from thirst during that time were frightful. They killed a turtle and drank its blood, and then for more than a fortnight they were absolutely without food. So terrible did their position become that at the end of Abe eighteenth day they deliberated as to the advisability of casting lots as to who should be killed to supply food for the others. The plan was proposed by the captain, but one of the men objected, saying it was better they should all die together, and the proposal , was not pressed. But after two days more of horrible suffering both the captain and the mate suggested that Use boy Parker should be killed, especially as his suf- ferings were so intense that he had become delirious. They also reasoned that he was only a lad with no responsibilities, while they were married men witb wives and families depen- dent upon them. Brooks declined to be a party to this act, and at first none of the others would undertake it. Even- tually, however, Captain Dudley and Edwin Stephens decided to kill Parker, it being arranged that Dudley should 1 strike the blow while Stephens held the lad down. Dudley first offered up a prayer for forgiveness, and then telling Parker that his time had come, ran a penknife through his jugular vein, and the boy died almost immediately. The survivors caught the gushing blood in their tins and drank it between them, then stripped the body of its clothes, cut out the liver and heart while Tet hot from the body, and devoured them voraciously. For the next four days they continued to live on the flesh which they tore from Parker's ' dead body, and they were still eating their horrible food when, on the twenty-fourth day from the time they left their yacht, they were sighted and rescued by the German barque Montezaraa. They then presented the appearance of living skeletons, and were so weak and exhausted alto they had to be lifted out of the boat and carried on board. The mangled remains of Parker were at once cast into the sea, and the survivors receivid every kindness and attention on board the barque. On arriving at Falmouth, on Satur- day, they were taken to the Sailors' Home, and later in the day they were apprehended under a warrant charged with the murder of Parker on the high seas.

div.head: PR'SONERS BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES
div.p: PR'SONERS BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES

At the Falmouth P,lice Court, on Wednesday, Captain Thomas Dudley, Edward Brooks, the mate, and Edwin Stephens, able seaman, the survivors of the crew of the yacht Mignonette, were charged with having, On or about the 20th of July, that they did wilfully and with malice aforethought kill and murder Richard Parker, a boy of nineteen years, who had been one of the crew of the vessel, and who, according to their own reports, have been killed and eaten by them to prolong their own lives after being shipwrecked and having suff,red fearful privations in a small boat at sea for 24 days.—Mr Tilly appeared for the prisoners. The only witness called wee Polic3-constable Laverty, of the harbour police, wbo said : I apprehended the prisoners under a warrant on the G.h instant. I saw them previously from time to time during the morning. When they were at the Custom House I asked Brooks his name and those of the other prisoners, and he gave them. I heard Dudley tell the Collector of Customs in the long room at the Custom House that the boy Rachard Parker was lying at the bottom of, the boat with his arm over his face, and that he (Dudley) offered up a prayer and asked God to forgive him for what he was about to do, and he then said, " Richard, my boy, your time has come." He (Dudley) then took a small knife from his pocket, and putting his linger to a place on his own neck, said he put the knife into tie side of the boy's neck, and that the latter never moved. The mate stood behind him, but could not see what was done. Mr Tilly objected to anything bAng said about the mate, as the latter was not present at the Custom House during the conversation,

Mr Genn (the clerk) said what had been said about the mate was only in his favour. Mr. Tilley (to Laverty).—Did you hear the captain say how long he had been in the open beat without food? Laverty.—l heard they bad been in one about twenty days. Cross•examined.—A waterman brought them on shore on Saturday forenoon, and they were taken to the Custom House. They voluntarily went to the Custom House and made their depositions. I only heard a conversation in the forenoon, and did not hear the depositions taken. I think the statement was made in reply to a question of the collector.

The bench then remanded the case until Thursday so that the Treasury may be communicated with. Mr. Tilley applied that they might be admitted to bail on the ground that any evidence that had been adduced bad been only a statement volunteered by prisoners. There had been no attempt at concealment. They made their depositions without reserve to the Collector of Customs respecting what bad occurred during the twenty days they were without food in the boat. The poor fellows from their con- duct to the present time showed they had not the least wish to shirk the facts of this melancholy case. The Mayor asked if they were prepared with bail. Mr. Tilley said any amount of bail could be given. The Mayor, after consulting with the other magistrates, said they had given the matter their serious consideration, but the circumstances were of such a nature that they could not grant the application. The prisoners were then removed to the police station. A Southampton correspondent writes t "Parker, the mur- dered boy, was the orphan of an lichen Ferry yachtsman, near Southampton, and was adopted by another yachtsman there with whom be sailed last year, and was offered a place this season, but be wanted to go to Australia, and perhaps settle there. Stephens, the mate, was a Southampton man, his father was captain of one of the Isle of Wight passen- ger steamers, and he himself was in the same service as mate. He was first officer of Union Company's steamer, European, lost several years since. He has a wife and five children living at Southampton." Dudley, Stephens, and Brooks, the survivors of the yacht Mignonette, were again brought before the Falmouth borough magistrates on Thursday morning, charged with the mur- der of the lad Richard Parker on the high seas on the sth July. The court was crowded, great interest being mani- fested in the case. Mr H Tilley again represented the prisoners. The Treasury had written asking for a further remand. Mr Tilly again made application to the magis- trates to admit the men to. bail. The roam, he said, in which they were confined at the police station was ill adapted to their health, suffering as they were from tho privations they had undergone, and there were difficulties in the way of preparing their defence. He also hoped they would not fix an impossible bail, for the men were only technically charged with the off mace of murder, and, quoting, from Stephen's Commentaries on the Laws of England," urged in their favour the great universal principle, that where a man is prompted to save his own life preferably to that of another, when one of them must inevitably perish, it amounted to justifiable homicide. The magistrates retired for several minutes, when, on the application of the Treasury, the case was remanded for another week, and the Bench further decided to admit the prisoners to bail, Captain Dudley himself in £2OO, and to accept one surety from Mr Burton, of "the Old Curiosity Shop," Falmouth, for a similar amonnt, Hail was alto ac.

cepted in £lOO, and a surety received for a similar amount for Stephens and Brooks, Barton again becoming surety for each. The announcement of the magistrates' decision WM received with applause in court. A brother of the murdered lad Parker was in court, he being a seaman belonging to the yacht Margarette, at present in Torquay.

GOLBORNE. ANNIVERSARY SERMONS.—On Sunday the chapel anni- versary sermons were preached in the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Go!borne, by Mr John Drought, of St. Helens. The collections amounted to £8 us 4d. Both services were well attended.

EXTRAORDINARY SUCCESS.—At the Royal Manchester, Liverpool, and North Lancashire Agricultural Show, which terminated at Stockport on Saturday, Mr Thomas Wakefield, of Golborne, was awarded the first and third prizes for his Rouen ducklings. Out of eighteen entries, we believe Mr Wakefield has taken the prize fifteen times, this being the eighth year in succession. ANNIVERSARY OF ANCIENT SHEPHERDS.—The members of the Verbena of Golborne Lodge met at their club room on Saturday, at which place an excellent spread were awaiting them provided by the host and hostess of the Asssessors Arms. Ample justice having been done to the good thing!' provided, the cloths were removed and P.M. Wm. Moly- neux was called to the chair, supported by Brother Edward Andrews. The Chairman having given the loyal toasts dancing at once commenced to the harmony supplied by Mr. Jos. Pickup, of Wigan, who gave an excellent violin 8010 during the evening —The Chairman said he was proud to see the district secretary present, and also gratified to be able to inform their brothers that they had added ten young men to their lodge that day—The Secretary gave a satis- factory report of the lodge funds. l hey bad appointed trustees, and a portion of their funds were to be invested in the Warrington Savings' Bank.—The Chairman proposed a vote of thanks to the host and hostess, which was heartily responded to.—Brother Last proposed a vote of thaeks to the chairman and his supporter, which was given with musical honours.—After spending an enjoyable evening the party broke up by singing the National Anthem. PARocuter., COMMITTEE MEETING.—The monthly meet- ing was held in Mr Brewis's office on Wednesday ; present —Messrs William Mitchell (chairman), David Garton, Tay- lor, William Garton, Thomas Mitchell, and Bennie (sur- veyor).—The Surveyor reported that during the past month a short length of the brook on the north side of the railway had been cleared of stones and rubbish so as to allow the free passageeof water under Mill-lane bridge. He called at- tention to the fire hose which was in a very imperfect con- dition, and he believed that in the event of a fire they would probably be found wanting with their present„ extinguishing appliance3.—The road at Brick-bridge was in a bad condi- tion owing to the subsidence caused by the mining opera- tions of Messrs R Evans and Co, and it was necessary that something should be done to it before winter. the con- sumption of water for month ending Sept 5 WS 9W GOO gals. The committee sanctioned repairs suggested for Heath street and High-street, and instructed the surveyor to defer his contemplated alterations at Golborne Dale 'Brow for a month.—The Surveyor stated that out of IGO yards of hose pipes halt of it was utterly unfit for any thing.—MrThornas Mitchell: Suppose you get new pipes, have you anywhere to keep them P—The Surveyor: No ; the present ones are kept in my office.—Mr William Mitchell: Have you a cart to take them out in ?—The Surveyor: No. Enquiries respecting a reel cart were made about four years ago, but nothing came of it.—Mr William Garton : I have often thought we should be awkwardly fixed if a fire occurred. move that the Surveyor get an estimate for a reel cart and pipes,—Mr Thomas Mitehell eecended the proposal, which was Carried.—After discussion of the subsidence at Brick Bridge, the Surveyor was ordered to make a claim for dam- ages on Messrs Evans and Co.—The question of a separate committee room apart from Mr Brewis's office was discussed, and the Surveyor was ultimately instructed to have an inter- view with Mr Bretvis, and report to the next meeting. -- Accounts amounting to £94 was passed for payment, and the meeting concluded.

ITAYDOCK. ACCIDENT.—WiIIiam Swift, a collier, employed in the Havannah Colliery, belonging to Mess-s Richard Evans and Company, received severe injuries in the pit on Wednesday evening. Swift was assisting in the laying of a new road, when a dirt-cart running along the line came in contact with his legs, and precipitated him to the bottom of a dry' well, 20 feet deep. The cat followed him, but fortunately for Swift's life, it got stuck in the middle of the well, which tapers towards the bottom. As it was, Swift escaped with a few bruises and a severe shaking. Under the care of Dr Hayward he is now progressing favourably at the Haydock Cottage Hospital. - - .

INSTALLATION OF THE VICAR OF HAYDOCK.-St. James's Church, Havdock, was filled with an attentive congregation on Wednesdiy evening, when a special service to cornmemorate the inatallation of the Rev A H Kearney as vicar of the parish, in place of the Rev H H Sherlock, was held. The Rev H Mason, curate of the parish, read the prayers, and the lessons were given by the Rev W J Melville, rector of DownallGreen. The installation service was then read by the Ven..Archdeican Bardsley, of Liverpool, who in a few substquent remarks expressed the hope that the affairs of the parish would continue peaceful, and that everything would be done in a harmonious and straightforward manner. The hymns and psalms were selected appropriate to the • occasion.

FATAL COLLIERY ACCIDENT —On Wednesday afternoon Benjamin Lowe, a sinker in the employ of Messrs Richard Evans and Co., at the No. 2 New Boston Pit, Haydock, met with an almost instantaneous death while fallowing his em- ployment. About half-past one the deceased was engaged in 'tunnelling," and had tunnelled about three yards when just as be was beginning to brick up the tunnel a large stone weighing about 2cwt. fell from the roof. The stone alighted on his back and neck, and pressed his chest against a waggon. He was removrd as soon as possible, but it was evident the poor fellow was mortally wounded, and he expired shortly afterwards. He was unmarried. His body was removed to his house at a place called Butter houses, Downall Green, Ashton, where it awaits the coroner's inquest._

POACRING AT BILLINGE —At the Wigan County Police Court on Friday, Timothy Shaw, John Foster, Richard Litt- ler and Henry Boardman were charged with poaching at Bininge-Higher-End on the 29th ult, and there was a charge against the first-named (Shaw) of assaulting Police-con- stable Hodgson whilst in the execution of his duty.—Mr Clavdon (Peace and Ellis) prosecuted, and Mr Kenney de- fended.—Thomas Gee, gamekeeper to Mr Thomas Crippin, of Billings-Chapel-End, said that on the morning of the 30th ult be was in a field occupied by Aun Wilcock about half past three o'clock and RIR, Timothy Shaw there. Mr Crippin had the right of shooting over the field in which were hares and rabbits. He ran across the field and found the other three defendants, Littler, Foster, and Boardman taking up a long net.—Each of the defendants was fined 20s and costs, and Shaw was fined 103 and costs for the as- salt on the police. PROPOSED READING Room AT HAYDOCK.—Mr Arthur L Evans has previously manifested a sincere desire for the improvement and increased comfort of the workmen and their families, resident in Haydock, as is evidenced by the many movements for their benefit he has originated and taken part in. He has latterly been completing arrange- ments for opening a public reading room—a greatly felt want by the working-men of Haydock. A shop near to the post office has been secured, and in the hands af the pain- ters, decorators, 61c, it is being transformed into a sort of club premises. Up to the present 14 newspapers and 35 magazines and other journals have been promised for the use of the room, which will be open from eight in the morn- ing until 11 at night. From two to five in the afternoon it will be reserved for the use of lady members. In order to defray the necessary expenses, a charge of 2d per week will be made upon the members. It is expected that the reading room will be opened on October Ist.

GREAT COAL FIRE AT HA.YDOCK.—SERIOUS DAMAGE. Since Tuesday last an extensive fire has been raging in a stack of coal near the Queen Pit, Haydock, owned by the firm of Messrs Richard Evans and Company. The stack in question is of some years' growth, and when smoke was il first observed issuing from it it was estimated that about 5,000 tons of coal had beefs accumulated. The smoke gradually increased in volume until it was evident that something was seriously amiss, the only conjecture being that by same means tbe centre of the stack had " struck fire. Since then efforts have been put forth to extinguish the "internal enemy," but up to yesterday they were un- availing. By means of hose pipes, wooden troughs, dic., a continuous flow of water has been falling upon the burning stack, and a gang of men have been employed cutting a way' into the centre of the immense pile. Owing to the dense volumes of smoke which issue forth, and the heat arising from the hot coals, however, the work is one of great dia" culty and inconvenience. On Thursday a vast quantity of coal had been destroyed, and undoubtedly the firm will have suffered a great loss when the fire is extinguished. A large number of persons have been attracted to the spot by the singular outbreak.
Lieut. F. A. Grogan, RE., has been suddenly ordered to the Cape on special service.

A company is in process of formation for running cattle ships from Canada direct to Holyhead ;, but the more important venture is the establish- ment of a line of cotton Ships between America and lioir head.
