EVPT AND THE SOUDAN. THE NILE EXPEDITION. . The Government have taken up another email transport. Her name is the Neptune, and ebe belongs to Tatham and Co., Liverpool. She is of about five hundred tons register. She will be ready to load with stores and provisiens for Egypt on Monday. WADE HALFA, Severunas.—The fall of the Nile has put a stop for the present to the operations for taking the steamer 't Nassifhera over the 'cataract. CAIRO, Streneet.—The transport Goorkha, with 200 Mounted Infantry on board, arrived at Alexandria last night. Four naval steer' pinnaces have passed the First Cataract. Nubar Pasha has been sent by the Khedive to inset Lord Northbrook, CAIRO, Meeroay.—The mounted infantry left thismorn- ing for Wady Haifa. News has reached here from Dongola , that the Sheikh Harowi, a chief of great influence and authority, has tendered his submission. The adhesion of this Sheikh is looked upon as of much impartance.—DaiiN IVetes. NEW YORE, MONDAY—The Canadian Voyageurs who have been engaged for service on the Nile will embark on Saturday. They will number about 500 strong. Father Breechand, who has been for two years in Egypt as a mis- sionary, will accompany the expedition. The hired transport Frutera left Liverpool on Saturday for the Clyde, where she will embark 93 of the Nile boats for conveyance to Egypt. The military authorities have fixed Saras, a little above the Great Cataract, as the fiaal base in the Nile expedition. instead of Wady Haifa. The transport from Wady Haifa to Saras will be made by rail, by Which the Second Cataract and six miles of rough broken water will be avoided. The telegraphic communication will be extended from Cairo to Saras by the time the expedition leaves there on November Ist, and will be continued by the telegraph section as fast as the expedition progresses. Major Martin, ILA., has left with the first part of the boat flotilla for the expedition up the Nile, in the steamship Pelican, which sailed on Monday afternoon from Woolwich. He is accompanied by a naval engineer and three aesistants, who are to re-build to stern paddle steamer and take charge of her up the Nile. The Pelican is expected to reach Alexan- stria about the 28th inst. The officials at Woolwich having despatched the first half of the stores and equipments for the Nile Expedition, are preparing the seemed half for transit. Fourteen hundred tons of commissariat stores have been already despatched. The transport President Garfield was engaged during the whole of Tuesday in the steam basin at Portsmouth, in get- ting on board stores, &o, and seine of the boats to be used in the e epedition. A number of boats arrived at Portsmouth by train during the afternoon, and zeveral were towed over from Cowes. The steamer Bulimba, Captain J Darcy Clarke, belonging to the British India Company, has been taken up by the Government for four months, and will leave the Royal Al- bert Docks, Woolwich, OR Saturday, for Portsmouth, where she will embark 700 troops for Egypt. The Post Office Volunteers who, after the Egyptian cam- paign of 1882, were attached to the First-class Artillery K, Reserves, have received notice that they will be medi- cally examined this week as to their fitness for service. It is understood, however, that only twelve men will be re- quired. Baker Pasha has left England for Egypt, and is proceed- ing by easy stages to Alexandria. via Trieste. Col. Hender- son, King's Royal H flee, left London last night for special service in Egypt. He, too, travels 'via Trieste. ALExANDRIA, TUESDAY.—Her Mii!Sly'S despatch vessel Iris arrived here at noon to-day, with Lords Wolseley and Northbrook on beard, who were received by Natoli. Pasha on behalf of the Khedive. Their lordships started for Cairo at 3-50 p.m. Her Majesty's transport Poonah has arrived at Malta 'from Queenstown, and will sail for Alexandria, conveying drafts for various reaiments. The transport President Garfield, having completed the shipping of her stores, left Portsmouth yesterday afternoon for Egypt. Shortly before her departure, a number of boats intended for use on the Nile were towed into the harbour and placed on board. The hired transport Ravenna loft the Royal Albert Docks early on Wednesday morning, and em- barked at Tillbury several officers for service in Eaypt. CAIRO, THURSDAY, 5 20 r pursuance of general orders Major General Earl, who proceeds up the Nile to- morrow, will take commaud of all troops at Wady Haifa and south of that place. Colonel Stewart will go up the Nile to Dongola and assume the command there, while Col. Maurice, of the Artillery, will be in command at Assiout. LORD NORTHBR )01i. AND THE KHEDIVE. CAIRO, WEDNESDAY.—LOrd Northbrook had an audience of the Khedive this morning in which he presented to His Highness a letter from Earl Grenville containing Lord Northbrook's credentials as High Commissioner, and reques- ting the assistance pf the Egyptian Government in the so- lotion of the important questions pendin r, and principally with regard to the fiaancial difficulties of the country. Dur- ing the audience the Khedive displayed great cordiality to- wards Lord Northbrook. His Highness Ids expressed him- self highly satisfied with Lord Northbrook's declarations. The Khedive returned Lord Northbrook's visit shortly afterwards. DEFEAT OF THE REBELS BY THE MUDIR OF DONGOLA. WADY lietva, Mudir of Dongola tele- graphs from Drebeh that a large force of rebels, consisting of the force from Kordofan, and another from Meravi, under Ameer Ahmed Liedin, has been totally defeatedoaear Ambi- kol, with great slauzlater. The Mudir says Ahmed Iledin was killed, but Major Kitchener says he is reported to have escaped. The Mudir hopes to return to Dongola within the next few days. THE FRANCO-CHINESE WAR.—BRITISH GUNBOAT FILED ON. Panes, SUNDAY.—Xdrniril Combat. after leaving the mouth of the river Min, went on Board the B ward, and proceeded to Kelung to inspect the Chinese defences. The French man of-war had approached within a short distance of the shore when the Chinese, unmasking a mounted gun, fired on the Bayard. The Ere told, and four sailors were wounded. The Bayard then replied, and with three shots demolished the Chinese battery. Having completed his in- spection, Admiral Courbet returned to the Min whence he communicated with the Admiralty in Paris and with M. Patenotre at Shanghai. The Admiral appears to be wateh- hag the movements of the Chinese fleet in the Gulf of Petcheli. HANOI, MONDAY—General Millot, accompanied by Col. Guerrier and his oelerly officers, left hers this morning. General Briere de Lisle arrived yesterday to take over the command. A telegram has been received from Vice-Admiral Dowell at Foochow, reporting that two shells were fired at her Majesty's gunboat Zephyr on the 6:11 lost, when coming up the Min river from the Chinese forts, under a misapprehen- sion. A further telegram, dated Monday, reports that the Chinese authorities have offered an apology and reparation. An officer and a men were wounded. Beth are doing well. The Zephyr is a composite screw gunboat, carrying four glans and about eighty men. Her commander is Lieutenant George Pollard. The Pall Mall Gazette learns that the declaration re- .-apecting hostilities between France and China issued by the latter has taken the form of a manifesto by the Emperor of the Chinese people, setting out the acts of tha French in the past, declaring that he regards these constituting a state of war, and calling upon his subjeats to aid him in repelling the French attacks. Saationer, WEDNEWAY.—The Chinese authorities have commenced operations for blocking Woosuag Bar with junks filled with stems. Pants, WEDNESDAY —M. Jules Ferry has written to all the Ministers now absent from Paris requesting them to re- turn to the capital by Saturday next in order to attend the Cabinet Council. All this evening's journals agree as to the importance of the forthcoming meeting of Ministers, at which the date for the convocation of the Chamber is ex- pected to be fixed. The Temps, indeed, thinks it possible that Si. Gr6vy may return to Paris in order to preside at the Council. Contradiction is given to the report that the French Go- vernment intend to recall M. de Brazz a from the West Coast of Africa. THE CHOLERA—DREADFUL STATE OF NAPLES. —VISIT OF THE KING. ROME, MONDAY—The official bulletins show a great Increase at Naples. There were reported on Saturday in the province 175 cases and 74 deaths, in the city 168 cases and 69 deaths; on Sunday in the province, 235 Cases and 67 deaths; and on Monday, 353 Cases and 11.6 deaths. Signor Grimaldi, Minister of Agriculture, hag requested the bank of Naples to advance to the municipality £50,003 lire for the relief of the poor. NAPLES, MONailt —lt is under consideration to form encampments outside Naples for the people inhabiting the poorer quarters of the city. The relief service organised by the principal iohabitants, without distinction of party, is being well carried out. —715 p.m. During the last 24 hours there have been-451 cases of cholera here and 154 deaths. King Humbert arrived here at 4-5 this afternoon. His Majesty was received by Signor Mansini, Minister for Foreiga Affairs, and Ike local authorities. An immense crowd had assembled outeida the railway station, and wel- comed the King as "The second father of his country." Previous to his departure from Venice, his Majesty received a request to attend the racee at Pordenone ; but he replied, "At Pordenone one amuses one's self; at Naples the people are dying. I shall go to Naples." MADRID, MONDAY.—The official bulletin issued to-day reports that during the last 21 hours six fresh cases of cholera and four deaths have occurred at Novelda, and three cases and five deaths at Monforte. MONDIS.—Sis deaths from cholera occurred yesterday in the department of Pyrai-335 Orientxles. There seers also 14 instantaneous deaths at St. Remeze, in .Ardeche. MinsEILLEs, Moni.lay.—The deaths from cholera have numbered 4,5, and 2 for the last three slays. Ne.p.t.cs, Tocenmr.—Ta-day's official bulletin reports 633 cholera cases and 211 deaths in the city of Naples. In ad- dition 1.4 of the cases already under treltnaent have termi- nated fatally. Toe King will commence visiting the hospi- tal in the poorer quarters. Evening: Daring the last 21 hours, 300 deaths from cholera have occurred. MADRID, TUESDAY —The oftcial bulletin to-day reports that during the last 24 hours four deaths from cholera have occurred at Novels and tan at IVlontforte. Hong, WEDNESDAY.—The official bulletin issued to-day reports the undermentioned cases in the following provinces: Aquila, one case; Bergam a, five cases, four deaths; Campo- basso, three cases; Caserto, six cases, four deaths ; Canso, 16 eases, 25 deaths ; Mies Carrara, six gases, eight deaths.

MADRID, WEDNESDAY.—ThO official bulletin repents the death of one of the five Children from Alicante, who fell ill after arriving here and were received in the le4 vette a short distance from this city. At Mahe, yesterday there were 18 cases of cholera, and four deaths ; 'Novelda, eight cases, and three deaths; and at Monforte one death. At Torres de Segre, in the province of Lerida, a person has died from what the bulletin describes as suspicions illness. Two fresh tans of cholera have occurred at Balaquer. The King leaves to-day for La Granja. NAPLES, WEDNEsnay.—During the twenty-four hours ending yesterdag evening there were 721 cases of cholera and 210 deaths in this city. Eleven hundred bodies have been interred up to the present in the portion of the cemetay in which persons who have died from cholera are buried. The King will visit the poorer quarters of the city to-day. MALTA, WEDNESDAY.—VesseIb arriving from Italian, trench, and Spanish Mediterranean ports are not prohibited ' from entering any of the harbours in the island of Malta. FRANCE AND MADAGASCAR. rents' SATURDAY.—A telegram of yesterday's date re- ceived from Z anzibar states that Admiral Miot has taken possession of Passandava Bay, in the Sakalava territory, Madagascar, without encountering any resistance. The oc- cupation of Tainatave by the French forces continues. BOMBARDMENT OF ANOTHER MADAGASCAR PORT. TAMATAVE, AUG UST 30.—The port of Mahanors, on the east coast, was bombarded by the French fleet on the 22nd mat, and it is rumoured that the French have temporarily occupied the place. Admiral Mist, the French commander, continues to reconnoitre the position of the Malagasy forces. FRANCE.—DESTRUCTIVE FIRE AT ST. PIERRE LES CALAIS. . LILLE, WEDNESDAY —A large fire occurred at eight o'clock yesterday evening at St. Pierre lee Calais, in the factory of Messrs. Dubrencq, situated in the Rue des Quatro Coins. The conflagration raged with great fury, and was not under control until two hours later, by which time the building was destroyed. Three firemen were injured, one of them seriously. THE BELGIAN EDUCATION BILL —RIOTOUS DEMONS [RATION. 13nussEr,s, SUNDAY.—The long-proposed Clerical demon- stration took place to-day, and led to a succession of scenes of turbulence and riotous disorder. The Clerical manifest- ants, of whom a lame number were brought in special trains from the provinces, assembled at half-past one. The pro- cessionists, who numbered many thousands, began their march ainid indescribable confusion, heightened by the con- duct of the onlookers, who hiss* hooted, and howled with the utmost vehemence. The passage of the procession was blocked in all directions, and a series of fierce struggles be- tween the demonstrationists and their opponents was the result. Banners and mottoes were wrested from the men who carried them and torn to pieces. A body of gendarmes then took the lead of one section and, meunting civil guard, exerted themselves to re-establish order in the procession. , Their efforts, however, proved futile. By three o'clock the confusion of the cortige became general, its advance was completely stopped, and the demonstrationists began to die- perse.-11 p m. The city has been in the most excited state the whole of the evening. The number of persons injured in the fighting is very large. In all 175 arrests were made. BRUSSELS, MOND AY.—About one hundred trrsons were wounded, several of them seriously, during yesterday's riot- ing. Disturbances occurred yesterday evening at the rail- way stations in several provincial towns on the return of the Clerical partisans from taking part in the Brussels demon- stration. At Antwerp the gendarmes were obliged to charge the crowd several times, and several people were wounded. Several journals demand the dismissal of the Burgomaster. BRUSSELS, TUESDAY.—The Senate to-day passed a resolu- tion strongly condemning the excesses of which Brussels was the scene last Sunday. VIE CZ R'S VISIT TO WARSAW.

BERLIN: .EITND—A7SC —Warsaw is rapidly filling in anticipa- tion of the visit of the Czar. All the streets are being pat- rolled by members of the St. Petershurgh police force, who number more than 1030, exclusive of 5,000 secret police. The pickets to be posted along the line by which the Em- peror of Austria will travel to Warsaw will muster 13,000 men. Wansew, MOIRDA.Y.—The Emperor and Empress of Rus- sia arrived at ten o'clock this morning. One of the saloon carriages of the Imperial train was filled with thwers pre. sentecl to their Mijesties during the journey. At the station bread and salt were presented by a deputation from the town. At half .past eleven the Empress drove to the Kulokoff Plain, the Cz tr riding. Here over 50,000 troops had assembled, and the whole force was inspected. The town is brilliantly illuminated,

PARIS, MONDAY.—The Temps publishes a telegram stat- ing that the Czar intends to be crowned King of Poland. BERLIN, MESDAY.—Advicas from Warsaw to to-lay an- nounce that the precautions taken for the Czar's safety have been much relaxed. There were two accidents during the review on the Mokotoff Plain, one dragoon being killed and another fatally injured. WARSAW, TrEsnias.—The visit of the Czar and Czarina to the theatre yesterday evening was quite unexpected, even by the police. Their Majesties occupied General Gourko's box, and were accompanied by Baron Fredericks, Chief of the Gendarmerie. On leaving the theatre at eleven o'clock their Majesties returned to the Lszienki Palace in an open carriage, driving 'through the side streets quite unkn )wn to the crowd or police, and took such a devious course that Baron Fredericks could scarcely keep them in sight. Na arrests of importance were made yesterday. WARSAW, WEDNESDAY.—The effect of the illumination of Warsaw, viewed from the Palace yesterday evening, was strikingly magnificent. The iron bridge over the Vistula facing the Palace was festooned with small lamps. The river was crowded with illuminated boats, and the Palace seemed one blaze of light. Seven hundred invitations were issued to the ball, at which th Czar and Czarina arrived at eleven o'clock, accompanied by the Grand Dukes present here. Their arrival was announced by a display of fire- works. Their Majesties walked through the long suite of apartments into the ballroom, bowing right and left to the assembled guests. The Emperor did not dance, and held long conversations with members of the Polish nobility and gentry. The Empress opened the ball with General Gourko, the Czarewitch dancing with Madame Gourko. The Czarina afterwards held a reception of Polish and Russian ladies present, addressing them individually ira the most gracious terrne. The reception lasted more than an hour. Her Majesty subsequently danced with Prince Dolgorouki. The Imperial supper was served, on a table decorated with 8,000 roses brought specially for the occasion from Eisen- bac!). After supper their Majesties retired to Lazienki Palace. _

Novo GEORGIETSIC, THURSDAY.—The Emperor and Em- press of Russia arrived here at eleven o'clock last night. The Wilna manceuvres will commence to-morrow morning, and will last until the 14th inst. THE MEETING OF THE EMPERORS.

BERLIN, TRIIRSDIY.—I6 is stated on good authority that houses have been taken for Prince Bismarck and Count Kal- noky at Skierniyiee. The Emperor and Empress of Russia will leave Warsaw to-day for Vilna, in order to attend the manceuyres.

CAIRO, SATURDAY.—The annual caravan conveying the Holy Carpet to Mecc I left Cairo today, with the usual ceremonial, in the presence of the Khedive. Lieut.-General Stevenson also attended at the head of the British troops, who were paraded for the occasion.

div.p: GERMAN ANNEX ATION IN AFRICA.

Capn-rowx. SATuttnas.—Tne commander of the Gatman gunboat Wolf has annexed the South-Western Coast of Africa between the Ifith and 2611 degrees of south latitude, with the exception of Walfisch Bay. RANK FAILURE AT NEW _JERSEIL—SUICIDES.

NEW YORK. MONDIY.—P Mahlon Ruiyon, President of the National Bank of New Jersey, at New Brunswick, which has suspended payment in consequence of the defalcations of the cashier, committed suicide to-day. It has been dis- covered that the total defalcations amount to 51,000,000. A depositer of the bank, on learning the facts of thecase, also committed suicide, thus making the third victim. The affair has caused groat excitement. INDIA—LORD DUFFERIN APPOINTED VICEROY.

CONSTANTINOPLE, ToEso-av-.--Ll:ord Dufferin has been appointed Viceroy of India. His Excellency will leave here on the 16th inst. on board ILM. yacht Imogene for Varna, on his Way to London, and is expected to arrive ha Calcutta in December next.

CAPETOWS, VIA PLYMOUTH, AUGUST 20rn.—Umquikela has issued a proclamation announcing that customs duties will be levied on all goods passing through Fondaland as a measure of opposition to the occupation of St John's by the Cape Colony. Ho announces that he is determined to pre- vent the passage of troops through Pondoland. It is reported that Bechuanaland is in a most disturbed state, and that Montsioa is now in great extremities, most of his fighting inn having been slain, including M. Bethel, late lieutenant in the Imperial Intelli,ent Department. TELE CIVIL WAR IN PERU: SEVERE

"A MISERABLE SQUABBLE."—The Rev J W Meyrick, rector of Beinmaris, on Wednesday sued the Bishop of Ban- gor in the Menai Bridge County Court to recover 14s. Some time ago the plaintiff's living was sequeatrated for noncom- pliance with an order to repair his church. The Bishop received the tithes, and on the groan: that the writ of sequestration was invalid the present " test " action was brought to recover the sum named.—The Judge after hear- Mr Meyrick's evidence adjourned the matter, remarkiag that it seemed to be " a miserable squabble." THE,. STonat Ow TILE SCOTCH COAST.—The gale which broke over the Shetland coast on Friday was attended with much more serious consequences than was at first reported. The fishermen have sustained heavy losses in nets, some boats having lost as many as thirty. Some buts rode out the gale, lying at their nets, and much apprehension was felt for their sarety, but all have returned with the ' exception of four—namely, Bonny Lass, Hive, and Sun- beam. of Port St. Mary, Isle of Man, and the Guiding Star, of Leavenwick. The crews of the missing boats number 23 men. DromEsTrorr.—The main cause of nervousness is indigestion, nd that is caused by weakness of the stomach. div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 13, 1884.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 13, 1884.
GENERAL NEWS.

- - During a gale off the Tyne on Sunday two South Shields pilots were drowned. , Electric lamps are being used to light a baker's oven in the Health Exhibition. Mr. Parnell, M.P., returned to Avondale, Co. Wicklow, on Tuesday, to resume grouse shooting. An epidemic of smallpox is raging at Crewe. Seven fresh cases have been reported during the week, and one death has already occurred. At Stonehaven, on Tuesday, Charles Newton Biggs, late captain in the 69th Foot, was committed for trial on a charge of placing an obetruction on the railway, near Drurnlithie, on Friday. Sir John Duntze died on Monday at Exeleigh, near Exeter, from inflammation, resulting from a cold caught whilst shooting. He was 75 years of age, and well known as a sportsman. THE MURDER O' A FAMILY.—A labourer named Duane has been arrested, charged with complicity in the murder of the Sheehan family, at Castletown Roche, seven years ago. The bodies of the victims were recently discovered in a well. Charles Darnell, aged 42, one of the eleven men injured in the explosion at Hall End Colliery, West Broinveich, on Saturday, died in the hospital on Tuesday evening. The recovery of two or three others is considered very doubtful. Lieutenant Wyatt, of the &rap's, was tried by court- martial at Portsmouth on Sunday, for leaving his ship without leave while temporarily placed in command. He was sentenced to lose a year's seniority and be dismissed from his ship. Nzw RISFIOP OF RIPON —Dr. William Boyd Carpenter was on Tuesday enthroned, inducted, and installed as third bishop of the diocese of Ripon, at the Cathedral, Ripon. The nave of the Cathedral was crowded, and the choir was occupied by about 400 clergy from all parts of the diocese. SERIOUS COLLIERY EXPLOSION—At Hall-end Colliery, West Bromwich, on Saturday, a serious explosion of gas I occurred, owing, it is believed, to a sudden depression in the atmosphere. Eleven men were seriously hurt, and were re- moved to the hospital, some being in a very precarious con- dition. DUBLIN CASTLE is now almost bereft of its chief officials. The Lord-Lieutenant is in Kerry, the Attorney-General is on a month's holiday, Mr. Jenkinson is looking after the dynamitards in London, Dr. Kaye and Mr. Samuel Lee Anderson are on their holiday, and all business de- volves on the Solicitor-General and Sir Robert Hamilton, Under-Secretary. THE DEBTORS ACT.—At Bolton Police Court, on Monday, Mr James Frederick Taylor and Mr James Wilson, house furnishers, trading as J F Taylor and Co., were committed for trial, under the Debtors Act, charged with falsely repre- senting the financial condition of the firm. They stated that their stock was worth £5,000, whereas the prosecution allege that it is not worth half that amount. The Treasury directed the prosecution. INDUSTRIAL REMUNERATION CONFERENCE. Arrange- ments are being made for holding a conference of artisans, capitalists and persons interested in the study of social problems, in London, next January, when the questions con- nected with the distribution of wealth between the labouring and capitalist classes may be discussed from all points of view. The plan originated with an Edinburgh gentleman, who hes generously given £l,OO towards carrying it out. This sum has been vested in the hands of Mr Thomas Burt, M.P, Mr J Burnett, Professor Fox veil, Lord Dalhousie, Sir Thomas Brassey, Mr F Harrison, and Mr R Giffen as trustees. CANON W J KNOX LITTLE ow Music —The Triennial Worcester Musical Festival cammenced on Sunday with a special morning service in the Cathedral. The Canon in office, the Rev. W J Knox Little, in his discourse was re- peatedly emphatic in exhorting his hearers not to forget during the week that the cathedral is the house of God, and that the festival, in the abstract, is an act of worship. Preaching from Zechariah ix, 17, "For how great is His goodness, and how great is His beauty !" the rev, gentleman said he could perceive how many composers, even those en- dowed with the highest capacity, might, lacking the dis- cernment of right or wanting susceptibility of grace, turn this heavenly endowment into the medium of sensation and sensualism. Could the choir or orchestra believe there was no danger in music? While the delight of sensation pre- dominated there would exist a materialism which stole God's robe to enwrap it. Beauty and goodness shonld ever go hand in hand. THE CORPORATION FRAVES AT WIOAN.—At Wigan Police Court, on Monday, William Holt, late borough trea- surer, John Caldwell, late professional auditor, and John Reynolds, formerly managing clerk for Caldwell, were charged with conspiring to defraud the Corporation of Wigan. Mr Brown, cashier, Wigan branch of Parr's Bank, produced books to show that in 1871, when Caldwell was treasurer pro. tent., an account was opened for private im- provement expenses, and cheques showing that in 1876 the amount of over £1,700 was transferred by cheques to other accounts of the Corporation. Mr Byrom, one of the elective auditors, produced the Corporation cashbaoke, containing lentry of payments to the bank, but no debit against Holt as having received such cheques from this account The yearly abstracts also contained no entry referring to this. Several letters were read, from which it appeared that Holt had fur- nished from the borough moneys several sums to Calde ell and Reynolds. All the prisoners were committed for trial, the magistrate remarking that it had been apparent to his mind throughout the whole of the inquiry that negligence and carelessness had marked the proceedings in connection with the Wigan Corporation accounts. How THE AMERICAN PRESIDENT IS ELECTED.—SOrtIe Of , our English readers who have perused the telegrams from I the United States respecting the Presidential campaign, I have been puzzled to comprehend the system by which a president is elected; and strange as it may appear, many Americans have but vague and often erroneous ideas as to the manner in which the highest office id the gift of the , nation is filled. Under the p-ovisions of the Federal Constitution, Americans do not vote directly for a President and Vice-President, but for an intermediate body of electors, , each State is entitled to as many as it has members in both houses of Congress. There being at present:32s representa- tives in Congress, and 76 Senators, the Electoral College , consists of 401 members, of whom 291 constitute a majority. I The Electoral nominees having the highest number of votes in any State, even though that number is not a majsrity lof all the votes cast, are legally elected. It may thus hap' I pen that the electoral votes of a State may be divided be- tween two or more nominees. This, la lwever. is of very rare occurrence. The electors meet in their respective States, and their vote, duly certified, is forwarded to Wash- ,lington, where the formal count takes place in the presence of both branches of Congress. Should any Presidential , nominee obtain a majority of the electoral votes he is de- clared duly elected. Otherwise it devolves upon the House of Representatives to choose a President from among the , three candidates having the largest number of electoral votes. When an alternative of this sort arises, each State must vote as a unit, the majority of the delegation deter- mining the vote. Should the election of 1834 be thrown into the House, the votes of twenty States will be re- {paired to name Mr. Arthur's successor. The American Traveller. THE MAAMTRASNA MURDERS: ASTOUNDING " REVELA. PIONS " BY INFORMERS.—AII extraordirary story, contain- ing some astounding "revelations," is published in the Dub- lin Freeman's Journal of Saturday regarding the massacre ,of a family at alaamtrasna. Casey is alleged to have given a correspondent an account of the massacrealtating that there I were seven murderers, and not ten as stated at the trial. These were himself and Michael Casey, now undergoing penal servitude, Patrick Casey and Patrick Joyce, who were hanged, and three others whose names the correspondent de- clines to publish. Two of these—father and son—are still living in the district of the murders, and the other has gone to England. The father was the author of the massacre. He held the lamp while the family were murdered, and, the murderers having left without killing the old grandmother, be compelled them to slay her also. The two meetings at which the murder was planned were held at the house of this man, and Casey was present. He gave the names of the others present, and alleged that Myles Joyce, the man who was hanged, Philbin, the second informer, Tom Joyce, Martin Joyce, Pat Joyce, and John Casey, all undergoing penal servitude, were not at the scene of the murder at all. Asked who were Kelly and the persons supposed to have escaped, Casey said there were no such persons, and that these were false names for the father and son already mentioned. The author of the mas- sscre mentioned is a wealthy farmer in the neighbourhood, Joyce, the murdered man, was alleged by this man to have attempted his life three times, and that he was determined to kill him, and leave no one behind him to tell the tale. He explains that the people selected were all relations by blood or connection by merriage, and this was for the she of safety. The son of this man, six weeks before any of the meetings were held, gave Casey £3. "I suspected," Cesey added, "that there was bad work to be done, but I wanted the money, and I took it, hoping to avoid the bad work afterwards." At a recent fair this son handed Casey £4, "because of all the trouble and sorrow that had been occa- sioned him." All this, he alleged, is we'l knowri in the district. At the murder the author of it had a revolver, and the man who is free in England had a dagger. It was, however, a hammer found in the honse by Pat Joyce that did most of the job. It was impossible for the Joyces, who brought. the murder home to the men hanged, to have tracked the assassins as they described at the trials, for the night was bright, and there was little covert for them. Philbin was allowed to mix with the witnegi Joyce at Kilmainham gaol, and they had time to make their tales coincide, although Philbin was not at the rgurder. Casey further asserted that Mr Bolton, the Crown Solicitor, said he would give £3OO for his information, and even up to £5OO and per- mission to leave the country. "I did intend," added Casey, "to leave the country last spring, but I would not have gone without giving to my priest a full statement of the truth." He said he did riot care what became of him if he obtained forgiveness from God and snarls all the atonement in his power. Be alleged that on their way to the murder Ina party called on a man named John Joyce, of Cruig, and I that he was called out to join them. He came out in his trousers and shirt, and pleaded that he had pains and could not go. Pat Joyce then covered him with his revolver and said" he would soon give him pains." "I then," says Casey," took hold of Pat Joyce and dragged him away. I told John Joyce to go in and go to bed and not mind. He did so." The correspondent says he left Casey with a vivid impression that he was telling the truth. Casey declared that he would tell everything above related on oath at a public investigation. Philbin, while in Casey's house, does not hesitate to confirm what he says. The _Freeman's Journal again presses for a public investigation.

THE POLITICAL VIEWS OF THE PRINCE OF WALES.— The Prince of Wales having been recently represented in a leading journal to hold somewhat advanced political views, and the favouring on economical and other grounds Repub- lican prineiples of -Government, the attention of his R iyal Highness was called by a correspondent to the matter. In reply, Mr Francis Knollys, secretary to the Prince, writes : —"I am desired by the Prince of Wales to acknowledge the receipt of your letter, and to inform you in reply that as his Royal Highness is not holding any office, any opinions to which he may give utterance must necessarily be unofficial." OUTRAGE BY A MADMAN:A shocking affair is reported from Homerton, a suburb of London. A man named Stock- ham, who is said to have been suffering from melancholia, stabbed his wife in the breast, caused serious injury to their infant (two days old), threw on the fire another of their children (a girl under two years of age), and finally nearly accomplished his own death by hanging. Toe little girl lies in the Hackney Infirmary in a serious condition, and the wretched father is under treatmmt in the same institu- tion. Stockharn, who was described as 29 years of age and a boot and shoe finisher by trade, was taken before the Wor- ship-street Police Magistrate on Wednesday and remanded. It was stated that the elder child was likely to die. THE LORD LIEUTENANT'S VISIT TO KERRY: SAD ACCI- DENT—When Earl Spencer, now at Killarney, was visiting Tralee this week, the contractors. of the extensive pier works, and the loyal portion of the inhabitants, decided to give his Excellency a royalealute in contrast to the black and insulting flags hung out of the windows of the N Alen- alists. In the absence of artillery a royal salute was impro- vised in the shape of 13 blasts, which were fired on the ap- proach of the Viceregal party, but with a lamentable result. All the blasts exploded but one in charge of a young man named Corkerry. The latter went to set it right, when it suddenly went off, blowing out his eyes and frightfully mu- tilating him. He died on Wednesday night in great agony. AN ADVENTUROUS CYCLIST —Among cyclists there are many venturous spirits. By them remarkable feats, requir- ing boldness and endurance, have been not only essayed but accomplished. So far the tricyclists have perhaps effected more than the two-wheel men, their machines being better adapted for rough work, and capable of conveying requisites for long journeys. There is, however, a young Englishman named Thomas Stevens, who, with his bicycle, has already beaten all previous achievements, and is bent upon an effort which can never be surpassed, except peradventure in the matter of speed. He has traversed the American continent, San Francisco being his starting place, and has even crossed the Rocky mountains, his average journey per day being 50 miles. This is what he has done. What he intends to do is to go right round the world—that is, of course the land sur- face. He has set himself to a tremendous task, and on the score of pluck he deserves to succeed. DESTRUCTIVE FIRES.—A Burnley Hotel Partly Gutted: On Thursday morning a fire occurred at the Thorn Hotel, Burnley, and ins few minutes the kitchen (where the flames originated) and the billiard-room were completely gutted The fire brigade extinguished the fire in a short space of time. The damage, which is estimated at about £7OO, is fully insured.—Dantage at a Bolton Mill: A fire was dis- covered at six o'clock on Thursday morning at the mill of Mr J J Hilton, Bow-street, Bolton. It originated through the breaking of a cylinder, and was communicated to the spinning mules, and through the reef to the attic. Three pairs of mules were destroyed and ether damage done before the flames were subdued by the Corporation brigade. The damage., which amounts to several thousand pounds, is covered by insurance.— Fire at a Cotton Warehouse. —Early on Thursday morning the Liverpool tire and salvage brigades were called to a fire which had broken out on the second floor of one of the block of Atlas warehousea at the corner of Atlas-street and Love-lane. Owing to the prompt attention of the firemen, assisted by salvage officers, the conflagration was prevented from spreading, and the damage was confined to a destruc- tion of 400 bales of American and Egyptian cotton,— Fire at Glasyow —A destrective fire broke out last night at Messrs Sandeman's oil works, Reechill, Glasgow. Many barrels of oil were destroyed. Poecurern AT lELLM—At the County Police Court Strangeways, on Monday' before Sir John Iles Mantel', a young man name' John Leonard Byard was charged on re- mand with poaching on land belonging to Sir Humphrey de Trafford at Irlarn on Wednesday last. The case had been adjourned in order that the prisoner might produce his father to swear that he had been in bed all night. Mr Byard, sen, now said he was "up, mad with the toothache," at three am, and his son was in bed then, and stopped there until the police and the gamekeepers fetched him from be- tween the sheets at five o'clock.—lnspector Kelly, however, said that when he went into the prisoner's bedroom he found the young man in bed with his trousers and stockings on, saturated with moisture. His boots, standing by the Jed- side, were also wet. He had, moreover, run out of the house i by the back door when the officers entered the room, and was then caught by another constable, placed there in readi- ness for such an emergency. Two gamekeepers, it will be remembered, had seen the youth poaching at Ham, and had followed him home to Patricroft between 3 aud 4 a.m.— Sir John asked the father whether it was not a strange thing for his son to go to bed in his trousers and wet stock- ings on his feet, to which the witness said it had been the wakes the day before and his lad had been to them. Sir , John said he believed the father was perjuring himself.— The prisoner would go to gaol for two months with hard labour. . . .

THE NEW VICES= OF INDIA.-1I is authoritatively an- nounced that the Marquis of Ripon will retire from the Viceroyalty of India before the dose of the present year, and that he will be succeeded by the Earl of Dufferin. A correspondent telegraphed from Pera, on Wednesday: The Earl of Dufferin, who has been appointed Viceroy of India, leaves Constantinople on Tuesday for England. He will probably return here early in December on his way to for- mally present his letters of recall. The Earl of Duffsrin, who succeeded to his father's barony in 1941, when he was fifteen years of age, after being educated at Christ Church, Oxford, entered public life as a Lord-in-Waiting in Lord J Russ,l Ps first administration. He was attached in 1835 to Lord J Russell's mission to Vienna ; and was sent by Lord Palmerston as British Commissioner to Syria in 1860. He was under Secretary of State for India from 1864 to 1866, and in the War Office subsequently for a few months. Under Mr Gladstone's AdmMistration, which commenced in 1868, Lord Dufferin was Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster for four years, and then assumed the direction of the Go- vernment of Canada, a post which he held until 1878. He was suhsequentiy Ambassador at St. Petersburg from 1879 to 1831, and was appointed to Constantinople in April, 1881. The following year be went on a special mission to Egypt. He was created an Earl in 1871. The noble Earl became known as an author in 1860 by his "Letters from High Latitudes." and he has written several pamphlets upon Irish questions. Lord Dufferin married, in 1852, the eldest daughter of Captain Hamilton, of county Dawn. CO-OPERATIVE WHOLESALE SOCIETY.—The balance sheet for the quarter ending June 28th shows a business for the three months amounting to Ll 206,323, which is an increase of £45,336 upon last year. The net profit, after providing fcr all expenses of production and distribution, interest on capital and depreciation, of property according to rule, amounts to £12,691 2s 61, which the committee recommend should be distributed thus :—Dividend on members' pur- chasers at 214 in the pound, £10,955; dividend on non- members' trade at 41 in the pound, £283 Hs; and the balance of £1,451 to reserve. In the bank department there is a net profit of £239, on a turnover of £4.000,487, and the following division is recommended :—Dividend to members on credit balances at * pet cent. and on debit balance at * per cent. £171; dividend to non-members at half these rates, LI Is 76, and the balance of £64 53 to the reserve. Six new accounts have b2en opened during the quarter, making the present number 166. The shipping business shows a profit of £lO2 14s, after charging all expenses, including repairs, depreciation, and interest on capital at the rate of 5 per cent. The society was established in 18134, and its business for the first year amounted to £Bl, 426, and its business now exceeds this sum. Ita total business during the 21 years it has been is existence amounts to £38,609,674, and the net profit realised to £460,067. Its majority celebration is to take place at London and Newcastle on Saturday next, and at Manchester on the following Saturday, when it is expected that upwards of 2,000 delegates and friends will be present at a dinner and meeting in St. James's Hall. CARDINAL MANNING ON RELIGIOUS EDucanoss.—Car- dinal Manning preached two sermons on Sunday at St. Wer- burgh's Roman Catholic Church, Chester, in aid of the Roman Catholic day schools. There were charges for ad- mission of from 55 downwards, but both morning and even- ing services were attended by large congregations. In the morning, the Cardinal preached from the words, " This is life eternal, that they may know Thee, the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom Thou hist sent." He said from the time that Christianity was restored in England there had never ceased to be in the country Christian schools and Christian education until the other day. It was a mournful truth, that 300 years ago England ceased to be Catholic, but it did not cease lobe Christian. It lost indeed the per- fection of that one universal faith which was one and the !lame in every place, which by its luminous universality was its own witness, and a witness for God and Christ. Never- theless, the tradition of Christianity, that was of the Apostles' Creed, the Baptismal Creed, the Baptism and Regeneration of the offspring of Christian men, the doctrine of the Holy Trinity, of the Incarnation--that was the knowledge of God and Jesus Christ, whom He had sent—the great laws of the I Divine Law-giveros they were written for us in the Gospels- all this,which was the very substance of Christanity, by God's infinite mercy, was still preserved, mutilated in part, but nevertheless in its substance inviolate. Therefore the schools of England were Christian schools, and it was Christian schools that made the English people. It was not warfare, nor the Legislature, nor any art or power of man, that made England to be one people. It was not until 14 Years ago that, with a heavy heart, they were obliged to declare that the unbroken tradition of the Christian educa- tion of England, which from the sixth century to the nine- teenth century had continued uninterrupted was cut asunder. Schools were established and multiplied in this land, in which nothing but the knowledge which was purely human was given. God only knew the future—whether what were called new the voluntary schools of England, i e., the ancient schools which formed the English people—whether they would multiply and survive, so as to check and turn aside this evasion of education in the knowledge of God and Christ, He only knew. In conclusion, Cardinal Man- ning congratulated Chester on the fact that religious in- struction was given in all its schools.—Another large con- gregation assembled in the evening, when Cardinal Manning chose as his text the words, "From henceforth all genera- tions shall call thee blessed," hie sermon being principally a defence of the Catholic Church and its honouring of the Virgin.
THE REFORNI AGITATION.

MR. TREVELYAN AT GLASGOW. A great demonstration in favour of the Franchise Bill was held in Glasgow on Saturday. The men taking pert in the procession through the streets, and who numbered about 70,000, mustered in Melvin Grove Park, in the west end of the city, and marched to the Public Green or People's Park, in the extreme south-east. Very amusing Orgies and other devices were borne in the procession, some of the ideas represented being similar to those mentioned in connection with the Burnley procession a few weeks since. Addresses were delivered from eight different platforms. Before each the following resolution was carried:—" That this meeting, while expressing approval of the general policy of Her Majesty's Government, desires specially to record its heartiest thanks to Mr Gladstone and his colleagues for their efforts to carry, during the past session, their measure for the enfranchisement of two millions of our fellow-country- men; views with the utmost satisfaction their decision to hold an autumn session in order to secure its enactment; strongly condemns the action of the Tory majority in the House of Lords in refusing to pass the bill, and expressea the deep conviction that, with its present constitution and powers, the Hereditary House of Legislature is inimical to the best interests of the nation." Public meetings were held in the three great halls of the city in the evening, all of which were crowded. At the meeting in St. Andrew's Hall —Mr Thomas Russel in the chair—Mr Trevelyan, M.P., was the principal speaker. Mr. TREVELYAN, in the course of his speech, said : It had been the hope of some of us that the greet measure confer- ring citizenship upon the half of the nation which is at pre- sent excluded might have been the work of both the great partiesand both the Houses of Parliament. It is a very signal benefit to the country at large when a great reform is the work of the nation and not exclusively the work of a party. But Lord Salisbury chose otherwise, and he alone has turned what might have been a national undertaking into a gratuitous, an unnecessary, and a most arduous con- test. In that contest we intend to fight till we have got the victory. While Lord Salisbury announces that he looks for the opinion of the country nowhere except in the exist- ing constituencies, I.ord Carnervon goes further up still, and he will look for it nowhere but in the House of Lords. He claims for the House of Lords that it has grown to be a representative of all that is worthiest, and noblest, and most educated in this nation. Now this is a very serious matter for the House of Commons. If the House of Lords repro. sent all that is most worthy, noble, and well educated, I suppose there is nothing left for the House of Commons, and the vulgar mass in whose name they speak and vote, except what is unworthy, ignoble, and ignorant. It is lucky for Lord Carnarvon that he was not born a generation ago ; for that speech would infallibly have earned him the most conspicuous place in Thackeray's immort "Book of Snobs." The excluded householders of Great Britain, in proportion as they are intelligent and public spirited, regard the action of the House of Lords as insulting to themselves, and injuri- ous to their Cause. The county householders know that if it had not been for the Conservatives in the House of Lords they would at this moment have the franchise irrevocably and unconditionally secured to them ; and that now, in con- sequence of the action of the Lords, they are as completely outside the pale of the Constitution as ever. If the Lords had passed the bill these men would be political citizens. Because the Lords did not pass the bill they are still politi- cal pariahs. If the Lords really wanted to extend the fran- chise they would have rased the bill; and everybody who like the bill, and everybody who fears it, have interpreted their action as it deserves to be interpreted. What is this system of redistribution upon which the Lords place such great value? Lord Salisbury, speaking at Manchester, im- plied that they were burning with desire to distribute seats in proportion to population. Lancashire was to have 63 members; London, 59; Yorkshire, I suppose, 50; Glasgow, at the very least, 10. When we come to redistribution, I daresay that Lord Salisbury and Mr. Chamberlain, working together on those lines, could knock out a very good scheme between them. But is it credible that the rank and file of the Tory peers who came up from the country on July 9th to vote for Earl Cairns' amendment, and who, to their dis- may and disgust, had to stay in town until July 17th to I vote against Lord Wemyss—is it credible that their reasons for opposing the Franchise Bill was that it was unaccom- panied by a Redistribution Bill allotting seats to the various districts of the United Kingdom in exact proportion to the population ? In showing the need of union among Liberal politicians of all grades, the right hon. gentleman remarked: The Ameri- can general Sheridan, the greatest fighting officer of modern times, at the critical moment of a battle used to say, "Now, let everything go in ;" and that is the moment which has arrived in the constitutional history of our country. As great a political leader as ever Sheridan was a military one has given the word, and everybody who has the soul of a freeman, everybody who is proud of our national traditions and confident of our national future, will march shoulder to shoulder into the conflict, the prize of which is the enfran- chisement of two millions of our countrymen and the estab- lishment on a firm and undisputed basis of the inherent right of the people to settle the details of their own representation in spite of the opposition of an assembly which is not repre- sentative at all. (Loud cheers.) Mr TREVELYAN spoke in somewhat similar term at the other gatherings. At the meeting in St Andrew's Hall and the City Hall he had a most cordial reception' but at the gathering in the Grand National Hall he was hooted and hissed by a small number of Irishmen, who for a time inter- rupted the proceedings with hooting and cries of "Sea-weed Treveiyan." The more orderly of the audience who were in the vast majority, turned the tables upon the Irishmen by giving three ringing cheers for the Chief Secretary. Speeches were also delivered at the different meetings by the Lord Advocate, Mr George Anderson, Dr Cameron, Mr Barclay, and Mr Summers, M's.P. The proceedings were characterised by great enthusiasm. MR. JOHN MORLEY AND SIR W. LAWSON. M.P. A city and county demonstration was held on Saturday on the Carlisle racecourse to protest against the action of the Lords. There were between 12,000 and 15,000 people present. A procession, four or five abreast, which occupied twenty minutes in passing a given point, perambulated the principal streets of the city with banners and bands of music, and flags were dieplayed from houses. Rain fell as the procession reached the racecourse, and the downpour became so heavy that the proceedings had to be curtailed. There were three platforms, presided over by Mr George Howard, M.P., Mr R A Allison, of Scaleby Hall, and Mr J S Ainsworth, of Harecroft. The following resolution was proposed from all three platforms :—" That this meet- ing of electors and non-electors hereby protest against the action of the House of Lords in rejecting the Franchise Bill, and pledge themselves to use all legitimate influence to prevent the decisions of the people's elected representatives being set at nought by a hereditary Chamber.' —Mr JOHN Monte:se M.P., who was received with enthusiastic cheer- ing, said they were not there to support the Parliamentary chiefs, because chiefs with a majority of 130 in the popular Chamber required no support ; but they were met to give expression te the opinion that the time had now come when they would have to light it out with the hereditary Cham- ber. (Cheers.) This feeling against the House of Lords had not sprung up like the prophet's gourd in a night. The cup which had long been too full was now overflowing. Mr Gladstone was reluctant to undertake constitutional changes. but, if the Bill were rejected a second time, he might think the time had come for undertaking them, and if Mr Gladstone did undertake them and asked the country to back him, it would go hard witle the hereditary Chamber. (Cheers.) Such proposals as that of putting a later date on the Franchise Bill were all traps, and what they meant was that the Tories were to dictate the terms upon which the House of Commons was to set about its own reform. A com- promise such as had been suggested would not be a compro- mise, but a surrender and a humiliation to the Commons. (Cheers.)—Sir Wilfrid Lawson, who spoke at Platform No. 3. said the cry of the day was once described by Sir Robert Peel in his time as "Register, register, register! " Now it was " Demonstrate, demonstrate, demonstrate !" (Laughter.) The House of Lords, which had knocked the Franchise Bill to pieces, was a representative assembly. They represented the pride, passion, and prejudice of an obsolete oligarchy. (Cheers.) They had set themselves against the nation, and would the nation submit to it? (Cries of "No.") Surely we had bother enough getting any reform passed in this country without setting up a House of Lords to bother us more. It reminded him of the Irishman in the song—
There was a young man of Ballinacrasy, Who wanted a wife to make him unaisy.

That was just what they wanted the Lords for—" to make us unaisy "—(laughter)—and, in his opinion; we had been unaisy long enough, (Cheers.) —The resolution Ira§ Carried with great enthusiasm at all three Platforms, and the crowd dispersed.

There was a great Reform gathering of 50,000 persons near Swansea on Saturday, and a procession took place through the principle streets of that town. Among those who spoke were Mr Dillwvn, MP, Sir H Nivian, M P, and Sir J Jenkins, M P.—Largely attended meetings of Liberals were held at Beverley and Parsley (in which the districts were represented), in support of the Franchise Bill. A demonstration of the Conservatives of East Cheshire was held on Saturday, at Adlington Park, near Stockport, the seat of Mr Clt B Leigh. The incessant rain interfered with the success of the proceedings, which, however, were enthusiastic. Mr T W Tatton presided, and the speakers included Mr Cunliffe Brooks, M P, who moved a resolution supporting the House of Lords in its action with regard to the Franchise Bill. Colonel Legh, MP, seconded the reso- lution, which was supported by Lord Stanley of Alderley and the Hon. Cecil Raikes, MP. Mr Raikes said that the enforcement of redistribution was the only means they could use to make a certain number of Liberal members, who had a personal interest in preventing a redistribution of votes, vote for a complete Reform Bill. If the Franchise Bill alone was passed the Ministers would be left masters of the situation, and the Crown and the people would be de- prived of the power of compelling a dissolution. Lord Egerton of Tatton also supported the resolution, wliich was unanimously carried. The Earl of Zetland preside& at a Conservative gathering in his lordship's grounds at Upleatnarn on Saturday. Mr James Lowther, M.P, expressed his firm intention of oppos- ing the "sham measure of reform," which was but a "fraudulent attempt to swamp existing constituences." Resolutions protesting against the spirit of partisanship displayed by her Majesty's Ministers in dealing with Par- liamentary Reform, and the unconstitutional agitation against the House of Peers was passed.—There was a " Con- servative afternoon," concluding with "a grand display of fireworks," at Cowdray Park, Sussex seat of the Earl of Egmont. More than 6,000 tickets of admission were issued, but it is estimated that not more than 500 persons attended the meeting for speaking.

; The Pall Mall Gazettee publishes its weekly record of ' meetings, from which it appears that there were last week thirty-three meetings against the action of Lord Salisbury and eight in support of it. In these circumstances the St. James's Gazette is frank enough to hint to its Tory re idets that " To continue to hold meeting for meeting and proces- sion for procession would be simply to play into the hands of the enemy." Sir H Selwin-Ibbetson, M.P., speaking at a Conservative "fête" in Hertfordshire at which there were several wag- gons crowded with agricultural labourers," said he would be the last man to oppose the extension of the franchise, but he thought the effect of the Government policy would ba to destroy the vote of the agricultural classes. A Conservative gathering took place on Thursday, at Berwick Park, Shrewsbury, the seat of Mr James Watson. There was a large attendance, and the meeting in the park was addressed by Messrs A R Scoble and J Watssn, Conser- vative candidates for Shrewsbury. A resolution was adopted approving of the action of the House of Lords.
