div.head: TRADES UNION CONGRESSi
div.p: THE TRADES UNION CONGRESSi

The seventeenth annual Trades Union Congress com- menced on Monday at Ate3rdeers. Mr. A. B. Bailey (of Pres- ton) presided in the early stage of the meeticg.—Tiae CHAIRSIAN said it was gratifying to him, as the chairman of the Parliamentary Committee, to congratulate them and the societies they represented upon their appearance in the city of Aberdeen. He was likewise proud to be able to say that during the past year they had been most successful in connection with the receiving of funds towards the Associa- tion, and were in a pecuniary position far superior to what they had been in any year of their past history. (Applause.) Being so far distant from the centre of the Association, it must be gratifying to them, and certainly to the Parlia- mentary Committee, also to those who supported the reso- lution for the Ceneress to be held in Aberdeen, to know that 140 delegates had already sent in their names, which proved, if there was any necessity for proof, the stability, the use- fulness, and the earnestness Of the trzeles' unions of the United Kingdom, the necessity of a Congress such as this, and the importance of the work which it had accomplished in the past. (Applause.) They had frequently been told that the objects of this Congrese was selfish, and in some instances that the officials in connection with the various institutions and societies were working, though assiduously, for their own interest. He could only refer them to one circumstance that had taken place within the last nine or ten years as showing that some amongst them at least were not as selfish as their opponents insinuated. That circum- stance was that their secretary, while receiving a sum of only £2OO for his services to Congress and the Parliamentary Committee' was offered a Government situation of £5OO per annum, which be declined. (Applause.) He was proud to see so large a number of the familiar faces of men who were still labouring for the cause of the class to which they be- longed, and who proved by their presence that the various trade organisations which they represented were not dis- satisfied with the past efforts of the Congress and the work it had year by year endeaveured to accomplish. (Applause.) He would only say that he hoped they would, in the discus- , sion that took place, give that credit to others which they , expected to get for themselves. (Hear, hear.) Mr J C Thompson, president of the Aberdeen Trades Council, was elected president. The other officers and committee were: —Mr James Swift (Manchester), vice-chairman; Mr Arnaud, of the Aberdeen Trades Council, secretary ; Standing Orders Committee: Messrs Battersby, Brummond, Bailey, Pickard, and Wilkie. Mr Wilson, of Durham, and Mr Ashton, Old- ham, were appointed auditors. Mr Bliley at this stage vacated the chair in favour of Mr Thompson, who in assum- ing the presidency offered a few words of thanks and wel- come to the Congress.—Mr Broadhurst, M.P., read the Par- liamentary Committee's report, which strongly condemned the rejection of the Franchise Bill, and attributed the loss of the Merchant Shipping Bill to obstruction. The com- mittee expressed the opinion that the Employers' Liability Act should be made compulsory. The passing of the Muni- cipal Elections (Corrupt Practices) Act, and the extension of the hours of polling, were referred to with satisfaction. Mr Chamberlain's proposed Railway Regulation Bill was described as one which would have been a most valuable one to railway workmen and the families depending upon them; but the determined opposition of the railway interest, together with the pressure of time on accouet of the Fran- chise Bill, had compelled ite withdrawal for the present. The interested opposition of the banking interest in the House of Commons to the Savings Bank Act Amendment Bill was also alluded to in terms of condemnation. After generally favourable reference to the bill, which did not obtain a place for debate, for extending the Factory Acts to evorkshops, the report touched upon the part taken by the trades union representatives at the last Co-operative Con- gress in a movement fur promoting an extensive propa- ganda amongst working-class organisations in favour of productive co-operation.—The Congress adjourned after formally receiving the report. On Tuesday the PRESIDENT delivered his inaugural ad- ' dress bidding the delegates welcome. He assured them that ' this Congress of the working classes in Aberdeen recognised a potentiality for good done not merely for trades unionists, but for all who bad to earn their bread by the sweat of their brow. Dealing with the dullness of trade, he asked if it was too much at this crisis to ask employers of labour to wisely consider their mode of dealing with their work- people, especially those who, by busy hands and brains, had helped to make them rich. Much lay to their hand in the way of turning the minds of men in certain directions with the view of relieving the glutted labnir market. In this connection he instanced the revision of the land laws. The dispersion and expatriation of our rural population was a matter to be deplored. This order of things must be reversed. Having urged the delegates to inculcate sobriety, he next spoke of the relationship between employer and employed. His own opinion was that the only remedy for existing grievances was productive co-partnership, Turning to poli- tice, he said the action of the House of Lords had tended to mutilate and subvert all good legislation. To allow that House to exist en its present footing would be a decided anomaly. Personally he believed only in direct representa- tion, and favoured the payment of members of Parliament by the State. In the meantime it would be wise for the trades to organise a special fund for the express purpose of working-class representation. Having referred in terms of approval to the codification of the criminal law, the com- mercial law, and the necessity for securing a change in the law of public inquiry in sudden and accidental death in Scotland, Mr Thompson said be sincerely hoped that the present Congress would outshine all former ones in the spirit of forbearance and the conciseness of the speeches, dignifying by every word and vote the labour movement.

In reply to a delegate, Mr BROADHURST denied that there was any truth in the statement published in The Times, under the signature of '‘ A Trades Unionist," to the effect that he had nominated working-men as sub-inspectors of mines, or that the appointments already made had proved in any way unsatisfactory.—On the motion of Mr LAHR& (Newcastle), seconded by Mr SMITH (Sunderland \ the re- port of the Parliamentary Committee was adopted. Mr JOSEPH ARCH moved is resolution expressing deep regret that the House of Lords had 'ejected the Franchise Bill.—Mr WILSON (Durham), in seconding, said he did not personally regret the action of the peers, as it forced for- ward into public notice the anomalous powers of that as- sembly.—Mr SIMMONDS (Maidstone) thought the resolution did not go far enough, and moved an addition to the effect that the time had come to insist that legislation should be entrusted solely to the representative assembly.—Mr TIMED. FALL (Southport) seconded this addendum —Mr KNIGHT (Newcastle) and Mr BURNETT recommended that, in order to avoid any question of a partisan or purely political character, the Congress should confine its resolutions, as originally proposed, to the simple question of the extension of the franchise, which both parties profess to be agreed on.— Mr. Harris (Preston) defended the legislative functions of the House of Lords, and proposed as an amendment that the Congress should express regret that the Government had failed to introduce a Redistribution Bill accompanying the Franchise Bill. (Groans, hisses, and laughter.)—Miss Wilkinson and Mrs Ellis (Dewsbury) claimed the support of trades unionists in favour of female suffrage.—Mr Carson (Glasgow) suggested that the resolution should express deep indignation at the action of the Lords.—Mr Simmons with- drew his amendment, and the original resolution was unani- mously passed, with the addendum advocating continued popular agitation for the Reform Bill until it is passed. Other resolutions passed urging the introduction of the Employers Liability Amendment Act, the extension of Lac- tor:, and workshop inspection, and an Engineers' Certificate Bill. It was resolved to ask Mr Gladstone to address the 9,4DETeSS; PRESENTATION TO MR. RROIDNITRST.

The first bdsiness before the Tra les Union Congress on Wednesday was the presentation of an address and £1,200, contributed by the working classes of the United Kingdom, to 'Mr. H. Broadhurst, M.P., in recognition of his long and valuable services to the cause of labour as secretary of the Parliamentary Committee. Mr. BROADHURST, in returning thanks, spoke of the opportunities now within the reach of every man, high or low, for achieving distinction in the ser- vice of the State. He said the blame would rest with work- ing people themselves if within a few years they had not a number of direct representatives in Parliament, and be even predicted that ere long the masses of the people would have a spokesman within the charmed circle of the Executive: In its subsequent discussions the Congress dealt with a variety of subjects. Resolutions were adopted asking for the speedy appointment of additional inspectors of mines, expressing satisfaction with the spread of co-operative productive !inter- prises, and thanking the Government for the extension of the hours of polling in municipal elections, whilst regretting that that measure hid not been exten- ded to county elections. A further resolution was car- ried in favour of a larger direct representation of labour in Parliament, and advising the working classes to organ- ' ise for the purpose of electing their own candidates. An amendment to this motion calling for the State payment of members was rejected by a large majority. In the evening the delegates were entertained by their fellow-workers of Aberdeen. The principal feature in Thursday's proceedings was an address by Lord Rosebery, who was accompanied by the Countess of Rosebery and Lord Aberdeen. Representatives of the Corporation, the University, and other local bodies were also present. Lord Rosebery expressed his high ap- preciation of the federalism of the Congress, which combined strength for mutual objects with separate management for separate objects of different Unions. This principle equally applied to the relationship of the mother country and the Colonies. Proceeding to illustrate the great importance of colonial federation, Lord Rosebery said it was of special in- terest to the working classes that the bonds which united our Colonies to the mother country should be made stronger and more definite. It was time for people to mike this
question one of prac'ical politics. Lord Aberdeen also briefly addressed the Congress. A resolution was passed urging thecoditication of the criminal law and of the law relating to petty sessicns.

div.head: MEMORIAL TO LORD BEACONSFIELD
div.p: MEMORIAL TO LORD BEACONSFIELD
AT ORMSKIRK.

On Tuesday afternoon a statue of the late Earl of Beacons- field was unveiled by the Earl of Lathom at Ormskirk. Ormskirk is one of the strongholds of Conservatism in South-West Lancashire, and shortly after the death of Lord Beaconsfield a project to perpetuate his memory was set on foot by the Conservatives of the polling districts of Orms- kirk and Maghull. Various proposals were discussed, and ultimately it was decided that the memorial should take the form of a statue, to be placed in a central position in the town of Ormskirk. A site at the top of Moonstreet was chosen, and the work was entrusted to Mr G H Margetson, of Chelsea, whose design met with the approval of Lord Barrington, Mr Ralph Disraeli, and the Earl of Lathom. The statue and the pedestal upon which it rests are of free- stone. The figure of the Earl is of heroic SIZ3, and repre- sents his Lordship attired in his robes as a Knialt of the Garter. The pose of the statne is admirable, and though the expression of the countenance is somewhat stern, a faithful likeness has been obtained. The whole cost of the memorial is estimated at about £4OO.

The unveiling of the statue was the occasion of some ceremony. At half-past four o'clock, amid the cheering of a considerable crowd, the Earl of Latho:n entered the enclosure formed round the statue, accompanied by the Right Hon Sir R A Cross, M.P., Colonel J Ireland Black- borne, M.P., Lord Gerard, Colonel Wilbraham, Colonel Hesketh, the Rev Canon Blundell, Mr Margetson, Mr J Forshaw (Mayor of Preston), Mr A B Forwood, Mr F B Hoyden, the Rev J Wilson (Raiford), Mr H F Addenbrooke, Mr T Dale (Manchester), Mr T E Priest, Mr J Prescott (chairman of the Memorial Committee), Mr S Brighouas, Mr W Parr, Mr W L Hutton (hon. secretaries), and a num- ber of other gentlemen. Mr. PREscarr, on behalf of the Committee, requested Lord Lathorn to unveil the statue. The Earl of LATHOM having unveiled the statue, said it represented a great man whose memory would always shine out in future ages. (Cheers.) The nettle of Lord Beanne- field was a name that would not die out of this country in a hurry. (Hear, hear.) There afght be present some who differed from him in politics, but they would agree that he was a shining example of a man who had raised himself to the highest position by hard work and by a love of his sovereign and his country. (Cheers.) His name would re- main permanent even when the names of many other great , men who were now known would have comparatively sank into oblivion. (Hear, hear.) It would stand befo e teem as that of a man who hod always worked for the good of his countrymen' and who entered with heart and soul into the great battle he was fighting. He congratulated the men of Orinskirk upon having reared in their midst a statue which would recall to their memory what Lord Beaconsfield did for the great cause of Conservatism in this country, and would inspire many to follow in his footsteps. Upon his death they knew, to a certain extent' what a loss they had sustained, but they did not know thoroughly, and they had only ju3t begun to realise how deeply and how heavily his loss bad affected the welfare of this country. (Cheers.) He again congratulated the people of the town on the posses- sion of so faithful a likeness of the great leader of the Con- servative party, and also the sculptor upon the success of his work. (Cheers.) ; Sir R. A. Cnoss, M.P., proposed a vote of thanks to the Earl of Letbone. He said Lord Beaconsfield was a man whom he believed every one present honoured and revered. (Cheers.) Colonel IRELAND BLACEBERNE seconded the motion, which was passed, and Lard LATHOM having briefly replied, the ceremony was concluded. In the evening a banquet took place in the large ball of the Working Men's Institute. Mr. J. Prescott presided, and was supeorted by Sir R. A. Cross, id P, Colonel J. Ireland Blackburne, M.P., Lord Gerard, and the majority of those who were present at the unveiling of the statue. After the preliminary bests, Mr. T. B. ROYDEN (Liverpool) proposed "Success to the Conservative Cause." Sir R. A. CROSS, M.P., in responding, said that the enemies of the man whose statue they had unveiled that day could not deny that he was a great man. He was a man only seen once in a century. We had our great men of the pre- sent day, and there was no doubt that he who was at the head of the Government was a great man, and that he was a man also who was only produced once in a century. (A Voice : " A good job too," and laughter.) He (Sir R. Cross) ventured to say there was no man living who had done so much to meintain the Empire and to benefit every part of it as the man whose statue had that day been un- veiled. It seemed to be rather the view of the Prime Minis- ter and of some of those associated with him that if we could only have a little England we should be happy here- after. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) But a little England could not live. We must never Ise afraid cf our resoonei- Unties, and the fault he (Sir R. Cross) found with the Prime Minister was that he dare not be great. (Cheers.) He was quite aware that at the last election Mr. Gladstone accused the late Government of wishing to extend the Em- pire, and of wanting to go into wars unnecessarily, and he should not have alluded to that if Mr. Gladstone had not spoken upon the subject in Scotland. He was bound to say there never was a greater mistake made. (Hear, hear.) Did they think if Lord Beaconsfield had remained at the head of affairs we should have beard of those terrible mas- sacres and tortures of men and women. those burnings of property and cutting and maiming of animals which hod oc- curred in Ireland? No man ever spoke a truer word about Ireland—and no man knew the character of the people bet- ter—than Mr Parnell, when he said the Irish were a very bad people to run away from. What was wanted was that the Irish should always have felt that there was a firm band, but at the same time a just and a merciful one, upon them. But they were now told to think nothing of those things; by and by they might be allowed to discuss those grave questions of foreign and Irish policy, but there was one thing of paramount importance which must be done first, and that was to pass the Franchise Bill. (Laughter.) TO say that the Lords rejected the Franchise Bill was an absolute, a wilful, and a deliberate lie—(cheers) ;—and in proof of what he said they had only to look to the words of the motions of Lords Cairns and Cadogan, which showed: that the House of Lords had never objected to the extension of the franchise. The Conservative party would not have an election upon an extended franchise without redistribu- tion. In North-east Lancashire, for instance, there was a i population of 233,000 living outside the Parliamentary , boroughs: and out of that 238,000 147,000 were living in towns of from 10,000 to 25,000 inhabitants. There were no votes he (Sir It Cross) would more readily give than a vote in favour of the House of Lords and a vote for the dissolu- tion of the present Parliament. (Cheers.) 1 Several other toasts followed.

It is said that Mr James Ellis Frencb, ex-Inspector of the Royal lash Constabulary, now awaiting trial for his alleged share in the Dublin scandal case, is in danger of dying from inanition, as he persistently refuses b take food.

FRIGHTFUL ACCIDENT:A shocking accident occurred to a pleasure party on Tuesday night near St Mary's Loch. A horse attached to a coach bolted, and the occupants were precipitated over an embankment. An Edinburgh butcher named Todd, and his niece, were picked up dead, and the others were seriously injured. . . _ _

A Mr. Crisp, of Walthamstow, was on Wednesday re- leased from Holloway Gaol, after undergoing fourteen days' imprisonment in default of paving a flue of £1 7s 63, in- flicted on him for r fusing to have his child vaccinated. Mr Crisp was met outside the prison by a brass band and a number of sympathisers with the anti-vaccination move- ment.

ACCIDENT TO A/4 ISLE OF MAN STEAMER.—When leaving Menai Bridge, or. Tuesday, the steamer Fenslla, belonging to the Isle of Man Steamboat Co, having on board about 200 excursionists, ran on a rock a short distance from the landing sage. The passengers safely disembarked, but the vessel on Tuesday evening had canted, and was in a danger- ous post;cn.

LANCASHIRE POLICE-OFFICERS DISMISSED.—The stspen- s:on of Police•constables Clarke and Smith by the Liver- pool magistrates, in connection with a charge of drunken- ness the officers had made against Edward Mason and Elizabeth Chantry, of Derby-road, bas been followed by their di Salina' from the force. The Head Constable made a thorough inquiry. STRIKE AT CHORLEY.—The whole of the weavers and other workpeople at Messrs Lawrence's mill, Chorlev, have been locked out in consequence of the spinners, who "struck" last Week, refusing to return to work. About 700 Ipersons are thus thrown out of employment, and unless the dispute is speedily settled the other employers in the town will resort to a lock-out. THE SALVATIONIST DISTURBANCES at Worthing and Brighton, on Sunday, were serious, and the members of the army received a good deal of ill-usage. At Worthing, the nut, after stoning the "barrack," attacked the shop of a Mr Head, who fired a revolver at them, with the result that a young man named Oliver was shot in the neck. Head was afterwards arrested, and stands remanded.

_ . - DEATH OF A CENTENIRIAN.—Mr T.. Brougb, a farmer, died on Sunday night at Seaham Park, Seaham Harbour, aged 100 years. He was born in 1784, and for the past 13 years had been bedriddm. Up to 12 months ago his memory was good, and he could talk of events which came under his observation during the closing years of the last century. He saw Lord Byron's marriage, and knew Lady Byron intimately when living with her father, Sir Ralph Milbanke, at Seaham Hall. LORD PETRD.—The Catholic Times of yesterday (Fridray) s ys—" It is not correct, as the daily newspapers have •an- flounced, that a Jesuit will take his seat in the Upper Cham- ber at the opening of next session. Mgr. Lord Petre is riot a Jesuit, but a secular priest; and although two or three 1 members of his sacred profession have been peers of the realm since the pre-Reformation times, he will, we believe, be the first Catholic clergyman since that perial l to sit in the House of Lords. He will no doubt be found fon the side of the Administration. THE PHFADEI2 IN SCOTLAND.— Mr Gladstone, P.CCOM- panied by Mrs and Miss Gladstone, drove, to Balmoral on Monday forenoen, and had luncheon wilch the Queen. On a Wednesday, Mr Gladstone,-accompani,d by the Earl of Fife, '.; left Balmoral, and drove to Fife Lode. In the afternoon k the Prince of Wales and Prince Albrt Victor drove from Abergeldie, and took lunch at War Lodge, returning in the afternoon. The balloons selected for the ascents on Monday, in cele- bration of the centenary of the first aerial voyage in Eng- land, are "The Colonel" and "La Ville de Boulogne." Notices were roosted on Thursday in Woodford, near Loughrea, threatening anyone who should work for Mr Page, agent to Lord Clanricarde. The police tore down the notices.

DEFRAUDING TUE RAILWAY COMPANY : AN OLD TRICK REVIVED.—At the St. Helens Town Hall, on Tues- day, before Mr A Sinclair and Mr Alderman Mcßryde, James McNully, a young man hailing from Liverpool, was charged with defrauding the London and North-Western Railway Company by travelling from Edge Hill to St. Helens without having previously paid his fare.—Mr For. rand, of the solicitors' department, Lime-street, station, ap- peared to prosecute. He stated that that case was one in which an old trick was revived. On the arrival of a train at St. Helens station on the previous day, the prisoner with two men passed the ticket collector. The prisoner gave up three tickets, two from Huyton to St. Helens and one from Lime-street to Edge-hill. The ticket collector named James Wild followed the prisoner and spoke to him about the tickets, whereupon the prisoner said he had given him a ticket from Lime-street to St. Helens ; but no such ticket was collected from the passengers by that train. He (Mr Preston asked for the infliction of a heavy penalty.—James Wild, ticket collector, and Detective Wright, in the employ of the company, gave evidence in support of Mr Ferrand's state- ment; and the prisoner who said he was drunk at Lime. street and trusted to a friend to get him the right ticket, was fined lOs and costs. A JUVENILE SIIOP-DREAKEE.—At the St Helens Town Hall on Tuesday, before Mr A Sinclair and Alderman Mcßryde, Themes Manuion, 15 years of age, was charged with breaking into the lockup shop of Henry Martin, Nay- lor-street, and stealing therefrom Is 61 in money, a scarf, and several tie, together of the value of 8s 61.—An assis- tant to Mr Martin, named Beresford, stated that on the 22nd August he locked up the shop when everything was safe. When he entered next morning he found that Is Gd had been abstracted from the money drawer and several articles had been stolen. The socks produced were his master's pro- perty.—James Bradley, 14 years of age, deposal that on the date in question the prisoner asked him to go with him to Mr Martin's shop. They went about halfpast ten at night, and the prisoner smashed one of the cellar windows. He then entered the premises and shortly afterwards came out with several ties and socks.—P C Walsh apprehended the pri- soner, who, ar the time was wearing the socks produced. On being charged with the offence the prisoner said he knew nothing about it.—The prisoner now stated that his mother knit the socks produced, and 'said the lad Bradley was tell- ing lies—he would tell as many as would get one hung.— He was committed to prison for six weeks; and on hearing the decision he buret into tears and cried "Ob, eir, I did not do it at all."

div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 13, 1884.

The Trades Union Congress—the Parlia- ment of Labour, as it has been aptly termed— opened its seventeenth annual session in Aber- deen on Monday. Representing, as it does, over half a million of the best workmen of the Kingdom, it is natural that its movements should excite considerable interest. The time has gone by for treating-Trades Union- ists as disloyal and dangerous men; they have, step by step, fought their way to the front; they have compelled the Legislature to recognise their claims to protection ; and are now regarded by both political parties as an important factor in moulding the opinion of the country Indeed a section of the Tories not long since, believing it to be of importance to get the Congress on their side on the question of Fair Trade, tried to " jerrymander " a number of delegates; but the trick was speedily found out and it igno- miniously failed. The latest move has been for Mr. JAMES LOWTHER, M.P., ex-secre- tary for Ireland, to advise the Congress to have nothing whatever to do with politics. They may be members of various Trades So- cieties, and, as such, vote at their meetings on the business that is being done; but it is altogether different with them as members of the Society described as the State; they must be content—large numbers of them at any rate—to do witliout votes, and when the question is raised as to the advisability of putting them on a level with others of their• fellows, they are recommended to sheepishly stand aside and open not their mouths. It is needless to say that the Trades Unionists were not such "dolts and idiots " as to act on a suggestion of that kind; and the outcome is that they are now pledged to assist the Government in their endeavours to carry the Franchise Bill. The report of the Parliamentary Committee was read at the 11 Congress, on Monday, by Mr. BROADHURST, M.P., the secretary, and it pointedly refer- red to the "sacrifice of time and labour" which had been "thrown away by the ac- tion of the House of Lords" on the Fran- , chise Bill. Another point touched upon was the decision of the Government to appoint a number of sub-inspectors for mines. This ; may be claimed as the direct result of the ' 'action of the Congress, for the matter is one which has engaged its attention for ; I several years. It may not seem to be ; of much moment to those who have given no thought to the subject, but it ' means more than is apparent on the surface. It means that the State is more and more recognising it as a duty to see that the law for the regulation of mines is properly carried out ; and it follows that, if this be done, a number of valuable lives will every year be saved to the country that would otherwise have been lost. It is a significant fact that the percentage of loss of life frpm mining accidents has been reduced in proportion to the stringency of mining regulations But it is notorious that the present staff of In- spectors is too small to accomplish the task assigned to it. Accidents happen through breaches of the law which might have been prevented under efficient inspection; and it is therefore a legitimate inference that an increase in the number of inspectors will be followed by a reduction in the average loss of life. The Employers' Liability Act, the existence of which is due almost solely to the efforts of the Trade Unionists, has also I,proved of great service in protecting the workman. By ensuring greater care in the use of machinery and plant of every des- cription, it tends to reduce accidents to a minimum; and, although the incidence of ita operation is to throw a cost of insurance upon the employer, there is every reason to believe that there will be a more than equivalent gain in the lessened loss by accidents—to say nothing in this connection of the limbs and lives of workmen. The Report pro- ceeds to give some account of the Interna- tional Conference of Trades Unions held in I . ails last year; and it is noteworthy that the

! conclusion come to by the English delegates I is that they were far ahead of foreign work- men in the matter of organisation, and that little could be done until they were more on a level vith ourselves." It will be remem: bered that there was "wild talk" at the Paris • Conference on the part of some of the Con- tinental representatives, and fears were ex- pressed by timid onlookers that it would be a bad look out for this country if these were the opinions of" advanced" Trade Unionists. It would seem, however, that the Anarchists so far from being the advanced guard are rather in the background in the way of or- ganisation. When they get really ahead and can look about them, they will begin to see, with English working-men leaders, that they have more to gain by peaceful Reform than by warlike Revolution, and ultimately shed, as a snake sheds its skin, their present coating of destructive doctrine. Let us by all means have progress, and progress we shall have when toilers the world over obtain such a field as they are getting in this country. On Tuesday the Report was adopted, and the Congress proceeded to give the chief feature of it practical effect by considering a resolution moved by Mr. JOSEPH ARCH, ex- pressing deep regret that the House of Lords had rejected the Franchise Bill,and promising the Governmen: "the hearty support of the Congress in the accomplishment of this great and desirable object." The motion was duly seconded and supported, but it was not al- lowed to pass unchallenged. An addendum was moved stating that it was the opinion of the Congress "that the power of the House of Lords, as a legislative institution, should be withdiawn." This brought out a distinct amendment to the effect that it was to be re- gretted that the Government had failed to in- troduce a Redistribution Bill along with the Franchise Bill. The quarrel was now " a very pretty quarrel as it stood." It was one which wou]d have kept the House of Com- mons wrangling for a score of nights ; but the trade delegates are sensible men—they got rid of it in one sitting, with the result that Mr. ARCFI'S resolution, after being strength- ened in the direction of pledging support to, the Government was adopted "unanimously.' Toryism, it is satisfactory to see, has not much chance amongst Trades Unionists.

The result of the Brewster Sessions in Warrington is somewhat disappointing, al- though the licensing justices, true to recent traditions: have no granted any new licenses I except in one case Where they had no option in the matter. There wis an impression in the public mind, as the result of certain statements made last year, that some steps would be taken this sitting in the way of considerably reducing the number of off- licenses; but beyond dealing with two or three offenders nothing has been done It would seem that the Temperance party in the town have been relying upon action being taken by the police authorities ; and on the other hand it is not unlikely that the Chief.constable has concluded that, if notice of objection was to be given to holders of off-licenses, it would be better that it should come from outsiders. At any rate, between the two stools, the opposition to these licenses has come to the ground, and the holders of them are scot-free to make the best or worst of them for another year. The Mayor, as presiding magistrate, ad- mitted that "there was a concensus of opinion that off-licenses were a great hindrance to I the sobriety of the town ; " and Mr. BROAD- BENT went the length of urging that the con- sideration of their renewal should be adjour- ned to the 29th inst. It is a pity that this Isensible suggestion was not adopted, for it would have given the Chief-constable, or a ! representative of the Temperance party, an opportunity of taking formal objection, and Ithe case for each license would then have to be taken on its merits. As it is, they are re- newed in a body, notwithstanding the expres- sed conviction that there are far too many of I: them. It is beyond question that all over the Icountry the off-licensing system has led to an appalling increase of drunkenness amongst ; women, and it is certain that Warrington has been no exception to the rule. Alderman DAVIES remarked that in 1875 there were 124 convictions against females for drunkenness in the borough, as against 174 for the past ;year, showing an increase of so. Bat he might have put the case stronger, for as late as 1878 the convictions for female drunken- ' ness were as low as 81—that is less than one half of the number for the past year. It is true that, taking women and men together, ; there is a slight decrease in the twelve months ; • but, unhappily, the decrease is amongst the males rather than the females. And it can hardly be otherwise so long as , there are so many off-licenses in Warrington. lAs one of the pantomimes had it last Christ- i mas
The grocer's as a,drink.shop.does.great harm,

Wheii wives get " beer" Enid put itt' lawn to ' barm." There is in Warrington a sufficient number of off-licenses to flood the town with beer. In Blackburn with a population of I to, 000 there are 33 off-licenses, and there is a strong feeling that there are too many; Watrington with a population of 4.6,0a0 has as many as 77. It has more than twice the number with less than half the population! In view of such a startling fact it is not sufficient merely to de- plore the prevalence of female drunkenness; it is a case for deeds rather than words. The magistrates must stop the cause if they are really anxious that the effect should cease.

SIR RICHARD CROSS, as One of the dozen or so of Tory leaders, is an admirer, and an imitator in his way, of the late Lord BEACONSFIELD. Providence has not blessed him with brains to enable him to imitate him in his higher intellectual qualities; but he manages pretty well as to the lower—that is. in displaying an audacious disregard for truth. Speaking in Scotland. on Wednesday, the Ex-Horn SECRETARY said "Mr. GLAD,. STONE had got this Franchise Bill so much on the brain that he honestly thought the House of Lords had rejected the Bill;, but nothing could be further from the fact.." What nonsense! What has Sir RICHARD. got on the brain that he should spout such, rub- bish ? It is no wonder he met with interrup- tion from a Scotch audience, who have yet ringing in •their ears the fine outburst of sarcasm with which the PP-lAIE MINISTER referred to the action of the House of Lords as—not a rejection—but an " effectual stop- page" of the Bill. Not only is it not rejected by the Lords, but, we are told "nothing could be further from Ow fact." In- deed! But suppose their Lordships had passed the Bill, would not that have been "further from the fact" of this so- called rejection ? Or are we to suppose Sir Richard has himself got so far from the fact that he does not know how to get back again He indulges in the usual stale talk about an appeal to the people; but, while, professing ,to deal with anomalies, he shows himself

THE NEW FIRE ENGINE AT WIDNES.— Under the superintendence of Mr J Carr this engine was tested on the the market ground on Tuesday, and the result was con- sidered to be satisfactory. DITTON Cut:ram—The Rev C W Wooll, for eight years curate of St. John the Divine, Fairfield, Liverpool, has been appointed to the living at Ditton, vacant through the resig- nation of Rev J 13 Cassells Brown. WIDNES C.E.T.S.—The Rev C Ranfitt presided over the weekly meeting on Thursday night, and delivered an address on temperance topics. An entertainment was given by Messrs J White, J Farrant, T Young, T Atherton, and Holmes. VICTORIA-ROAD- WESLEYAN •CHAPEL, WIDNES' The annual sermons were preached on Sunday by the Rev John Leathlev, of the Haslineden circuit, formerly of Widnes. There were good congregations, but the cellectione were rather under last year. ST. MICHAEL AND ILL ANGELS' CEIMICH, RUNCORN.— Mr John Llezlelaurst, of Roche House, High-street, Ruecerre has presented a donation of £l.OO towards the chancel feuds of this church. The main portion of the building is rapidly approaching completion, but as the Building Committee could not provide funds for the erection of a chancel that portion has not been commenced. Sr. PAUL'S WESLEYAN CHAPEL, RUNCORN.—Theanniver- sary sermons in connection with this chapel were p-eached on Sunday, large congregations attending at each service. In the morning the Rev E J Robinson, superintendent of the circuit, occupied the pulpit, and in the evening the Rev Themes Hackett, the successor to the Rev George Hack, preached. A collection was made at each service. MARRIAGE AT RUNCORN. —At St. Patine Wesleyan Chapel, On Thursday morning, Miss Robinson, daughter of the Rev E J Robinson, superi3tendeet minister of the Run- corn Wesleyan circuit, was married to Mr Frederick Oak Bell, of Cheltenham, the bride's father officiating. Miss Emma Louisa Bell was the brideem aid, and Mr E C Robin. son was best man. Messrs Yarwood and S-on supplied the carriages. During the af:ernoon the happy couple departed for Berwick where they intend to spend the honeymoon. FATAL ACCIDENT (TN THE WEAVER Mr H Churtone county coroner, has held an inquest on the body of Robert Leach, 40 years of age, who was accidentally killed at Dut- ton Locks, near Acton Bridge, on the river Weever. The deceased was in an empty lock, from which he ascended to assist another boatman. While he was engaged turning the handle which opens the lock, it slipped from his grasp, owing to the weight on one side of the cylinder giving way. The rapidly revolving handle struck hi 3 forehead, and killed him instantly. A verdict of "Accidental death " was returned. ROBBERY AT RAINHILL. At Widnes Police Court on Wednesday, Patrick Farrell, a labourer, was brought up in the custody of P C Palmer, charged with stealing a spade belonging to William Talbot, farmer, Rainhill. The spade was missed from the farm on the 7th July, and a few days- later the prisoner sold it Walter Heys, of the Home Farm, Rainhill, for Is 61, the prisoner stating he had -purchased it in St Helens.—The prisoner pleaded guilty, and put for-- ward that he was drunk as an extenuating circumstance. There was a long Bet of previous convictions against him, and in default of paying a fine of 203 and costs he was sent to gaol for 14 days. HARVEST FESTIVAL AT HAITON.—The annual harvest thanksgiving service in connection with Halton Parish Church took place on Thursday evening, when the Rev William :Yates, vicar of Worleston, Nantwich, preached an 1 appropriate sermon. The sacred edifice had been charm- ingly decorated for the occasion; Lady Brooke as usual 1 having reserved to herself the privilige of adorning the I chancel, which presented a beautiful aspect. Cereals. fruits, dowers, and plants had been forwarded in generous abund- ance by Sir Richard and Lady Brooke, Miss Short, and , Messrs Joseph StokeeeW Stokes, T Wright, IV Baker, J S I Jeecock, W West, Jan, J Yapp (churchwardee), T F Ac'on (churchwarden), and Beggerley. ' FIRE AT A WIDNES, FARM.—AbOIIt Midnight on Tuesday a cabman in the employ of Mr Lee, Victoria-road, wa. driving several gentlemen from Farnwor hto Widnes. On passing the Plimpton Cross Farm occuoied by Mr John Bennett, be observed flames issuing irom the shippon, and he immediately stopped the conveyance and informed the passengers. The gentlemen alighted, and bursting open the door of the building, which was of wood, discovered 1 that t ere were no cattle inside. They awoke the occupants of the farm and set about extinguishing the fi tmes, in which I endeavours they were assisted by S,rgeant McGregor and 1 several constables who had been warned by the cabman. , The Local Board fire engine could not be obtained, but a : hose and reel was despatched, but arrived too late to be of any assistance. The shippon.was almost totally destroyed, 1 - , and the damage is estimated at £5O. CHESTER AND THE SUNDAY QUESTION—The Chester Town Council on Wednesday discussed a recommendation from the Free Library Committee to open the Reading and Reference Libraries on Sunday afternoons. A telegram from the Duke of Westminister to the Council was read, stating that the libraries were now open in several of the principal towns on Sundays, and he honed Chester would 'follow the example. After a warm discussion the Council decided in favour of Sunday opening by a very large ma- jority. In addition to Mr Guest having destroyed a considerable portion of the road by aperrying operations, that gentleman had erected a wall and a wire fencing which effectually blocked the way. On Fri- day the Commissioners, through their Clerk, gave Mr guest notice to remove the obstructions and place the road in proper condition in three days. Instead of doing so, however, he still further destroyed the road, and Mr Linaker, the law-clerk, at once set about collecting evidence for an action. A plan drawn up- in 1853 was discovered, in which the road was clearly shown, and several old in- habitants made statements which confirmed the view that there had been a rood in that spot from time immernmial. It is pleasing to be able to record that an amicable solution has been arrived at. Mr Guest has undertaken to remove the obstructions at once, to place a strong fence on the edge of the (Ivry, and when he finishes operations there to fill the place up with solid material, and make a good road. PRESENTATION AT RUNCOIAN.--A presentation was mad, on Wednesday afternoon by the teachers of Bethesdee Congregational Sunday School to Mr J E Tunna, grocer, who on • that day left Runcorn for Port Hope, Ontario Canade, It was only a few days ago that Mr Latina made known his resolve of proceeding to Canada, and his friends, while hearing of his departure with sincere regret. were hopeful for his future success. The officials and teachers of the school named' above decided to mark their apprecia- tion of his long and useful connection with the institution by a suitable gift. On Wednesday Mr 'Panne wag waited upon by Mr W Handley,Mr F Beek, asd Mr F Fairhurst, and presented with a Gladstone travelling bag land a dressing cons. Oa making the presentation, Mr Fairhurst appropriately re- ferred to Mr Tonnes connection with the school and chapel since he eine to Runcorn, 13 years ago. He remarked that in every movement the church had had the active sup- port of Mr Tunna, and they regretted his loss very deeply. They trusted, however, that success awaited him in Canada. Mr Tunna, who was evidently taken by surprise, and was much moved, expressed the sorrow he felt to part with the friends with whom be had associated in Runcorn. Although he was going to Canada, he felt that he shou'd not remain away for ever, and that he should return in a few years, when he hoped to find that the ties of friendship, though severed for a time were net irrevocably broken. FRODSH.I3I WATER SUPPLY.—A special meeting of the Frodsharn Parochial Committee was held on Tuesday night, Mr A Thomas, J.P., presiding.—Mr Bancroft reported : " On the sth inst I inspected the trial well at Five Crosses with Mr Arthur Linaker and Mr Timmins. I found the well 21 feet flinches deep, and that the contractor bad been able to sink it without lining. At a depth of 15 feet a small spring was tapped ; teethe well was deepened more water was gradually met with ; it yielded on the day I inspected it 9,300 gallons in 24 hours. Mr Timmins reports this morning he has got down another foot, or 22 feat 0' inches from the surface, and that the yield is now at the- rate of 12,480 gallons-in 21 hours. . This considerable in, crease in the yield at only one foot lower depth is.very sat- isfactory, and it confirms tny opinion that by persevering in lowering the well, and by driving adits or levels, we shall ha able to obtain an ample supply of water for the district. Providing the well when sunk to the contract depth (24, ft.) does not yield 30,000 gallons per day, which is the mini- mum quantity you require, I would advise you. to. allow Mr Timmins to sink 6 feet lower and drive am edit. Fol- lowing the course of a fault which is clearly indicated in the cutting, much more water would then in all probability be obtained. Mr Timmins is in favour of sinking a bore hole. This might bs tried at no very great expense, but without the water rose very near to the bottom of the well it would necessitate pumping. By driving adits a greater collecting area is obtained, and at that level it could be conveyed into the district by gravitation."—Mr Timmias was present at the meeting, and submitted a sample of the water for inspection, and so far as the committee could judge from appearance and taste, it was very satisfactory. Mr Timmins advised a boring to be made, as 'cheaper than driving an edit, and it would test the existence of the water below the present depth of 25 feet, and the artesian force, as a standpipe and valve could then be arranged to test the yield of water from the boring apart from the well.—After some consideration, it was resolved uneniumusly that Mr Tim:nine proceed at once with a trial boring, on the terms set out in the tender submitted by him.

In answer to defendant witness said she had been prom's d half bridge fare.—The father alleged that his daughter could only earn about 7s per fort- night, and out of this there was Is per week bridge fare, and sometimes fines. He stated that Mr Mostyn was in corn- municetion with Mr Shaw on the matter. —Minnie McCuley was celled and stated she could earn Is per week. She paid full bridge fare.—Mr Mostyn said he had a room cep- able of holding 30 frames empty through apprentices absenting themselves from work.--Annie Gardener, an apprentice, and Mary Ann Stoke, her suety, was summoned under similar circumstances —The defence was that Mr Mostyn had promised to pay half the bridge fare, and had not done so, and that it was impossible for the girl to obtain 73 per week as she was promised..—Gardner said if her knife broke she had to wait an hour or two before it was mended, and if a hole was made in a piece it was always put down to carelessness whether it was so or not.--Mary Jane Whelan, an apprentice, and Patrick Whelan, her father, were summoned to answer a similar claim.—Mr Thomas said the Bench were of opinion that the aperentices understood they would only have to pay half fare over the bridge, and it was because they had to pay full fare that they absented them- selves. They were induced to sign the indentures by a pro- mise that half fare only should be charged.—Mr Burton contended that the Bench must ha guided by the written in- dentures. They could not take any verbal evidence against the indentures.—The Bench, however, dismissed all the cases.—Mr Burton asked for a case as to the reception of the evidence respecting bridge fares, and the Bench granted his application. A YQ ING RORSH STEALER AT RIM/RN-1340re Mn A Thomas and Mr James Handley at Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday Frank Allman, apparently about 14 years of age, was brought up in custody charged with stealing a black mere, value £l2, the property of Themes Bricknall, and a bridle value 4s, the property of Joseph Brown.— Thomas Bricknall, boatman, Town's End. Middlowich, said he brought his boat to Runcorn on Friday afternoon and put up his horse at Williams' stable Welsh-row. About nine o'clock next morning he sent the prisoner, who had been employed by him for about three weeks, to the stable with a feed of corn for the horse. As the prisoner did not return he went to the stable and diecovered that both boy and horse had gone. He gave information to the police.— The prisoner alleged that witness told him to take the horse on the " Old Quay Cut side" to a field to get a feed of grass. He let the mare eat as far as Warrington.—Thos Walker, ostler for Mr Williams, said he bad charge of the stables. The prisoner took Bricknall's horse away with a bridle on about ten o'clock. He said he was taking it for Mr Bricknall to look at.—P.C. Johnson, of the Warrington Police Force, deposed that he found tile prieoner in Parker- street, Bank Quay, about ten minutes pact one on Saturday. He asked him what he was doing there, and be replied that he was seeking employment. He stated that his name was Arthur Wilson and that be had come by the 8.30 train from Runcorn. He said he had not seen any mare. He was then taken into custody, and on the way to the police station he admitted that he had left the mare tied to a rail on the canal side near the iron bridge. The prisoner was handed over to P.C. Bennett —P.C. Bennett deposed to walking along the canal side in search of the prisoner and the horse. Near Walton he found the horse on the canal side, and at Walton Arches he received the prisoner into custody. When charged he said "1 knowed I'd serve him out for what he did for me." He gave his name ps James Williams, and afterwards as Frank Allmen.—Joseph Brown, boatman, Gila bert-street, Runcorn, identified the bridle as his property.— The prisoner asked the Bench to send him to a reformatary school. He had a brother in one in Newcastle, Staffordshire. —Mr Thomas said they could not send him to a- reforma- tory. He would be committed to Knutsford Sessions for trial and he must make his request there.—The prisoner caused much laughter tAr claiming a previous acquaintance, with their worships, and Mr Ashton and Mr 3etanson.

RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD. The monthly meeting was held on Wednesday. Ms P Briscoe presided, and there were also present Messrs Nor- man, Coleburn, Moss, Whittaker. Rogerson, and Saflteld (secretary).—The Secretary reported that during the five months ended August 25th there had been 149 interments, against 135 in the corresponding period of last year. The fees received for the same period amounted to les 33 31, representing an increase of £135 2s 81.-1 r Mess moved the confirmation of the minutes of the Finance Committee, which reconimended payment of accouna amounting, to £6l So 3d. It was argued that people cannot very well get into a righteous passion in connection with an event that may or may not happen two months later. div.p: r his friends for smite days WY grave anxiety was aroused. Ths assistance of the police was sought, and after prolonged search the Lord Mayor of Dublin was discovered on bed with nothing on but his chain of office. Rortly by compul- sion and partly from necessity he had ported with every- thing else. But the sacred cham of office he clung to to the last.

I went to the Tepper giv,es Lvt the Prince's Theatre on Tuesday night, to celebrate the 100th representation of "Called Back." This run is a triumph, the more remark— -- able just now when thCre is scarcely a theatre in London that has paid its expenses of the season. The triumph is due simply to intrinsic merit, "Called Back " being one of most striking melodramas placed on the English stage with- in recent memory. Supper was served under a tent on the stage and must have formed a very pretty and animated scene, looked down upon from boxes and gdleries. There . were one or two speeches in which manager and company felicitated each other upon their succeestie and were heartily applauded by their brother acttrs and actresses. With a very few exceptions the company was entirely composed of members of the profession. With-alcnowledge of this fact, I was much struck by the way in which speeches !aped into recitation. One would imagine thetetc,tes and actresses had enough of elocution and acting on the stage. But it would be difficult to find anywhere an audiesce that hung more breathlessly on Mr Fernanelkees recitation of "the lifeboat." I sat opposite a well-known actress who was worked up into a state of intense excitement ae the accom- plished reciter unfolded the simple story of MA verse. She listened as a little child might hear resreemoving and tender tale. Her bosom heaved, her fingers nervously clutched the table cloth, her eyes filled with-teare, and, when the happy denouement came she heaved i sigh of relief. coarse this may have been acting. leolt was exeeediligf; t , well done. But the lady had no one to play to, for everyone else (with the exception of a furtive observer), waoequally absorbed in the recitation. Other recitations followed, and it was four o'clock in the morning before- the company be- gan to break up. But what a simple and unexpected way ,of spending an occasional festival! Mincy a nuraber of 'literary men meeting to celebrate sap the tenth edition of 1 la.poptalar work, and by way of amusement reading to each Other portions of leading articles, or bits from their miscel- laneous writings.

ILLNESS OF CARDINAL MANNING.
VISIT TO WARRINGTON PCIrSTPONED.

The meeting which was to be held in the Drill Hall, War- 'iington, on Wednesday evening, in support of the temperance cause has, unfortnnately, had to be poatponed owing to a sudden illness of Cardinal Manning, who. was to, he the chief speaker. His Eminence concluded his brief etay,at Chester on Monday morning, when he left by the ten ,o'clock train to pay a visit to St. Bede' College, Manchester, The Cardinal, accompanied by the c'ergy of St. Werburghle.. Church, in- spected the Roman Catholic schools, Qeteenetreet, shortly before proceeding to Manchester. The appearance in War- rington of his Eminence, wile is one ,of the- mast distin- ,guished, if not the most distiegniebed, of the active advocates of temperance,, in., this country, was being looked forwetel to with, great interest, as was evideaced by the velv large sale. of tickets, and the sadden and unexpected announcement of his inability to Wend was conseqteently eeceived, with propor- tionate disappointment. , Contidetalehe preparations had been made to.suitably welconas the distinguished visitor. The Drill Hell, in which the meeting nes .te he held, had been hung with mottoes and in other ways. band9omelr decorated be Sergeant O'Brien; and arrangements had also been made fur a procession frdm the Inagua thil In 8.-twasy- street. Lit these arrangements were of • course rendered futile by the enforced elesertee a the Cardinal, as imme- diately upon the receipt of the information that he could not attecat placards were Asseed postppning the meeting sine 4ie. NOTES BY THE WAY. At Scarborough, on Saturday, the Australians finished off their match against I Zingari in most brilliant style, and gained an easy victory by eight wickets. The second in- nings of the English team, in which three of the best wickets bad fallen overnight for 45, was completed for 100, Spofforth again bowling with great effect. The match ended in a victory for the Australians by eight wickets. Score :—Aueralians, 233 and 137; I Zingari, 229 and 140. —Owing to rain on Saturday there was again no play at Kennington Oval, and consequently, after waiting about until two in the afternoon, the captains agreed to draw stumps and abandon the match. The final scores overnight were : Surrey, lot innings, 110; second innings, 11 for no wicket ; Yorkshire, first innings, 134. Many of the Glasgow ironrnasters have intimated that they intend to limit production unless the landlords agree to reduce royalties and the railway companies establish lower rates. It is stated that the business is carried oa at a loss, and that this cannot be wholly taken out of

wages. THE ST. LEGER.—The St Leger was run on Wednesday at Doncaster, and it resulted in the victory of Mr R C Vyner's The Lambkin, the Duke of Westminster's Sandi- way being second, a length behind; M. R Peck's Superba was third. The winner's time was three minutes fourteen seconds. DEATH OF A CHESHIRE COUNTY MAGISTRATE.—A Ches- ter correspondent announces the death at Trafford Lodge, near Chester, of Mr. Thomas Hogging, J.P., who fer a num- ber of years has taken an active part in the business of the Chester Castle petty sessional division. Mr. Hoggins, who was a Conservative in polities, had been ailing for some time. A Thu SUN% EY COLLISION : TWO MEN DROWNED.— A serious fatal Casualty occurred on Thursday morning off Shields Harbour. It appears that during foggy weather the screw steamer New I'elton of and from London was com- ing to the Tyne, and when off the bar she came in collision with the steam tug Belmont, of Newcastle. The tug was sunk, and the chief engineer and fourth hand were drowned. The rest of the crew were brought to the Tyne by the New Pet ton. THE SHAM CLERGYMAN AT BIENINGIIAM.—George Robert Lee, who described himself an an LL.D, and is alleged to be a clerical imposter, was brought up at the Birmingham Police Court, on Tuesday, on a charge of swindling trades- men out of goods by representing himself as a clergyman entrusted by the Bishop of Worcester with an evangelic mission. The police said they were informed that the prisoner had tried the same dodge on in Newcastle, Shef- field, London, ond other places. He was remanded in cus- ody. THE LATE Ma JOSEPH LIVESEY.—The following reso- lution has been passed by the executive committee of the Church of England Temperance Society (Manchester Dio- cese) :—" That this executive desires to place on record its appreciation of the great service rendered to the cause of temperance by the late Mr Joseph Livesey during his long and useful life ; and expresses to his surviving relatives its sorrow for the loss they have sustained by the removal of one so devoted and unselfish in his promotion of all social improvements." REDUCTION OF LICENSED HOUSES.—The Bradford ma- gistrates, at the adjourned brewster sessions, on Wednesday, followed up their recent action of materially reducing the number of Douses by refusing to renew twenty licensss to sell off the premises only, on the ground that there was no longer a necessity for them. It is expected that at another adjourned meeting there will be still further reductions in the number of persons engaged in the liquor trade. The town clerk, acting upon the instructions of the Council, on Wednesday, supported the objections to the renewals. STARVING A CHILD TO DEATII.-olle Of the most pain- ful stories ever recorded was told at an inquest held at Wal- ton, Essex, on Wednesday. The deceased, a child two years and nine months old, was proved to have been absolutely starved to death, and the doctors examined said its body did not weigh as much as that of a newly-born infant. The father, seemingly a widower. was a German baker named Dumas. He was of very dissipated habits—" scarcely ever sober." He lost another girl nine months ago, and was then warned by a surgeon who had been called in that if "any- thing happened" to the then two remaining children he would be criminally responsible. The child still surviving was described as having the. appearance of a heap of bones. Dumas was now committed for trial on the charge of murder.
