THE EAELESTOWS R&M:ELEM.—The Earlestown Ramblers plated their opening game of football, on Satur- day, in very we weather. Sides were chosen, but owing to the rain play was confined to half an hour. The players afterwards sat down to an excellent tea at the Cocoa-rooms, Legh-street, the rest of the evening being spent in a pleasant manner. A selecticn of songs was gone through by the members.

--- -- WESLEYAN SUNDLY SCHOOL TEACHERS MEETING.-- The quarterly meeting of the leachers and officers of the E erlestown Wesleyan Methodist Sunday School was held in the Lecture Hall of the school on Tuesday evening, when the Rev J M Fairbourne presided, and there was a good attendance. The attendances of the teachers and officers were brought before the meeting and tirLfly cammented upon, and several ministers were selectGd to be communi- cated with as the preacher of the anniversary services in May next. The subsequent business included the selection of sp3akers for the annual tea party on New Year's Day, and the appointment of a committee to arrange the gather- ing. A discussion followed on the general working of the school. _

GOOD TEMPLARS' ENTERTLINMENT.—At the weeny ' meeting of the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Tern- piers on Monday evening Bro George E Warburton- P W.C.T, presided. After the lodge business had been tran-1 stcted, an "open meeting" WAS held, when a goodly number , of friends attended. The chair was occupied by Bro George Clarke, D.M. Recitations were given by Bro George E tVarbarton, Sister M Clarke; readings by Bros .7 Barnard, E Newman, and the Chairman, songs by Bro W Kenning and Sister Whitty, and a duet by Sisters E and J Clarke. Mr B Tripp gave three violin solos in splendid style, and he was accorded a hearty vote of thanks on the moticn of Bro W Aitken, seconded by Bro Wallin, ton. A very pleasant even- ing was spent. RECM,BITE3 AT NEWTON —On Saturday about 200 members of the Independent Order of Rech Mites, Liverpool district, No. 5, paid a visit to Newton. A procession had been arranged, but in consequence of the inclement state of the weather it had to be abandoned, and the Congregational school-loom, Newton, which bad been placed at their dis- posal by the Rev J Allatt, was used. About 150 persons journeyed by rail from Liverpool, and the remainder, accom- panied by a band, were conveyed from St. Helens in wag- gonettes. Tea was provided in the schcol-room by Mrs , Jackson, of Earlestown. A public meeting WAS afterwards held, whe3 addresses on " Ittchabitism " were delivered by Bro. Zechariah Callow, 0.V., and others. The party left Earlestown about 8.30 p.m. PROPOSED PARR FOR EARLESTOWN.—For some time past tbe encroachments upon public land have formed a topic of conversation among the inhabitants of Eirlestown and Newton. The question, so far as it affects Newton Common, has been frequently discussed and commented upon, but a new suggestion to settle the mater has been made. A correspondent states that if Mr Legh (the Lord of the Manor) would allow a portion of the Common—between the highway to St. Helens and the bottom end of Eerie- street up to and including the Dingle—to be utilised as a public park, he would subscribe £lOO towards the expense 0. patting it in order. There cm be no doubt the spot in question could be made into a very attractive park if suffi- dent funds were forthcoming to carryout the work. As yet, however, no definite arrangements for carrying the sugges- tion into effect has been made. _

EARLESTOWN TONTINE SOCIETY. —The annual dinner to the members of this society took place on Saturday even- ing at the Griffin Hotel, Earlestown. About 60 members sat down to an excdlent repast, supplied by Mr James Lythgoe.—After dinner the chair was taken by Mr. James Gilman and the vice-chair was occupied by Mr. J. Muscroft. The secretary, Mr J Audley, read the year's report and statement of accounts, which showed that the financial position of the s'eciety was most prosperous and en- couraging. He believed that was due to the officers and members working mutually together. There were 79 mem- bers on the books, there having been 18 new ones during the year. The receipts had been £97 63 41., and there was a balance of £64 183 Id to be divided amongst the mem- bers, in addition to which was an amount carried to the re- serve fund. The usual loyal toasts were afterwards duly honoured, the proceedings being interspersed with a capital selection of songs by Messrs P Hastie, J Williams. J Lewis, E Smith, D Harrison, J Sharpe, G Jackson, and J Muscroft ; and Rand J Green gave a capital duet entitled "The Yankee Boy." The proceedings concluded with the sing- ing of the National Anthem.

DISCUSSIONS AT THE EABLESTOWN LIBERAL CLUB An additional attraction to the members of the Earlestown and District Liberal Club will be found in the weekly dis- cussion classes which hive been started in connection with the club. The discussions ought to prove of considerable ri interest and advantage to the frequenters of the club, and it,' is to be hoped that the venture will prove a success. The first of the meetings was held in one of the rooms on Wed- I nesday, and was of a very encouraging character. About 15 members were present, an .l Mr M Birkhead presided.—ln commencing the proceedings, the Chairman remarked that I he was glad these discussion classes had been started, and he hoped they would be continued, and prove of great 1, benefit to the club and those connected with it. He hoped 1 the discussions would be a success in every respect.—Mr • C A Luffman then read an excellent paper on "The House of Lords—what shall be done with it ?" He gave a care- fully prepared review of the House of Lords and its pro-li ceedings, and, while maintaining that It could be dispensed; with, he expressed the opinion that the country was I , scarcely ripe for that at the present time; but the House of Lords was greatly in need of reform. In the discussion which ensued, Messrs Birkhead, T Howard, W McEvoy, I John Davis, and Younger took part.—At the close a cordial vote of thanks was passed to Mr Luffman for his excellent paper. A similar cempliment WAS also paid to the chair- man. It is understood that next Wednesday Mr Birkhead , will read a paper on the reform of the House of Lords. FOOTBALL.—EABLESTOWN v. HAYDOCIL TEMPERANCE. —The meeting of the Earlestown and Haydock Temperance ,Football teams at Haydock on Sa•urday afternoon was an "Teat interest in local football circles. For three eietileleam; th had not met iu a contest. Owing to e tereaonr:t o 4 s le;del feeling Which Wee known to exist between them It was deemed advisable th et the twi club should not be brought together. However, during the last few months correspondence has passed between them, and as both sides appeared anxious to be on the best terms a match between the players was arranged. Unfortunately the weather on Saturday turned out very unfasourable, rain falling heavily throughout the aft,rnoon. Notwithstanding this drawback, however, there was a large attendance of spectators, many of whom were from Earlestown. The match was played on I I the new ground of the Temperance club, behind the Wagon and Horses Hotel. The Earlestown team were short of the services of R Green, F Emmett, A Dagnall, J Simm, and T Champion, but excellent substitutes were found : while the Haydock eleven also lacked the services of two fist team men. The Haydock captain won the toss and chose to play with the ground, wind, and rain in his favour. The visitors accordingly kicked off and at once assumed the aggressive. For a few minutes they severely pressed their opponents and Williams ultimately kicked a goal. The play was of a fast and exciting character, but at half-time the score re- mained unaltered. After the change of ends the backs for both teams played excellently and the attacks on each goal were repulsed. After about twenty &mites play Cameron from a corner kick landed the leather in front of the Hay- dock posts and the goal-keeper put the leather through, thus !scoring a second goal for Earlestown. The home team then I made a determined effort to scare, and in the course of a scrimmage in front of the Earlestown uprights Duxbury kicked the leather against one of the posts and it rolled through. As no other score was made the match resulted in a victory for Earlestown by two goals to one. Teams— Earlestown J Gray, goal; J Whalley (Capt.) and W Rich, , backs • R Bowker, Duxbury, and 11 Whalley, half-backs; I H Holcroft and S Williams, right wing; J Ellison, centre ; J Cameron and J Appleton. left wing. Haydock Temper- ance: J Green, goal; T Hatton and A Picton, becks; T Plant, J Baines, and J Carter, half-backs; J Blackey and T Alley, right wing; J Picton, centre; P Twist and J Harri- son, left wing. ALTERATIONS AT TILE NINE ARCIIES.—rne Lonnon and North-Western -Railway Company are at present engaged in carrying out extensive alterations and repairs at what are known as the "Nine Arches," Earlestown. The name is not inaptly applied to the nine monstre and tower- ing arches which span the valley containing the Sankey canal and Sankey brook, near the Viaduct Waggon Works. Being on the main line of the London and North-Western railway between Manchester and Liverpool, some hundreds of trains, including the quickest service of expresses in the kingdom, pass daily over the arches, and it will thus be seen that the company have a great responsibility as far as the safety of passengers is concerned. They have therefore for some weeks been gradually taking steps to render the arches, which were erected some 50 years ago, more secure and safe. Owing to the rapidity with which the trains pass along the lines, however, the alterations have to be carried out with much inconvenience and personal danger to the ,1 workmen employed on the job. The principal pert of the work was begun on Sunday last, when some two or three hundred men were engaged in taking up the old iron girders and placing new ones in their places. It was absolutely im- possible to do this without taking up both the up and down lines; and as this is out of all question on week days, por- tions of the lines will be taken up on succeeding Sundays until the whole work has been completed. As a consequence the traffic will be carried on, as was the case last Sunday, under singular circumstances. On Sunday, the neighbour- hood of the Nine Arches had a very busy appearance. To the passengers along the lines, unacquainted with the cir- cumstances, their experiences at the spot in question were of a novel character. As trains approached the arches fog signals were passed over, the engine whistle was sounded, men were hurrying backwards and forwards with red and green flags, while Just as the engine appeared about to pass on to the arches it stopped altogether, and soon men came up shouting "All change." The passengers bore puzzled looks, while alarm and fear were depicted on more than a few. As the parties alighted from the carriage monstre gangs of men were seen at work upon the arche4. Roil way inspectors and other officials were running about in all directions; and the passengers were asked to walk along a narrow " gangway " of three planks for a distance of about 40 or 50 yards. To prevent the people from slipping, "navvies" stood on each side, about two yards apart, hold- ing a rope some three feet above the level of the planks. On getting over the arches the passengers found another train awaiting them, and this they entered and were conveyed to their destinations. Some weeks will elapse before the work Is completed; but when it is done passengers along that line will feel that the company have but done a duty to their patrons in carrying out so important and necessary an alteration.

PEOGRESS OF TIM NEW CENETERY.—The work of completing the new cemetery for Earlestown and Newton is being proceeded with as rapidly as possible; but a con- siderable time will of necessity elapse before the grounds will ha ready for interments. The site of the cemetery ap- pears to give a greater public satisfaction than it did when it was first moOted. Situated in Park-road it seems to be a central spot for Earlestown, Newton, Wargrave, and the Vulcan. The ground itself is approached from the highway by a straight carriage drive; and the chapel is being built almost in the centre of the ground, which has been walled in. A delay, however, has arisen in connection with the erection of the chapel; the men en- gaged thereon being at present in want of terracotta bricks from Wales. In the meantime the roads are being procee- ded with and the boundary walls are being completed. The entrance lodge will soon be ready for occupation, and, it is stated, an occupier will not 'oe wanted one moment too soon. On Sundays a goodly number of persons visit the cemetery, and some wilful damage and trespass have been committed. The planting of trees, flowers, will not be commenced for some time. Mr Rothwell, of St Helens, secured the con- tract for the work; his charges amounting to about £2,400; ' while Mr Willam Cunliffe, of Leigh, is doing the draining ' and formation of the roads, at a cost of about £330.
NEWTON Of:LURCH. GIFT OF A. NEW BELL.

Mr. T. J. Gillespie, J.P., of Newton, has recently bestowed a kind and generous gift upon the parishioners of St. Peter's Church, Newton, in the shape of a inagnificent ball, which has been placed in the newly-erected belfry of the church. For many months past the church has been undergoing repairs, which included the pulling dowm of the old belfry—a structure acknowledged to be in an unsafe condition—the pointing and otherwise improving the appearance of the edifice. This work having approached completion, Mr. Gillespie intimated to the authorities of the church his willingness to present a new bell, and the offer was thankfully accepted. A new Loll was very much needed for the Parish Church, and the generous disposition of Mr. Gillespie having been manifested when help and assistance were greatly required, he has by his kindness sown himself to be a true friend in time of need. In effect his instructions to the church officers were that they could secure the very best and most serviceable bell regardless of expense, and a few weeks ago one was selected at the works of the eminent makers, Messrs. Bussell, of Liverpool. The bell is made of the beet gun-metal and silver, and weighs about 7i cwt.; while its cost was over £7O. It was placed in the belfry of the church about a fortnight ago, and its first public trial took place on Sunday week. Its tone was found to be very fine and splendid ; but unfortunately it was attend( d with a kind of " jarrine sound. This was found to arise from the fact that the boll had been affixed to a steel cross-piece. In order to remedy the unpleasant noise the bell will have to be taken dawn, and a cross-piece of wood placed in the belfry in place of the steel one. Tnis will be done as early as possible. Since the unsatisfactory trial of the bell it has not been rung. The bell, it should be stated, bears an inscription, stating that it was presented by Mr. Gillespie.

Surveyor should inspect the brook and report to a future meeting. RECEIPTS AND EXPENDITURE.—The Clerk stated that at the last meeting he was instructed to prepare a return of the receipts and expenditure during the year. The receipts amounted to £1,261, and the expenditure was as follows : Sorters £133, water supplies £ll7, dust removal and other sanitary work £l3l, loans, principal and interest repaid, £387, salaries, otc, £430, other establishment ch trges £65. HEALTH OF THE DISTRICT.—The Medical Officer (Dr E F Hall) reported for the month of August that the health of the district had been remarkably good. Since the ladt meeting there had been only two cases at all requiring his interference having occurred, namely, onset English cholera and one of typhoid fever, in neither of which could he find anything specific. The usual pre- cautions were taken. He thought it would be desirable that a sample should he sent to Dr , C Brown for analysis from the well that supplied the cottages at Mersey View, Halewood. It was in close proxi- mity to the midden ashpits attached (o the cottages, which were not roofed over, and were nearly always more or less wet and offensive.—The Chairman expressed the opinion that the medical officer's report was very satisfactory.—Mr Meadows : It is very satisfactory to hear that the health of the district is so good.

SURVEYOR'S REPORT. Mr Twist (surveyor), in his monthly report stated that several nuisances and unsatis- factory sanitary arrangements had been remedied. As di- rected he had inspected the brook from Whiston to Tarbock, and found that all the collieries in the district contributed to its discolouration. Upon the day of his visit there did not appear to be sufficient from any of them, or all combined, to produce the appearance at Tarbock Hall, but he was told the quality varied very much, and the day of his inspection must have been one of very favourable ones. The effluent water from the Prescot sewage farm appeared colourless, but from its outlet into the brook to the Carr' s pumping station there were unmistakeable signs of sewage; below that, however, owing to the water from the colliery being mixed with it, they were not so apparent. This was the principal business.

div.head: ASHTON.
div.p: ASHTON.

ASSAULT ON A SWING PEoPRIETort.—At the Wigan County Police Court, on Friday. James Parkinson was charged with assaulting and beating James Crook, a swing proprietor, at Ashton, on the 30th ult.—lt was stated that the defendant went to the complainant's place about 9-30 at night and asked for a swing. After he had been served he said to Crook I'll punch your neck out," and when he got out of the car he got hold of complainant, threw him on the ground, and kicked him.—Defendant was fined lOs and costs. _ .

BEATING A Boy.—Wm. Long was summoned at the Wigan County Police Court, on Friday, for having beaten a boy named John Warren, son of Mr. Warren farmer, Ashton, on the 27th ult.—Mr. Ackerley prosecuted—lt ap- pears that Mr. Warren has been troubled very much with jowls goinz into his fields, and he gave instructions to his son to send away any hens he might see on his father's land. Last Wednesday the boy saw a duck on the field and he ran to get it off. The defendant came up while he was driving the fowl away, and said he would break the lad's ribs if he would not let it alone, and began to kick him.—The Bench said the defendant had committed a very unprovoked as- sault upon the boy. Long had no business to interfere for the lad was only doing his duty. Defendant was fined 20s and costs.

THE ALLEGED THEFT OF A WATCH. At the Wigan County Police Court, on Monday, before Mr J C Eckersley, Francis Weldon was brought up, on remand, c'iarged with stealing on the 26th tilt, a silver watch from the person of Peter Unsworth, landlord of the Bay Horse Inn, Warring- ton-road, Ashton.—Peter Unsworth said the watch produced was his property. It was a silver lever watch, and was worth £6 10s. About two o'clock in the afternoon of the 26± ult he had the watch in his pocket, attached to a chain At that time he went into the taproom and fern asleep. There was no person in the room except.himself. He awoke a little after three o'clock, and found his albert hanging out of his pocket and the watch gone. He gave information to Sergeant Savage, and he and the latter went in a trap to Newton. Prisoner was seen coming out of the Oak Tree, Newton, and when searched the watch produced was found upon him.—Elizabeth Marriott, servant at the house of the prosecutor, said she saw the prisoner come into the Bay Horse about three o'clock end go into the taproom. He called fora pint of beer and took a seat close to Mr tins- worth's feet. She noticed that Mr Unsworth's watch chain was is its proper position. She left the room, leaving prosecutor and the prisoner together, and did not see the latter le we the hot.se.— Sergeant Savage stationed at Ash- ton, said he went with prosecutor to Newton on the 26th tilt, and apprehended the prisoner at ten minutes past four in Crew-lane, going towards Earlestown. He searched him in the presence of the prosecutor, and found the watch pro- duced in the watch pocket of his veet. He charged Lim with stealing the watch from the person of Peter Unswortb, and he replied, 'Guilty."—Prisoner, in answer to the usual challenge, said, "I am guilty of the charge, but at the time I was under the influence of drink." He was committed to to the next assizes for trial.
PRESCOT. PRESCOT RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

A meeting of the Prescot Rural Sanitary Authority was 1) held at the Workhouse, Whiston, on Thursday forenoon, when there were present: Messrs J Leatherbarrow (in the chair), eV A Meadows, T Syder, W Gilbody, and S FL Hartley (clerk.)—The minutes of the last meeting were read and confirmed. MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT,—The Local Government Board wrote asking for certain information upon points men- tioned in the annual report of the Medical Officer of Health, and the Clerk was instructed to consult with the Medical Officer and forward a reply. THE ECCLESTON SEWERAGE SCHEME.—With reference to the proposed sewerage scheme for the township of Eccleston the LOC.II Government Board asked the Rural Sanitary Authority to pass a resolution applying for sanction to bor- row the money required for carrying out such works of sewerage as they had determined to execute, and forward a copy of such resolution to the Board together with plans and detailed estimate of the conteniplated works with infor- mation as te the assessable value and existing debt of the Rural Sanitary district—The Clerk stated that it was neces- sary for the Board to pass a formal resolution in accordance' with the request of the Local Government Board.—A resolu- tion to that effect was passed, and the surveyor (Mr Twist) was ordered to prepare the necessary plans, atm WHISTON WATER RENTS.—The Local Government , Board wrote calling attention to a previous communication I with reference to the remark,* made by Mr Hazlehurst re- specting his audit of the accounts of Mr Barrow, water rent collector for the township of Whiston, and stating that they wished for a reply to a communication. The report of flee auditor was as follows :—Whiston Water Rents : The collection of these rents still remain in the same unsatisfac- tory condition, and I am of opinion it is extremely desirable that the Rural Sanitary Authority should take steps for pro- viding the township of Whiston with a satisfactory water supply. From the statements made to me, I gathered at the audit that the Rural Sanitary Authority are under an agreement with the Rainhill Water Company to take a supply of water from them in bulk for distribution, and which agreement the Rural Sanitary Authority are anxious to determine, owing to the water being objectionable to the inhabitants, many of whom refuse to use it on account of its hardness, and hence the loss which annually occurs to the township, the consumption not being equal to the mini- mum which the Rural Sanitary Authority are under agree- ment to take from the Water Committee, and which I am informed the Rural Sanitary Authority have endeavoured to set aside on more than one occasion.—lt was decided to leave the matter in the hands of the chairman and the clerk. ALLEGED POLLUTION OF A BROOIC.—The Local Govern- ment Board wrote forwarding copy of. a letter from the Widnes Local Board relative to a complaint of the pollution of a water course by sewage from the Rainhill sewage farm, and inquiring whether the tanks and other works of sewage disposal at Rainhill included in the estimates for which the loan of £4,000 was sanctioned in 167 d bad been carried out. The letter from the Widnes Local Board was as follows : " Widnes Local Board, 21st August, 1854.—Rainhill sewage farm.—Sir,—l beg to acknowledge yours of the 18th inst. As the statements made by the Rural Sanitary Authority of Prescot Union are so directly opposed to those made by I this Authority, I am instructed by the chairman of the Health Committee of this Board to repeat the request made ,by this B.)ard on the 9th July, viz., that your eßoard should send down an inspector to examine, I take evidence, and report. If this course is 'taken I the matter will be very easily settled at a I very slight cost, it would also prove to your Board the value of the statements made by both the local authorities concerned. TO-day the field has been again inspected, and I send samples without comment.—l am, yours, J T ALLEN, clerk."—The Clerk stated that the only course for that Authority was to ask their surveyor to inspect the brook and report upon it. He noticed from the Liverpool papers I that the Widnes Local Board were ,pressing for an inquiry I Into the matter, but their report was that there was no pol- lution. To obtain the samples of water some one must have done it without the authority of that Authority. They had no evidence at all that the samples sent to the Local Government Board had come from the Rainhill sewage farm—for what they knew it might have come from some of the Widnes sewers.—Mr Gilbody remarked if the samples had been taken jointly they might have acknowledged them, but under the circumstances they had no knowledge of a nuisance existing at all.—A motion was passed that the

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
WIDNES FOOTBALL CLUB.

A general meeting of the members of this club was held on Monday night, in the large room of Tilley's Norton Arms. Mr J Burgess was voted to the chair, and there were present Messrs W Ireland, A Brown. T Higley, 8 H Ken- rick, J J Lathan], J Briggs. T Laws, H Stirrup, R Rogerson, J H Smith, P Corns, E Farrell, R Johnson, A Hutton, J Wright, T Ridyard, E M Davies, H Cookson —The Chair- man, referring to the last meeting, said the proceeds of the charity match had been emeended in purchasing a couch and two or three pictures, which appear to have given great satisfaction to Miss Downie, the matron. The majority of the vice-presidents that were elected had accepted the posi- tion, but in addition the committee had elected Mr Leonard Pilkington, Sir R A Cros's, M.P., Colonel Ireland Black- burne, M.P.—(applause)—and these gentlemen had con- sented to stand. Mr J B Briggs was elected captain of the club, but he had since then taken unto himself a wife and could not come. (Laughter.) The committee bad therefore elected Mr John Briggs, the county cricketer, as captain— (applause)—and he trusted they would be able to command his services during the season. (Hear, bear.) During the last month or two the question of the amalgamation of the Cricket, Athletic, and Football Clubs had again been under consideration and there had been several meetings of dele- gates from the various clubs. The Football Club and the Cricket Club had come to something like a definite arrange- ment, which would enable the Football Club to rent a new field which the Cricket Club were about to obtain. He had an agreement in his hand, which required some alteration, and be did not think it would b 3 right to read it. He thought, howeve-, they would come to terms. The cricket club appeared to be a little hard upon them in one or two clauses. If the money could be raised to gat the field and put it in proper order for football, athletic sports, cricket, lacrosse, and lawn tennis, the question would be settled. Referring to the coming season the Chairman said the list of matches arranged was the best the club had ever had—(hear, hear) —and he paid a compliment to Mr Brown, the secretary, on his successful labours.—The Secretary read a list of the matches, from which it appeared matches had bean arranged with Oldham, Salford, Tottineton, Walton Barrow, Akan, Royton, and other good club-s.—The Chairman observed that they were likely to have to board the field round at the expense of the club, and they would want as many volun- teers as possible to erect the fence. (Hear, hear.) They would also want funds, and he appealed for subscriptions to be paid early.—Mr W Rogerson said suppose they could not COM to a favourable arrangement with the cricket club, how would the football club be then placed with regard to a field ?—The Chairman said they had got one in view. But he had no fear of the negotiations falling through.— The Secretary proposed that the resolution passed at the last meeting with reference to the sash be rescinded, but he was ruled out of order.—Mr Kenrick moved, and Mr Hut- ton seconded a resolution that a meeting be called to con- sider the question of the costume.—Mr Latham proposed, and Mr Farrell seconded, a direct amendment.—The origi- nal resolution was carried by 20 votes to I7.—A vote of thanks to the secretary and chairman concluded the meet- ing.

div.head: FASHIONABLE MARRIMIE AT FAUN WORTH.
div.p: FASHIONABLE MARRIMIE AT FAUN WORTH.

A marriage in which great interest was evinced was solemnised at St. Luke's Parish Church, Farnworth, on Tuesday morning. The contracting parties were the Rev. D. J. Llewellyn, formerly curate at Holy Trinity Church, Runcorn, and now incumbent of Maesteg Bridge End, Glamorganshire, and Miss Kershaw, eldest daughter of Mr. W. H. Kershaw, of Bryn Felin, Farnworth Mr. Kershaw, the bride's father, is a builder carrying on an exteneive business in Widnes, and was formerly a prominent member of the Local Board. The ancient fane was well filled with a congregation composed principally of the fair sex, and as the decorations for the harvest festival still adorned the chancel and other parts of the edifice, the scene was most bright and attractive when the wedding party took up their positions. The party consisted of Mr and Mrs Kershaw, Mr \V Kershaw, Mr James Kershaw, Mr and Mrs J W Carlile, Mr and Mrs R Lewis, Mr and Mrs Pritchard, Mrs Syred, Mr and Mrs Leith, Mrs and the Misses Bennett, Mrs Newell, Miss Hampson, Mr Corner, and Mr Ridmayne. The bride wore a dress of cream coloured cashmere, with an orange wreath and veil, and she was adorned with a beautiful diamond brooch, the gift of her father, while clasping the folds of her dress was a gold brooch, the gift of the bridegroom. The brides- maids, Miss Pritchard and Miss Newall, were attired in wile blue cashmere dresses, trimmed with white satin, and wore white straw hats trimmed with crenn coloured satin. Miss Pritchard were a gold locket, a present from tb.e bride's father, and a brooch from the bridegroom, while Miss Newell was wearing a gold beacelet and a brooch the gift of Mr Kershaw and the bridegroom respectively. The ceremony was performed by the Bev G Bond, vicar, assisted by the Rev W Preston, of Holy Trinity, Runcorn. The Rev R Edwards, curate in charge of Newtown Mission, Runcorn, was the best man, and Mr J Kershaw was the groomsman. As the party left the chancel, Mendelssohn's Wedding March was played onthe organ, and the bells sent forth a merry peal. At the door of the church the villagers and friends were assembled to greet the happy pair, and a number of girls from the seminary of Mrs Syred strewed flowers in their path. The party then drove to Mr Kershaw's residence, where breakfast was laid for 32 guests. In addi- tion to the ladies and gentlemen already mentioned, there were present Mr and Mrs S Sadler,Mr and Mrs F H Pankhurst, r Miss Hampson, and Mrs Bend.—The toast of the bride and bridegroom was proposed by Mr Carlile, and responded to by Mr Llewellyn, who gave the health of the bridesmaids coupled with the name of the Rev R Edwards, who respon- ded. "The Clergy" was propos3d by Mr R Lewis, and responded to by the Rev G Bond and the Rev W Preston. Daring the afternoon Mr and Mrs Llewellyn left for South Wales. Annexed is a list of the present :—Gold watch and chain, Mr W H Kershaw; diamond brooch, Mr W H Ker- shaw; locket, the Bridegroom; gold brooch, Miss M Hemp- son ; desert spoons and carvers. Master W Kershaw; majolica jar, Miss baby Kershaw; dinner cruet stand. crown Derby, Mr J W Carlile ; table tea kettle, Mrs J W Carlile; two engravings, Mr and Mrs James White; silver biscuit box and toast rack, Mr and Mrs F H Pankhurst ; silver fish knives and forks, Mr J T Allen; paragraph Bible bound in morocco, Rev R Edwards; Japanned table in crewel work, Mr and Mrs S Sadler ; silver batter knife, Master J H Bennett; sauce ladles, Mr J Kershaw ; salopian vases, Mr Richard Lewis ; two handsome china vases, Mr S Sadler; desert silver knives and forks, Mr Gogg ; silver tea kettle, Mrs Greenfield; tea pot and coffee pot, Mr J Kershaw; biscuit box, Mr and Mrs A G Kyle; oak and silver butter cooler and antemacasser, Mrs ii Syred ; purse, Mr T Redmayne ; silver salt cellars, Miss Pritchard ; silver butter dish, Mr and Mrs C Taylor ; silver preserve spoons, Mr George Stead; silver fish knife and fork in case, Mr and Mrs Leith ; silver butter knife, Miss Knight ; silver pickle fork, Master Jamas Kershaw ; salt spoons, Miss H Burgess; mats and hearthrug, Miss Bennett ; book of music, Mrs John. Davies ; water jug, Mrs William Gerrard ; ornaments, Mrs Ford; ornaments, Mrs Hindley ; dessert service, Mr and Mrs Deakin ; brackets, Miss M Bennett ; wall bracket, Mrs J W Davies; crayon drawing, Miss L Jones ; hand-painted flowers, Miss Katie Walter; crystal flower stands, Mr and Mrs W Copland ; egg stand, Mr T Webster; marmalade dish, Mr Grayston ; butter cooler, Mrs Bennett ; a dozen forks, Mrs Roberts ; dozen dessert spoons, Mr H Corner ; dozen teaspoons, Miss Newell ; dozen small forks and large spoons and four table spoons, Mr and Mrs Newell ; album, Mr and Mrs D Forster; bride's bouquet, Miss M Forster ; pair flower brackets, Miss M Stead; papier mache trays, Mr and Mrs Williams ; pictures, Mr T Ben- nett; five o'clock tea service, Mr and Mrs W S Pritchard ; two crayon drawings, Miss Pritchard ; two macraime brackets, Miss Thompson ; lace curtains, Mrs Hy Lee.

div.p: FATAL MISADVENTURE.—On Tuesday evening Mrs Char- lotte Mannington, of Little Melton, Sussex, was shot dead by one of her sons, a young man of 22. The latter, a Rifle Volunteer, was, according to the evidence given at the in- quest by a younger brother, " joking " with his gun while under the influence of liquor, and the jury found that the fatal occurrence was the result of misadventure.

TERRIBLE RAILWAY ACCIDENT AT BOWDON.—A 'youth named Arnold, of Barrington-road, Altrincham, and about 14 years of age, met with a frightful accident on Thursday morning at the Altrincham and Bowdon station. 141 at- tempting to enter the ten o'clock train for Manchester, which had started when he arrived on the station, he fell be- tween the carriage and had both his legs cut off. He was removed to the Altrincham Hospital.

div.head: BLOODTHIRSTY LITTLE ANIMAL.
div.p: A BLOODTHIRSTY LITTLE ANIMAL.

In the ermine, or large weasel, we have perhaps the most cruel and bloodthirsty animal in existence. Its in- tillet to kill is BO strong that, were it possible, it would destroy the means of its subsistence. It would leave none of its varied prey alive. The lion, and even the man eat- ing tiger' when gorged, are inert, and quiet. They kill no more than they want for a meal; but the ermine will attack a poultry yard, satiate itself with the brains of the fowls or by sucking their blood, and then, out of "pure cussedness," will kill all the rest within reach. Fifty chickens have been destroyed in a night by one of these remorseless little beasts. It makes fearful ravages among grouse, rabbits, and bares. It is the mythical vampire embodied. Only lack of material or bodily fatigue suspends its bloody work, and its life is one long career of carnage. It has a terrific set of teeth, which are worked by most powerful muscles. Dr. Coues, an eminent naturalist, has given a graphic account of him. His words, as I remember them, are a true portrait of a murderer. "His forehead islow, and nose sharp; his eyes are small, penetrating, cunning, and glitter with an angry green light. His fierce face surmounts a body ex. traordinarily wiry, lithe, and muscular, which ends in a singularly long, slender neck that can be lifted at right angles with the body. When he is looking around, his neck stretched up, his flat triangular head bent forward, swaying to and fro, we have the imago of a serpent." This is a true picture of an ermine when excited Sr angry when at rest, and in certain conditions of his fur, there are few more beautiful, harmless, innocent-looking creatures. Let one of the animals on which he preys ap- proach, however, and instantly he becomes a fiend. In the economy of nature he often serves a very useful pur- pose. In many regions field-mice are destructive. The ermine is their deadliest fee. A rat will fight a man if cornered, but it gives up at once in abject terror when confronted by the large weasel. This arch enemy has a pride in his hunting, and when taking up his quarters in a barn will collect in one place all the rats and mice he kills. Sometimes a hundred or more have been found to- gether as the result of two or three nights' work. The ermine hunts, however, both by day and night,and climbs trees with great facility. He has been used successfully as a ferret. Having first filed the creature's teeth down, so that it could not kill the game, a gentleman secured 12 live rabbits in one forenoon.—Harper's Monthly Maga- zine.

div.head: NEIGHBOURS IN MANITOBA.
div.p: NEIGHBOURS IN MANITOBA.

The population round us chiefly consists of half-breeds and Indians, with a sprinkling of English settlers. They are most hospitable, but extremely iough, dirty, and un- civilised. Our post-office is four miles away, and we can send off and also fetch letters once a week. Let me de- scribe the interior of this post-office, one day last winter when I had occasion to call there. The post-master is a very rough Canadian; his wife is a half-breed, a tall, handsome woman. When we drove up she was out of doors in the snow, chopping firewood. Her lord and master was sitting in his only downstairs room, with his feet on the stove, and a pipe in his mouth. In the same room, which was bare of carpet or curtain, and contained the family bed, were three little children—a boy, aged seven, swearing lustily; a girl, about five, sucking her fingers, who began to howl as soon as I spoke; and a baby of two years, seated in a frying-pan on the floor, engaged in carefully wrapping up its bare feet in a dish- cloth. Their mother followed us into the house, and promptly seizing the handle of the pan, proceeded to eject the baby, and to wipe out the pan witl the afore-men- tioned cloth. Next she broke about a dozen eggs into the pan, fried them, and having made tea and produced her solitary teaspoon, she invited my husband and myself to partake, or, as she phrased it,to "sit in "with the family. It is needless to add that, after what I had just witnessed, I declined the hospitality as graciously as I knew how. This is my nearest female neighbour. Another interest- ing house is the home of a Justice of the Peace for the province, who is a settler near us. He is a Seotchman, and can quote Alison's "History of Europe." His house- hold comprises himself and his wife—a half-breed woman —a married daughter, her husband, and their two children; two other grown up daughters, a son of fifteen, another of ten, and two young men lodgers. The house is a log cabin, and consists simply of one fair-sized room. It is scarcely a cause for Eurpr is o that the whole of this family suffered from scarlet fever last spring. The only wonder is that they all recovered—All the Year Round.

div.head: HOW SHE SCARED THE BURGLARS.
div.p: HOW SHE SCARED THE BURGLARS.

As I watched the lightning from my window a flash I revealed to me two men climbing over the garden wall. What was to be done? There was little doubt that they knew that only three helpless woman and a girl were left in the house that night. As sudden, swift and stealing as one of those flashes, which were momently illumining the outer world, an idea shot through my brain. On the toilet-table was a jar of white tooth powder. I shook out a quantity, shut my eyes and proceeded to rub it thickly over my face, arms and hands. That done I drew the white coverlet off the bed and draped myself with it loosely from head to foot; then I unbound my hair which in those days was ebon black and reached below my waist; and shook it around my face and over my shoulders in "most admired disorder." I was now ready for the role I had made up my mind to act. Leaving Bessie watching by the window in case a constable should pass I stole noiselessly downstairs into the corridor. A moment later I was startled by a noise of falling glass. The burglars had effected an entrance into the drawing- room, and they and I were only separated by the drawing. room door. Quickly I sped past the docr to the opposite end of the corridor, where there were two more doors. The first was that of my brother's office; the second shut off a passage leading to the kitchen. This latter door I succeeded in opening without noise and took my stand a little way on the inner side of it. Presently a faint creaking told me that the drawing-room door was being opened. For a few brief seconds an almost overpowering longing seized me to get back to my room at any cost. i But it was too late, by this time the men were n the corridor. I knew it though I could not see them. "Where's the door we want ? " I heard one whisper to the other. "On the right—the first door we come to." As they advanced I did the same. "What noise was that?" asked one of them. "Don't be a fool. There was no noise." "I tell you there was. Where's the gHm ? " But the lightning was quicker than the bullseye. It came, smiting the darkness and flooding the corridor with the blinding intensity of its glare. One of the men gave a gasp and whispered to his mate, "What was that tall white thing at the end of the passage? Seemed to me like a ghost." "Ghost be dashed ! There ain't no such thing. Here's the glim. We'll soon see what it is." As he spoke, the light of his bull'seye lantern was turned full upon me. I advanced a.couple of paces and the men fell back in speechless surprise and terror. I have often tried since to picture to myself the appearance I must have presented when seen at such a moment and by that uncertain light, with my ghastly, death-like face, my dilated eyes, my black, snake-like lock,, my tall figure all in t% hits, and with one extended arm and finger pointed direct at the men. I cannot wonder at their fright. At 1 this juncture came another flash, and a terrible peal of thunder startled the air and shook the house. At the very instant, impelled thereto by something within me 1 that I was powerless to control, I burst into a wild peal of maniacal, blood-curdling laughter. One step nearer I advanced; but that was enough. With a loud yell of terror the men turned and fled. I heard a crash of shattered glass, and after that I remembered nothing ' I more till I came to my senses, to find Bessie supporting , any head on her lap and pressing her smelling-salts to my I nose. But John's ninety pounds were saved !—Clianibers's Journal.

A dog belonging to the B--s, which was a great favourite of theirs, and regarded as of thoroughly irre- proachable training, was charged by some of their neigh- bours with worrying sheep at night. The family rebut- ted this charge on the ground that the dog was fastened into their kitchen at night, and was never let out until the servants came down in the morning. The farmers, how- ever, persisted that they knew the dog well, and had seen him going from the sheepfold, though he had managed to escape them. When this was urged so strongly as to make it imperative on the B— s to take some further steps, one of the daughters volunteered to sleep in the kitchen, and watch the dog's behaviour. When they made up the younglady's bed,the dog seemed very restless and strange, but by and by he settled down, and all was silent. A little after midnight he got up, came to the bed, and sniffed about until he had satisfied himself that the lady was not awake. Then he leaped into the window seat, lifted the catch of the shutters and opened them. Then he undid the latch of tha window, which he opened and then disappeared. After. a long interval he came back, closed and fkstened the window'and shutters, and finished by licking his own feet, and the marks which he had left by springing on the floor. To the terror of the seeming sleeper, he now came and closely scrutinised her; but she kept still, and he at last crept off to his own bed. As soon as she heard the servants stirring, the lady rose softly and slipped through the door. But the guilty dog had marked her. He sprang up and made a dash at her with most undisguised fury, for he saw that his secret was discovered and his character blasted by one whom he now regarded as a hateful spy. Fortunately, she got the door fast shut in time,and at once alarmed the house. But the dog was now so furious that no one dared go into the kitchen, and at last a gun was brought, pointed through an aperture,and ho was shot dead. —Petland Revisited. 1311 Bev. J. G Wood.

A man who pretended to have seen a ghost was asked what the ghost said to him. "How should I understand," replied the narrator, " what he said? I am not skilled in any of the dead languages." A new minister has been installed in the parish church of N—, a gentleman possessed of stentorian lungs and hard, horny, fists, and he used both with great eneigy, shrieking out his sermon with the full power of the former, and hammering the pulpit with the latter. After hearing his first sermon and being disthissed, the members of the congregation assembled in groups outside the church gates, and began discussing his merits. Standing apart by themselves were Sandy Mackintosh and Jamie Tamson, two of the village worthies. "Eh, man," said Sandy to his companion, "he's a c'ever ane yon; man, I just likit him fiist•rate. Hon did you like him, Jamie?" "Like him!" retorted Jamie, as he made his one hand play crack into the other, as if to emphasise his answer, tae tell the plain truth, I just didna like him ava' ; for, od, man, whan we had oor sin auld, quiet minister, I got sleepin' a' through the sermon; but wi' this new billie, an' his roarin' and hammerin', I never got sleepit a wink trae the vas end o' the sermon tae the itkell! ,

TEE BEST DISINFECTANT.-Of all known disinfectantis carbolic acid is now generally admitted to be most efficacious, and it is the basis of most of the disinfecting agents now sold. The acid is too powerful to be used alone, and is therefore generally mixed with eighty or ninety per cent, of some other substance not possessed or disinfecting properties. Sometimes the bisulphate of lime and magnesia are added, and these substances are themselves possessed of disinfecting properties; but more generally chalk or sand is used; or the acid is simPlY diluted with wlter. A small portion of the mixture sprinkled in water-closets and other places where decom• posing matter is allowed to remain will diminish, if /4 entirely remove, the chances of contagion, and on" sweeten and purify the atmosphere.—Cassol's Magazine.

PARTNERS FOR LlFE.—Partners for life ought to be con- genial and harmonious in so many things. When rneEt., make a partnership in business they can't get along well a they are unlike in disposition or in moral principle or in business ways and business habits. They can dissolve and' separate at pleasure and try another man. A man and hio, wife ought to be alike in almost every thing. It is said that folks like their opposite, their counterparts, and so they do in some respects. But in mental quaaies and emotional qualities, and tastes and habits and urinci pies and the like they ought to class to-ether. Indeed, it is better for theta' to have the same politics and the same religion. The happiest unions, as a general thing, are those where the high contracting parties have known each other for a long time, and have assimilated from their youth in thought and feeling.

ECONOMY OF LIFE—The true economy of human lue adjusts expenditures to a moral scale of values. P 0 Quincey pictures a woman sailing over the water/ awakening out of sleep to find her necklace untied au°, one end hanging over the stream, while pearl after Pear' drops from the string beyond her reach; when 8110, clutches at one just falling, another drops beyond re- covery. Our days drop one after another by our careless- ness, like pearls from a string, as we sail the sea of life, until we learn that the waste of time ig a more serious loss than the extravagances against which there is such loud exclaim. The expenditure of a few dollars on taste is a small matter in comparison with the wasting cf months and years by thousands who have every advau- tage society can offer, and exact every privilege it affords as a right.

NOBLE SILENT MEN.—Tho noble silent men scattered here and there, whom no newspaper makes mention of ! They are the salt of the earth. A country that has none or few of these is in a bad way; a forest that has no roots, all turned into leaves and boughs, which must wither and be no forest. The first sign of a truly powerful nature is noticeable in the demeanour. Performance comes later and does not surprise us, for it has already been pledged by the behaviour. A man of this description may he' gentle, modest, and unassuming, never pressing himself into notice, and yet we do notice him, for we cannot he/P it; and he has an air of self-command and self-poise, an absence of heat, or passion, or strain, or exaggeration, t courteous hospitality to another's thought, a firm and decisive utterance of his own, an individuality which sur- rounds him, protecting him from assault by enforciug respect—all of which combine to assure us of a power In reserve that cannot fail to make itself known, though in what direction we may not be able to foretell.

MAIIKETING.—Before going to market it is a very good rule to determine what shall be purchased and in what quantity. This is especially needful when the butcher is to be visited. Another rule is to deal at shops where good articles only are sold, and if possible to take your money with you, because a ready money customer will, as a rule, be the best served. It is not always safe to let the butcher, poulterer, fishmonger, or other provision dealer choose for you, because he may be over anxious to sell what is not in the best condition, or what is frora other cause hardly saleable. Experienced persons will not fail to observe carefully the quality of what they buy; and they will reflect upon the quantity of bane, gristle, or other waste in it. They will also consider the require- ments of the family, and the uses to which they can put what is not consumed as soon as cooked. At the butcher" see the meat cut and weighed, and placed ready to be sent home; you will then know what you have bought. " Always buy good meat rather than inferior, and, if possible, from the best parts of the animal.—Cassell's Household Guide. •

Bonnowarc.—llave your own things. Accustom your- ' selves to be careful to keep on hand your own stock of writing paper, pens, pencils, and indiarubber. Do not depend, on mamma's workbasket for a thimble or needles, nor on her bureau drawer for ruffles and handkerchiefs. Do not consider that you have a right to borrow palmed knife, nor to make a foray on brother Tom's roam foe strings and wrapping-paper. Everybody should be inde- pendent of the home world, so far as some personal belongings are concerned. If you allow yourselves to form the habit of going here and there with Please lend me this," and "Do oblige me with that," you will often annoy people who are too polite to shew their feelings, and you will sometimes incur mortifying refusals. It is usually much better to do without the use of an article than to borrow it. This is especially true of things to wear. There are girls who put on their sisters' hats and aprons quite indiscriminately. There are boys who never have a collar in their box, nor a tie that isn't a perfect string., and not fit to be seen. Remember that a very wise man bas told you "the borrower is servant to the lender." This has many meanings, or rather the meaning of it makes itself plain in many ways as you go on in life. You will have a truer self-respect if you decide that you will, so far as you can, stand on your own feet and not borrow your neighbour's crutches.

SLOVENLY READlNG.—Slovenly reading is ruinous both to mind and morals. It is apt even to injure a nian's business-habits and prevent him from winning success in practical affairs In time it will confound all his faculties; it will destroy his capacity for clear preception, for precise thought, and for proper reasoning. It will throw into confusion his judgment and his memory. If he does not get rid of it, he can never become a good writer, or do any literary work of any kind worth looking at. How many slovenly readers are to be found in these times! They will; in their slovenly fashion, read a newspaper-article, perhaps a very excellent one, and, when they have got to the end of it, or, as they say, when they have "looked through it " or "glanced over it," you will find that they are unable to give any accurate account of its argument, or that they de not apprehend its fundamental points, or that they have lost one of its links, or that they have overlooked an im- portant illustration, or that they have failed to seize a word which is the very hinge of the writer's thought, or that they have wholly misunderstood the drift and purpose of the article which they have wasted their time in "glancing over." Slovenly reading is largely due to the slovenly way in which children are taught to read at school. Teachers must be very careful about this thing; they must teach their scholars to read with precision and understanding, thinking of every word, getting the sense of each sentence, and grasping the full meaning of any piece that may be before them.

TO CLEAN MARBLE. Brush the dust off with a piece of chamois, then apply with a brush a good coat of gum-arabic about the con- sistency of thick mucilage, and expose it to the sun or wind to dry. In a short time it will peel off. If all the gum should not peel off, wash it with clean water and clean cloth. If the first application does not have the desired effect, it should be tried again. Another method. is to rub the marble with the following solution: ilb. of soft soap, ?lb. of whiting, and loz, of soda and a piece of stone blue the size of a walnut; rub it over the marble with a piece of flannel, and leave it on for 24 hours, then wash it off with clean water, an& polish the marble with a piece of flannel or an old piece of felt; or take two parts of common soda, one part of pumice-stone, and one part of fine-powdered chalk, sift it through a fine sieve, and mix it with water, then rub it well over the marble, then wash the marble over with soap and water. To take stains out of white marble, take one ounce of ox-gall, one gill of lye, one and one-half tablespoonfuls of turpentine; mix, and make into a paste with pipe clay; put on the paste over the stain, and let it remain for several days. To remove oil-stains, apply common clay saturated with benzine. If the grease has remained in long, the polish will be injured; but the stain will be removed. Iron- mould or ink-spots may be taken out in the following manner: Take half-an-ounce of butter of antimony and one ounce of oxalic acid, and dissolve them in one pint of rain-water; add enough flour to bring the mixture to a proper consistency. Lay it evenly on the stained part with a brush, and, after it has remained for a few days, wash it off, and repeat the plocess if the stain be not wholly removed.

div.head: TEACH THE CHILDREN TO THINK.
div.p: TEACH THE CHILDREN TO THINK.

Strength of mind is not equivalent to perfect balance of judgment, or evenness of power. As a rule, specially strong-minded persons are given to single ideas, which are held with great tenacity. Inventors rppresent this, as well as advocates of particular ideas. What is called strength of mind is the result of independent thinking. Hence its basis is real thought. The first element toward it is inducing the young to think. Hence even incorrect thinking should not be rudely reproved, but kindly and gently corrected. Every encouragement should be given children to think. Thought stimulates thought, and hence living ideas put before children in the home circle, at table or elsewhere, has its value in this direction. On the other hand, the rude repression of an unguarded or iacorrect thought is injurious. Encouragement to hold fast to an idea till it is disproven is another step in this form of education. The mere circumstance that someone. does not agree with it proves nothing. Nor does it follow that the disagreement of an older per-on is to be accepted as final. Before an idea or opinion is abandoned it should be satisfactorily seen to' be wrong. The moment one accepts or abandons a thought or opinion at the ipse dixit of another they betray weakness. Leadership is one thing and dominancy another. It is well, if we have not the qualities of leadership, to be willing to be led; but to have our minds dominated and controlled is another and entirely different thing. The important lesson to impart to children is that of sound, independent thought. And if it lead to strong-mindedness—that is,. tenacity oi opinion—it will be well, provided opinions be carefully and thoughtfully formed.

A sufferer by a late railway-accident, rushing wildly about, was asked if he was hurt. "No," he said; "but I can't finil my umbrells." "My aim is always to tell the truth." "Yes," interrupted an acquaintance, "and you are probably the worst shot in the United Kingdom." History-class in American school. 'reacher : " Wha was the first man ?" First boy : "George Washington." Teacher: "Next." Second boy: "Adam." First boy indignantly: "I didn't know you meant foreigners!" An Irish country.doctor conversing with a friend about the high rates of mortality then prevailing,'rernarked, "Be. dad, there are people dying who never died before !" A short time before his death H. J. Byron's brougham. horse fell ill, and the coachman went to consult his master about it. There was not very much the matter, the man thought; a little treatment would soon set him right. "I think he ought to have a ball, sir," the man said. "Very well," Byron replied, "let him have one; but, I say, don't ask too many people." A funny mistake occurred lately in printing labels for a meat-preserving company. The printer had been in the habit of labelling tins of beef or mutton, as the case might be, with the words "without bone" prominently displayed. The company hsvingadded kidney-SOUP to its list, the new article was duly ticketed as "Kidney-soup—without bone." A curious incident happened once at Bowness church. There had been a good deal of dry weather in the south, and an Oxford man who occupied the pulpit began to read the prayer for rain, when the clerk pulled the skirts of his sur- plice. "You mustn't read that, sir," he whispered; "we don't want it." But it's a prayer for a good harvest, my man," reasoned the parson. "That's just it," rejoined the clerk; "the visitors are our harvest, and we want none of your rain." Shortly after the Crimean War two officers who were quartered in Dublin drove on an outside car from the bar- racks to the North Wall Quay, a distance of about four miles, and on arrival presented their Jelin with a shilling. Pat fixed his eye attentively on the coin, and ejaculated viciously, "II id leek to the Cztr of Rooshia!" One of the officers said," What do you say ?" Pat repeated, in a louder tone of voice, "Bad luck to the Czar of Rooshia!" "Why?" asked the officer. " Becos, bedad, he has killed all the gentlemen that used to be in the army !" A YOUNG Gist's HEROISM.—" I would like to ask you to take some ice cream, dear," he said, looked hesitatingly in the window of a saloon, "but after that disastrous affair in Brooklyn a few days ago lam afraid to," and he made an attempt to forge ahead. "What affair was that, George," she asked, holding him back with both hands. "Why, over one hundred and fifty people were poisoned from a single freezer." "It must have been terrible. Still, George, dear, there is a possibility of our escaping with our lives, and if we do die" here the heroic girl gave him a look of love un- utterable—"we will die together." FOLLOWING THE DOCTOR'S ADVICE.—" Doctor, I want 1 you to do something for me. My nerves are shattered com- pletely. I am not able to eat anything and I sleep very little at night. What would you advise me to do?" "What has brought about this condition?" "Drinking too much, I'm afraid." "Well, I would advise you to give up drinking." " Erm, that idea never occurred to me. What's your charge for the advice?" " Nothing." " Nothing ? I'm much obliged to you, doctor. Let's go and take something." THE ROAD TO TDB ALTAR.—The following astounding story, says a contemporary, appears in a recent number of the German serial Deutsche Dontan-Bibliothck, under the title of " The Road to the Altar." A younger son of the Duke of Arsyll having become engaged to Lady —, as in duty bound, asked his father's consent. The duke however answered, " Siece my el&st son, the Marquis of Lorne, married the daug`tter of the Queen, our Sovereign, he has become the head of our house. You must obtain his con- sent. If you get that, you may rest assured mine will not be refesed." To the marquis his brother accordingly betook himself; but from him he received the following answer:— "As lam son-in-law to the Queen, duty and respect require that the matter should be referred to her for her decision. I will at once lay the matter before her." To the Queen went the marquis immediately, and informed her of his brother's wishes. The monarch, however, replied, "Since Heaven de- prived me of my noble ever-lamented husband, I have made it an inflexible rule to take no step in the affaiis of my house without referring the matter to nay brother-in-law the Duke of Coburg. I will write to him." The Queen did as she promised; but from the duke she received the following answer, instead of the consent she expected—" Your Majesty, my beloved sister, is well aware that during the last four years important political changes have taken place in Germany, in consequence of which the centre of gravity has been shifted from Coburg to Berlin. I therefore consider it my duty to submit the matter to the Emperor William for him to decide. I cannot take the responsibility on myself." To Berlin accordingly went the duke, begged an audience of the Emperor, and acquainted him with the object of his visit. After considering the matter within himself a short time, the Emperor said, "What I have fought for and attained for my country is well known to the whole world. People, however, ' have no idea how my heart is tortured by discord and dis- agreements in the circle of my family and among my minis- ters. However I must honourably confess that the Prince Bismarck is the wieest and most clear-sighted of my ad- visers. I give you the commieion to refer the matter to him, and let him decide." The duke then directed his steps to the Wilhelmstrasse, and. sent in his card to the mighty minister. Being immeiiately admitted, he read the Queen's letter, faithfully reported the words of the emperor, and begged for a favourable decision. The Chancellor's answer was given without hesitation—" Why should the matter require any decision of mine? What have we to do with the Duke of Argyll, or with his son? If the young fellow wishes to marry, let him do so, and be hanged to him!"

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.

- - ST. Manx's Caterame.--In is expected that this new church at Cowley Hill, which is a fine structure, and can be seen for many miles round, will be opened towards the old of October. A few internal arrangements only need completing and then the edifice will undoubtedly be a very serviceable and handsome one for the district. TRAP ACCIDENT.—On Friday forenoon a trap con- taining three butchers, driven by Mr John Hatton, was proceeding down Shaw-street at a rapid rate when the horse slipped and fell. Both shafts of the trap were smashed, the splashboard broken, and the three men thrown into the road. Fortunately they received no injury with the excep- tion of a severe sleeking. STARR-BoWBETT BUILDING SOCIETY.—An appropria- tion in connection with the 1 hint St. Helens Starr-Bowkett Building Society took place on Thursday at the offices, Market-place. The chair was occupied by Mr A Lomax. Tbe result of the ballot was that Mr James Bath, of 103, Robin's-lane, Sutton, was declared entitled to an advance of £2OO for 12n years, free of interest. SWINE FEVER —A. special meeting of the Health Committee of the St Helens Corporation was called for Fri- day morning to receive a report that another case of swine fever had been found to exist on the premises of Charles Metcalf, 21, Eldon-street, Cropper's-hill, St Helens. A quo• rum, however, could not be obtained to make the neces- sary order as to the infected circle, and the meeting was adjourned THE WINDSTORM : DESTRUCTION OF Tattattnittaern Posrs.—On Saturday night and Sunday morning two tele- phone posts in Prescot-road, near the Old Toll Bar, were blown down by the high wind which prevailed. About a dozen wires were attached to the posts, n lid as they fell into the road the traffic on Sunday morning was seriously in- terrupted. In the forenoon, however, a number of men con- veyed the posts and wires into an adjAc nt field, and thus re- moved the obstruction. SUDDEN DEATIL—The Coroner, Mr. Brighouse, held an inquest at the Running Horses Hotel, Liverpool- street, on Wednesday morning, on the body of Ellen Turner, 51 years of age, residing at 23, Talbot-street. The deceased had been suffering from an ulcerated leg for a con- siderable time past, but was not attended by any medical gentleman. She was found dead in bed at a qearter past ten on Sunday night by her son,— The jury returned a vet- of "Death from natural causes." Sr. HELENS WATER COMMITTEE.—At the monthly meet- ing of the St. Helens Water Committee, held at the Town Hall, on Wednesday afternoon (Alderman Mcßryde presid- ing) the Water Engineer (Mr Gaskin) reported that the yield of the Corporation wells during the month of August had been as follows :—Eccleston Hill 18 974 053 gallons Whis- ton 22 340 160, Sutton-road 17,883,512, Knowsley (delivery for 16 days) 4,901,401, Fccleston old water (16 days) 230,400. The other business was of a routine character. BoWas GARSWOOD V. PILEINGTON'S CITY ROAD. The return match between the Garswood team and Pilking- ton's City-road team, St. Helens, was played on Saturday, on the green of Os Garewood club. After the game the teams had refreshments together at the Garswood Hotel, Mr Hertion, captain of the Crtrewood club presiding, with Mr Job Preston in the vice-chair, and a pleasant evening was spent with toasts, songs, and recitations. The score was as follows :—Garswood, previous score 201-407; Pil- kinaton's City-road, previous score 269-472. Majority for St. Helens, 65. THE Sr. HELENS ENGINEERS.—In accordance with the War Office regulations for giving territorial designations to boll the Regular and Velunteer Amy, the 2nd L.E.V. have obtained a local name as well as habitation. In com- pliance with their request the Duke of Cambridge has been pleased to grant them the privilege of bearing the special designation of " The St Helens Engineers" in addition to their numerical title of 2nd L.E V. It may be memtioned that in connection with the corps a branch of the St Helens centre of the at John Ambulance Association has been formed. The class has been organised mainly through the instrumentality of Lieutenant Brooker, a: d at present con- sists of tairty-two members. Surgeon Hall has undertaken to deliver weekly lectures, and he will be assisted by Mr Thomas Sherlock. ST. JcIIN'S, RAVENHEAD.— The Rey Canon Carr, L L D, of St Helens, has effered the perpetual curacy of the church of St John the Evanaelist, Ravenhead (rendered vacant by the death of the Rev R R Moore), to the Rev H S Bolton, who, we understand, has accepted it. The new incumbent, a native of 1 orkshire, received his ministerial training at St Aidan's Theological College, Birkenhead. He was ordained deacon in 1881, and priest in 1882, by the Bishop of Liverpool. Mr Balton was appointed curate of Prescot, where he laboured for less than two years; and then came to Ravenhead. Both at Prescot and Ravenhead Mr Bolton endeared himself to the parishioners by earnestness in preaching and kindliness in his general bearing, and at the latter place a pressing request was made to the Rev Canon Carr to offer the vacant office to Mr Bolton. A DISTURBANCE AT THE STATloN.—Samuel Marsh- land, a middle-aged mar, of Liverpool, who said he was a foreman in the employ of the Lancashire and Cheshire Telephone Company, was charged at the St Helens Town Hall on Tuesday, with being drunk and disorderly at the railway station and also with assaulting James Lyon, one of the officials of the company. About balfpast six on the pre- vious evening the prisoner was on the platform of the rail- way station, under the influence of drink. He asked what time the next train for Liverpool started and was told; whereupon he asked the name of the ticket collector. Lyon, the foreman porter, refused to tell him, and turned to leave the prisoner, whereupon the latter ran behind him and dealt him a violent blow on the face, and used very abusive lan- I guage.—He was fined 5s and costs for the drunkenness ' and for assaulting the porter he was fined lOs and costs. THE HUSSARS' ANNUAL DINNER.—The annual din- ner in connection with the B Troop (St. Helens) of the Lancashire Hussars Yeomanry Cavalry took place at the Sefton Arms Inn, Baldwin-street, on Set urday. The mem- bers of the troop marched to the Sefton Arms, headed bs the capital band of the regiment, but the inclement weather affected the display. The dinner served to those present reflected the highest credit upon the host, and was greatly enjoyed. The chair was occupied by Mr. W. G. Dixon, V. 8., and the vice-chair by Sergeant-Major King. The usual loyal and patriotic toasts were given ; the bealths tf the coloael of the regiment, Colonel Legh, and the ad- jutant, Captain Moreland, were also drunk, all the toasts being received with musical honours. In the course of the evening the prizes for shooting and sword exercises were presented. The first prize for sword exercise was presented to Private Joshua Sumner, and the second to Private Kearsley. The first prize for shooting was gained by Ser- geant Ashton. and the third by Farrier Sergeant Hall. The proceedings were of a pleasant description. FATAL ACCIDENT TO A COLLIER.—On Friday, John Burrow, 24 years of age, residing at Si, Lyon-street, St. Helens, died from injuries received while following his employment at the Phoenix Colliery, Ravenhead, about three weeks ago. An inquest on the body of the deceased was held by Mr Brighouse, coroner, at the Griffin Arms, on Monday forenoon. Mr Schofield, manager of the colliery, was in attendance.—James Frodeham, a miner, who was working at the face of the coal three yards in front of the deceased, said he heard something fall, and, turning round, saw a large stone partly resting on a waggon and partly on deceased, who had been knocked down by its falling from the roof. The stone was too heavy for witness to lift him- self, and deceased lay under it until assistance could be pro- cured. He was then taken home, and afterwards to the hospital. There were three props in three yards from the face, but no bars were set for ten er twelve yards. The roof had been good, and it was not thought they were needed. The stone which fell was just ever the waggon way, and there could be no prop under it.--In reply to the Coroner, witness said if there bad been a bar across there would have been less chance of the stone falling —The Coroner said the evidence only convinced him that it was important in all colliery cases that they should have a sketch of the scene of the accident, which should be made immediately after an accident had happened. If they had had one in that case they would have understood it a hundred times better.— The inquiry was adjourned for the attendance of Mr Hall, the Government Inspector. DEATHS OF CHILDREN: STRICTURES BY THE Ceneeenet. —On Wednesday Mr S Brighouse, coroner, held an inquest at the Running Horses Hotel, on the body of Bridget Murphy, one month old, daughter of James Murphy, who with his wife lodged at 18, Sandfield-crescent. The child was found dead in bed at half-past five on Monday morn- ing.—The mother of the deceased stated that she and her husband with the child went to bed as usual on Sunday night and the child was placed on her left arm. When she awoke on the following morning the child was dead on her arm. She heard nothing during the night. She was a sound Sleeper and perfectly sober when she went to bed.—ln ad- dressing the jury, the Coroner said it would be best to re- turn an open verdict of found dead in that case, because the police could afterwards take any steps in the matter they might like. He did not think the jury should be called upon to assume the responsibility of saying whether the child died accidentally or whether it died from natural causes upon the evidence they had had before them. There Peemed to be• many cases of children being found dead, and when they were found amongst a certain class alone they had, their suspicions aroused. If they found such deaths in various classes of society, from the highest to the lowest, then they might think it might not be in human neture to prevent them, but when they found them invari- ably happening amongst such a class of poor people then he thought their best course was to return a verdict of found dead, se as to leave it an open question in case the police heard anything fuither.—alr King (a juror) said there were 80 many cases of that kind that it made one feel reluqtant to gives verdict at all.—The jury ultimately returned a verdict that the child was found dead in bed, but by what means she came to her death the jurors were unable to
