div.p: 17etterti to the editor.

THE SCIENCE CLASSES. Sir,—Several letter have appeared urging the continu- ance of the science classes, and giving several reasons but the right one for their failure. Allow me to say the school is not closed for want of funds, for want of interest on the part of the committee, or for want of effort to popularize and make them accessible to all—both rich and poor. The failure is due entirely to the want of interest by those for whose benefit they were established, and if a reasonable number of young men bad shown sufficient interest in science teaching. the c.nnmittee wonld not have closed the school, even with en adverse balance from year to year. 'Cheri) never his been a better a r pointed laboratory in War- rington, and it is a s )1L cc of sincere regret to the writer and many other friends of the school that they have had to close it for want of stodents.—Yours faithfully, F. MONKS.
Brooillamb, Warrington, Sept. 12th, 1884.

THE TOWN COUY'CIL AND CORPORATE PROPERTY. Sir,—Many members of our Town Council mast be troubled with bad memorirs. It surely is in the recollection of many of them that upon one or two occasions the Coun- cil Chamber has been lent to the c'ergy of the Church of England. Further, the old Commil Chamber in Market- street was let to the Liberal party for a club room. Surely after these precedents already upon record there can be no wrong in letting the premises in John srreet for the purpose applied for by Welah residents? I am afraid the well-known "popularity" of Dr Mackie in the Council Chamber, whose speech upon the OCCASiOII referred to was charactetised by a, notorious councillor in rather unparliamentary language, had more to do with the decision arrived at than the (ora- tion at iseue. Ihe case of the Welshmen was in bad hands, and I would advise them to obtain a new champion and try again. la the face of fac's already mentioned, our Council would do well to again reverse their decision. A RATEPAYER.

THE WATER U AT SUTTON. Sir,—Wilt you kindly allow me space in your valuable paper for the following :—Some five months ago, as already reported in your issue, the typhoid fever was about com- mencing in the above village. The result of this outbreak was to have the water of the well known in the village as Taylor's well analysed, and it was found to be unfit for use. The well was closqd and the mrin water supply was cutoff, not qaestionirg the unfitness of the water for drinking. Sir, I have strong reasons for giving my opinion that the epi- demic is by no means the result of drinking the above- mentioned water. 1 here has been a plentiful supply for the villa:l:ere of this water Now, sir, I ask what is to be done ? There is now only nil,. small pump in the village ; and I am right in saying Chit not half of the people have a suffi- cient supply o water. White staving there a few days ago I heard many complaints. The following I lead brought uurPr my notice :—A certain farmer in the village, for con- venience, came to this scanty supply and well-drained it by six o'clock in the morning ; and for no other purposo was this yaluable water. used than supplying a thrashing Triachlue engirt°, the result 7:,_14; a COMplete water famine , for the whole day, as the water comes into the well Very I slowly. Considering the number of wells in the village, their being one in every filly or sixty yards, and the only one mentioned tit for use, I think the sanitary authorities, who have been the means of stopping the supply from Tay- lor's well, should have first given their attention to cleansing some of the numerous supplies mentioned.—l remain, sir, yours, Jm., VERITY,

"PERMITTED T) DRINK, Bur NOT TO PRAY." Sr,—The Rev John Yonge deserves mneh credit for in- venting en fine a tide as the above for his letter to you of last Saturday; but it is very deceptive. The notion con- veyed is, that somebody was preventel front praying; and OM is too absurd to need an instent's discussion. I, personally, am delighted that the Corporation refused ita eancticn for the purpose reqaired by the two Welsh Evangelists; not because I wish to see their efforts nneuc- cetsful, but because I believe co-partitions should steer clear of religious and uelitcil movements in every way. And then, the advec icy of this ceste at the Council meeting was enough to de:en it. The maudlin gush of those who posed as pious benef teors of the benighted town was equal to a sail on a rough sea for a had sailor. Shades of Mawworm, Pecksniff, and Sir Pertidex Micsycophant! where are ye now? Do these interesting philanthropists practice what they preach? Methinks they rather realise our greatest firm:tourists notion : A mere oeofe3sor elite of all hit mut, Is Not a whit be',:er than a An ins ins VG. f what clime I can't determine, That life, its paws most puma-like, and thence, By simple savages—thro' sh:rer pretence— Is rackon'd quite a saint am mg the vermin. There are nurne-ous pieces in the town that could be hid for a nominal rental, without nuking the Corporation the landlords of any sect or creed; and, althoLgh it is quite true, as Mr Y.,ege s.ye, that the London Guildhall and Mansion Rouse ire (low and then (though very rarely) used for political or religious !neetiegs, they aro not " let," in any sense of the term, to any disputative body. The Cor- poration, I repeet;are quite right in their action; and I re- joice that the sham sentiment introduced at the Council to , gratify the inordinate vanity of a few stale spoutere, has been detected and crushed. The Temperance qttestien is, in my opinion, much too wide for a letter. I miy, however, sty that I sympathise very much with Mr Yenge in wishing to STO drunkenness stopped, but I do nor agree with hint in the method of doing it. There ho been, since that very superficial lecturer, Mr Murphy, WAS hors, teld,•Llef to do mare then teach or per- steade, namely', to meddle with the iaterests of a business which are as inalienable and legal—aye, and I will say, as henest--as the teetotallers' own—be he either parson or tradesman. Ministare of the (level have their own vehicle —the pulpit—to sh3CV th 9 right way; but abstaining trades- men, who se r themselves up as censors of law and morals, and who would have everyone's appetite to be like their own, are forge:lW of two things : First, that they are not trying to " live ail let live ;" and secondly, that they are net minding their own business.—Yours, Sm, PENDENNIS.
-September 10th, 1834. "THE DitUA ECCLESIASTIC."

Sir,—Allow me to congratulate the Liberal members of the Town Council on having at lost found one of "light and leading" who ie able to act as their temporal and spiritual guide. Alderman Burgess and Councillor Crestield must feel ashamed of themselves at having, in such an innocent manner, fallen into the fowler's snare. Could they not understand that Councillor Burgess in this matter, as in most others, could do• very little "at his own option?" Could they not see tile* the big d,mrn was doing service to drive out the schismatics? No, they fell into the trap, add in the words of the Rev .1 Yonge they preferred to stop .prayer and encourage drink. Couucillor Mackie is "cute ;' he could see the fol'y of the narrow-minded policy of Coun- cillor -Burgess, and preferred to give a sermon on religious -equality. True, he lihn,df does not understand what this means in its entirety, but so far as he does he was willing to support the -young Welshmen. I, as an outsider, can only excleiql, "Behold bow these Christians love one another!" I think ratepayers neeht to have a word with respect to this unfortunate building in John-street, and ask what good .is it doing the town. If it cost nething that is no reason why it should stand idle, and I am sure had the rector, or the Bev E C E Carleton wanted the building, not a dis- sentient voice would have been heard from the party who claim to be established by law. The building is doing no good, and ought to he let for all and every purpose that is useful. While linking OR at this squabble lam strongly .reminded of the Kilkenny cats, and can only hope that those who are engaged in it will speedily bring about the same results that the cats did. Councillc r Mackie tells us that Warrington hae got an uner.viable name during the ,past twelve mouLtis—drinking girls and runaway .husbands. What a satire on the results of ,Christian teaching! Our Christian friends are blind to the truth, lost in their own superstitious faith, or they would see clearly there is no charity, no love, no -sympathy amongst thorn; not a chnrch or chapel but what is full of vain deceit and hypocrisy. Pride is rampant amongst them. It proclaims he presence in the gaudy trappings and surroandiegs of pulpit and alter. Stand any Sunday in Church-street and watch the followers of Him who had not where to lay his head; note the pride of dress, the haughtiness of carriage, and tell me those are worthy of all imitation. Go from there to the Dissenting places of worship, end what do you and ? The pride that anee humility ; the Wesleyan imitating the Churchman; the Congregationalist trying to outdo the rest in architec- tural display. And yet all these affect to despise "the 'day of email things." The poor Welshmen must put neoney in their purees, and they will soon be respected. Councillor Mackie lot drop a loving sneer at the Atheists. Let me turn his attention to Northampton, where from the bench to the press there is but one general opinion as to the high moral .standing of its inhabitants, the great improve- ment that has beet, noticed and reported on. Warrington has seen just recently a Murphyite campaign, a Moody and Sankey caonioaign, and last, but not least by any means, a mob of Salvationiets. And yet we have the miserable re- port of Councillor •Meckie as to our morality. It is time the Christians stood on one side ; weighed ip the balance, they are found wanting; better send for the Atheistic le4- turer to teach them humanity. cAprAiN COTTLE.

MORE DEATHS FROM YAOCSTATION. Sir,—A short tirno ago you published particulars of a' series of fatalities due to vaccination occurring in EL,g4nd within a few weeks, but as to which the medical journals and the medical department of the Local Government Board have observed their customary official reticence. It should not be forgotten that it is only on rare occasions that such cases come to liht at all, owlJg to the general custom of certifying deaths from vaccination as due to secondary causes, when the medical secret is buried with the body. Montaigne says, "The successes of medical men are every- where noised abroad, but their failures are underground." May I venture to briefly refer to a few of the latter. On the 10th Zane Leonard Walker, of Duseld, was vaccinated by Dr Skinner. Two days after the operation the child became ill, and, according to the mother, died from blood poisoning on the 23td. A surgeon, of Sheffield, leposed that the arm was much Inflamed and "brawny," and gave a certificate that death was dne to vaccination. The Leicester Mercury for June 13th, reported the death from erysipelas, superven- ing upon vaccination, of the infant child of Joseph Milburn, 13. Alexandria Terrace, Leicester. The doctor admitted to Mr Biggs that the fkaal dise.aa was due to vaccination. The coroner, however, declined an urgent request to hold an in- quest, and thereby nava4 a verdict adverse to the interests

of vaccine coercion. The London Eei.o of the 18th July gave particulars of an inquest held on the body of William Arthur Pleasants,of 23, Wellesley-street, Mike-end, who died three weeks after vaccination. The surgeon testified that the vaccinated arm was black and swollen—the verdict of the jury being "blood poisoning due to vaccination." An infant, Horace Best, of Hull, died through the effects of vaccination performed at eight weeks old, when in a thoroughly healthy state and free from blemish. Inflam- mation of the vaccinated part commenced on the fourth day after the operation, which ultimately spread all over the body. This case was referred to in the House of Commons by Mr Hopwood. Then comes the death of the infant child of Mrs Sturry, of Waltham - stow, who deposed that "the poor little thing had been one mass of corruption ever since vaccina- tion." On the 22nd of the 831119 month a photograph was lent me of a little girl in the same place, suffering in a frightful manner from vaccine svphillis, the parents and all other children being in good health, and on Saturday, the 9th August, a London newspaper furnishes the particulars of a demonstration made at Palace Yard, Westminster, by the friends of Mrs Harriet Phillips, of Peckham Rye, whose child, hitherto in robust health, was vaccinated on the 10th ;Ay, and died after agenisieg suffering on the 2nd August. Dr W J Collins certified the death as due to erysipelas fol- lowing vaccination. The coroner refused an inquest on the ground that the operation bad been properly performed. The body of the victim was conducted in the cortege to the House of Commons amidst thousands of deeply-interested soectators. The deputation, accompanied by Miss Jessie Craigm, was received by Sir J C Lawrence, and a petition setting forth the facts was p es toted to the House of Com- mons the same evening. Mr C H Hopwood, M.P., sent a message of sympathy to the afflicted parents. The Oldham Express for the 21st contains details of two other vaccine disasters, and on the 23rd the child of John Holloway, 51, Victoria-street. Westminster, succumbed to the same lethal rite. The St James's Gazettee remarked, when referring to the Norwich vaccine disasters, that these fatalities are oc- curring up and down all over the country, which these pain- ful records show to be true, and yet the Government make no sign. I ventured to suggest some time ago that if some [ powerful newspaper would have the noble courage to send a qualified commissioner into the haunts of the poor in Lon- don, and other large centres of population, and take down from the mothers' lips the simple narratives of suffering and death caused by vaccination, and publish these recitals on the wines of the press, they would create such an impres- sion in the public mind that this cruel system, invented in a barbarous and unscientific age, would be swept away amidet a storm of public indignation. A distinguished scientific observer, Dr Alfred Russell Wallace, F.R.G.S , has for some time been investigating the vaccination question from official returns, and estimates that the deaths directly due to this operation amount to at least 10,000 per annum, while he miintains there is not a particle of scientific evidence to support the theory that vaccination saves lives at all. Dr Wallace's arguments and conclusions are now in the press, and when issued must arrestetlae attention of every thought- ful reader.—Yours faithfully, WILLIAM TEBB. Devonshire Club, St. JAMB'S, London, Sept. Bth.

WRAT IS NEUTRALITY ?

Sir,—l have been' led to ask the above question in conse- quence of reading an article in the Fortnightly, written by His Grace of Marlborough. The article is headed On the Cross Benches," and will well repay perusal by those whose attention is now directed to what we are now pleased to call "Government by Party." Since the Reform Bill of 1832, and more especially since household suffrage in boroughs gave working men the right to take an active part in the political affairs of the kingdom, government by party has ceased to be the peculiar property of what is termed the "governing claeses." Certainly they have retained the power of appointing to all lucrative posts their friends and retainers. This power is gradually being scotched, and will, I have no doubt, be soon done away with. In the good eld times, so sadly bemoaned by our Tory friends, it was impos- sible for a politician, if he wished to make his mark, to con- fess himself either neutral or to take his seat on the cross benches. He also knew it was equally impossible for him to come in for his share of the good things dealt out to those whose political conscience was of the elastic kind. Each political party has, even to-day, the right to bestow on its ornamental adherents such silly sinecure posts as feeder of hawks at a salary of £1,312. A great duke is mean enough to take this office that does not exist for the sake of the money that does exist, and neither Liberals nor Tories seem inclined to disturb this happy state of things. Neutrality, as seen during recent years, seems to incline to Toryism. If seen in the House of Commons it contents itself with voting against the peoples' wishes. If seen in a newspaper editor, it becomes transparent at once, and is easily seen through. A neutral editor contrives in one column to place before each political party his facilities for giving publicity to their speeches; in the next column he, the year round, persistently uses his autocratic powers to place before his readers leaders of such a pro. nounced Tory type that his readers of both shades of politics recoil from him in disgust. Not content with making hie 'Neutral" paper the vehicle for strong Tory vituperation, be may occasionally offer his columns to the highest bidder, thus making it impossible to carry on the palitical straggle with peace anc. honour to either party. Neutrality of such a dark hue is to be detested of all honest men. Better, by far, that each man's politics be clear and pronoun-nee, and that each newspaper shoula cease to exist than that such mean paltry bids should be made for the sake of making " divi.' Such is our experience of local newspaper neutrality. With neteral politicians, we don't seem to have very much experience. I fancy the article can never be in such great demand, with working-men at least. They require their representatives to be men who have already made up their minds. Such men as Lord Carnarvon, who has twice deserted the leader he is now following, would clearly be out of place. Such men as Lord Randolph, who, at Aylesbury, denounced the House of Lords for even hinting at the rej c- tion of the Franchise Bill, and who now follows Sir Staf- ford Northcote in such a fashion that at every fresh angle the substance and the shadow change places with each other, will soon find their mistake in not having a definite purpose. With the Cross Benches in the House of Lora we need not trouble; ending, not mending, will soon settle their business. With the House of Lords, as a body of men, I should wish even at this important crisis, to be just. We cannot expect them, as now evisting, to endorse and swal- low all the House of Commons may send up to them. Yet we cannot at the same time allow them to stand in the way of reforms as they from time to time crop up To remain neutral would be to stultify themselves, a process we cannot for a moment expect them to undergo. It appears to ma that,we want neutrality superseded by open declaration of opinion ; and if we are to continue the system of eiovernment by party, Cross Benches must be de- serted for party benches. I am the more con- vinced of this by certain statements of the Duke of Marl- borough. "The conditions of party government tend in every way towards embitterment in parliament." This, I take it, the experience of the last three years proves, but how would it improve matters to have a large neutral body, to whom each party should be making bids, as, we see, the Tories now coquetting with the Irish Nationalists? His Grace tells us that the "Tory party are more violent and more inclined to the tactics of state socialism." This, I take it, is a fact that has been largely over-looked by the People, because its pauperising effects have been so insidious and have partaken so largely of the paternal and patriarchal cast. His Grace thinks that "amid all this toil and jostle " the "average tending" of our civilization is forming itself, and yet in another place we see the man of the world speak. ing out facts that betray themselves to all who care to see them. "For centuries, whether under the name of Whigs or Tories, the great aristocratic party et England has repre- sented virtually one system of government—the guidance of the people by aches of hereditary statesmen connected with the land, in opposition to the selection of the representa- tives of the people from out of their own class. Thus there is a perpetually increasing disparity of happiness be- tween the lives of the rich and the poor—the rich are be- coming more rich, and the poor mere unable to support the strains imposed on them in the fight for existence." What man, penning the above lines, could remain neutral, and feel satisfied that he was doing his duty. Are the cross benches a fitting place for one who believes that "education does little mere than help them—the people—to realise the misery of their lot ?" Is it possible that one can remain neutral and stand idly by while " the desperate resistance of the unreasonable Tory to all change" is going on? I say most emphatically, no. It behoves all men with brains and capability to stand well to the front, determined to do their share in the great work that is going on to make life better worth living than it is at present. Another important factor in the political world is to be considered of even greater Importance than the neutral nonentity. This is the would-be politician who fancies that his especial grievance must be considered to the exclusion of other and more national matters. We have noticed in Warrington, and I know it is the case in other towns, that the Tories twit us with the bad state of trade. Mr Gladstone, they say, promised us better trade. I ask where is the statement to be found? And yet there are a few men to be found who listen to this statement, entirely forgetting the fact that it was during the Beaconsfield Government that the greatest reductions and the keenest trade struggles occurred ; that succeeding a period when trade prospezed by leaps and bounds, we had a period of six years, a period of time entirely devoted and used ky the Tories for the furtherance of foreign aggression, when all home trade was so smitten that merchants betook them to foreign markets, and capital was diverted into other channels. And Toes try to per- scads working-men that this can all be remedied in a short fear years. Why, the injury done to our trade during the late Beaconsfield Government will never be remedied unless' those who now have the power nse it to prevent county potentates seeking opportunities ,for preferment& for their SODA and relatives. As in imperial politics, so in municipal matters, working- men have no right to temain neutral or stand idly by. There of f newspaperthe peo peony press. paper. is a mighty weapon ready to their hand. I allude to the Theil i grievance working-man canis the e there chief w f s usleo,retee tilatedt and I have been pleased to notice the publicity rem have given to the water question. While Dr Gornall is iseee- jog "precautions aeainst cholera," and advising against using " tainted water," we have great numbers of men and lads forced to drink rile "pop." While we have a public park presented to us, we have the Mayor shutting out the public and arrogating the right to himself to invite parties to lawn termite thus turning a public park into a private pleasure ground. There is no room for neutrality. England expects every man to do his duty. keptembar Ist, 1884. CLIFFORD DIX, •

RUNCORN AND WIDNES..,

ATTEIViiCi TO WRECK A TRAIN AT RUNCORN. An incident which can only be characterised as an at- tempt to upset a train occurred on the railway near Run- corn on Thursday evening. About a quarter to eight a goods train from Liverpool passed through Runcorn sta- tion, followed by what is termed a "bank engine." The bank engine aidedthe train as far as Halton Junction, where it was turned from the up to the down line, and started on the return j)urney to Ditton. When near Cawley' Bridge the dtiver felt a shock to the engine. He stopped as quickly as posatble,and commenced to examine the line. tie dis- c )vered that the wheels of the engine had coins in contact Iwith a thick plank and several bricks, whilst on the up-line which be had only passed over a fey minutes before, he found a bricklayer's hod and a considerable quantity of ' brick., Sr..). He removal the obstacles and proceeded on to Runcorn. It appears that a number of the company's men from Crewe are engaged repairing Cowley's Bridge, and on fobbing work for the night placed their tools and material on one side. It is supposed that some bays have perceived them, and in a mischievous spirit placed them on the metals. Fortunately the engine was travelling at a very slow rate of speed at the time, and the only effect of the obstruction I was to slightly injure the guard of the wheel.
WIDNES LOCAL, BOARD. The monthly meeting was held at the Board•room, Al- fordo Chambers, on Tuesday afternoon. Mr F H Gossaga „..

presided. and there were present—Dr 0 Keeffe, Messrs Forster, Pankhuret, Wright, Midwood, Dutton, H Gaskell, jour, Houebton, Martley, Webster, Johnsen, Sadler, J 'l' Allen (clerk), J Carr (gas engineer), Higginson (surveyor), and Dickson (nuisance inspeetor). THE BLOCKADE OF WEST BANK-STREET. The Clerk explained that it was the opinion of the solicitor that 14 days' and not 28 hours' notice should be given to Messrs Bolton and Sons to remove the obstruction in West B ink- street. He had accordingly given 14 days' notice.—Mr Midwood moved that this action he confirmed, and it was corned. GAS COMMITTEE—PROPOSED Ex HIBITIOII OF GAS STOVES.—The minutes of the Gas Committee contained the engineer's report, which showed that during the four weeks ending August 13th there had been 45,660,933 gallons of water delivered, being a decrease of 329 as compared with the corresponding period last year. There had been made during the earns period 3537,000 cubic feet of gas, and 3,563,000 cubic feet delivered, are increase of 23 01 made and 13 27 delivered. The illuminating power of the gas had averaged 15 87 candles. On the 26:h August 11 C Davis and Co. wrote off,ring to provide an exhibition of gas cooking stoves, dra., for five days early in October next, under the superintendence of Mrs Th vaites. Lectures, &e, at 3 and 7 p.m, All expenses, other than hire of room and gas, to be borne by El C Davis and Co. It was rec memended tbat the Volunteer Hall be engaged, the total cost to the Board not to oxceed £2O. At a later meeting it was recom- mended that Mr Goss age be asked to attend and open the exhibition, to be held on the 6.11 October and few following days.—The minutes were confirmed on the motion of Mr Forster. I HIGHWAY MATTERS—MR WEBSTER IN A CRITICAL VEIN. —The Highway Committee's minutes stated that the pro- perty owners in certain streets having failed to do the ne- cessary repairs as agreed upon in January lest, instructions given to serve final notices that unless the streets in ques- tion are satisfactorily repaired before the 30th September, 1834. it will be recommended to have them made under the provisions of the Public Health Act, 1875. Various tenders were opened, and the committee recommended that the tenders of J Heaton for each street be accepted, subject to his references and sureties being satisfectory. With respect to public lighting it was recommended that £2 per lamp per annum be paid; and it was recommended that "Kent's Lamp" be removed to opposite the police station, Mr Kent having kindly consented. On the 25th August a letter was read from H Wade Deacon respecting the suggested alteration in boundary wall to St. Paul's Caurch: seas to widen the entrance in new street. It was recommended that in consideration of his giving up about 200 square yards of land, for the foregoing purpose, the necessary sewer connections to the church be mode by the ißeard, and £5 paid for the cost of conveyance. It was recommended that a pipe sewer be made from the ditch near ,to Gerrard-greet to the new culvert in Lugsdale-road, upon T Robinson paying £2O towards cost of sane as offered. The plan for alterations to Railway Hetel, for P Langton, approved, subject to sanitary arrangements being passed by the Health Committee—Mr Midwood, in moving the con- firmation of the minutes, said the committee had had an interview with Mr Shaw, of the London and North-Western Railway Company with regard to Waterloo-road level cross- ing, and they had explained everything to him. He had promised to do everything possible to do away with the shunting operations, which had been complained of so mach. Referring to St. Paul's (Thu :b, Mr Midwood said the Building Committee could not t ,e their way to make any further offer, he wished the recommendation to be ex- empted from the minutes.—Dr O'Keeffa seconded the minutes.—Mr Webster said he saw that the committee had been inspecting West Bank district, and he should like to ask if they had visited Oakland-street and West-street, for they had been in a fearful condition for years. He thought the property owners ought to have notice to put the street right. The bottom of the greet was always blocked up. Flrteen months ago £250 was voted to repair the ferry ap- proach, but the work was not yet finished, and he questioned whether £6OO had not been spent upon it. He should like to know what it had cost. The speaker added that he had not seen the plans of an erection which was being put up at the bottom of Oakland-street. It had been explainip to him that it was for a museum. but he thought it was to be turned into a menagerie for he sew they had got lions there. (Leughter.)—Mr Midwood, in re- ply, said the Committee had twice called the attention of the owners to ihe condition of Oakland-street, and notice had been given that if they did not do what the Board asked at the end et this month the Board would make the streets. He was not in a position to state the cost of the ferry ap- proach at present. The reason the work was not concluded was because the workmen were waiting for three wagons of setts. He moved a resolution that the MIR of £2 for public lighting be increased to £2 2e, and the minutes were passed with this ccrrection, an amendthent by Dr O'Keeffe not be- ing seconded. . THE SEWERAGE SCHEME : RESIGNATION OF THE EN- OINEER.—The Sewerage Committee had received a letter respecting No. 2 contract, from R Perry (North Denbigh Building Society), offering to accept £5 in full settlement of all claims in respect of the alleged trespass caused by the ventilating shaft and flue connecting eAtlls with sewer, and it was recommended that this offer be-accepted. A letter dated 30th Augnet was received from Mr Copland, giving three months' notice of his intention to resien his appoint- ment of engineer of sewerage works, in consequence of the works approaching completion, and the Board having deci- ded not to proceed with any new works at present. It . recommended that the notice be accepted, and that the Board give Mr Copland a testimonial in acknowledgment of the efficient manner in which he has performed his duties as engineer of the sewerage works. In consequence of the , sewerage works approaching completion, it was also recom- mended that Mr Colquitt (clerk of works), be I given a week's notice to terminate his appointment. L —Mr Webster moved the adoption of the minutes, observing that although he did so he did not entirely approve them. , The Board had made a mistake in taking the sewerage 1 affairs out of the hands a the Committee, because in con- seqtrence Mr Copland had been compelled to resign. The ' Board would have done far better to allow the Commit- , tee to decide what sewering was required and have retained Mr Copland who had the matter at his finger ends until the town was thoroughly sewerel. He contended that the Board had taken an unwise position, and by preventing a proper-system of seweriog being carried out, had put the health of the inhabitants in danger. It was all very well of gentlemen who retired to some nice spot each evening, and left others to fight the matter out.—Mr Midwood seconded the motion. He differed from Mr Webster very much in- deed. The Board had done a good deal towards sewering the tows, having spent something like £20,000. The Bo erd had not work for two surveyors at present. Mr Higginson was well able and qualified to carry out all of the work re- quired.—The minutes were passed. HIGH DEATH RATE—Die. O'KEEFFE ON THE LOCAL GOVEENUENT BOARD.—The minutes of the Health Com- mittee contained the Medical Officer's report for August, which showed that there were 78 births or 35 32 per 1,000. and CI deaths or 28.29 per 1,000. The deaths include 22 children under one year and 27 between one and five years. Zymotic diseases caused 32 deaths. The Local Government had forwarded the following letter:— "Copy. Prescot Union, Union Offices, Whiston, Prescot, 9th August, 1834 IMy Lords and Gentlemen.—l am directed by the Rural Sanitary Authority of this district to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 14th ult., an extract from a letter which you_have received from the Widnes Local B ,ard complaining of a nuisance arising from the pollution of a water course by sewage from the Rainhill sewage farm. The Sanitary Authority notice that the Widnes Local Board's communication to you is dated 9th July, 1884. The Inspector and Surveyor to the Authority has reported that on the 3rd or June, 1884, he visited the Rainhill sewage farm and found very little sewage flaw- ing on to the land, and owing to the exceedingly dry weather and the perched state of the ground no effluent water from it. The ditches at its boundary were very dry and without traces of any recent pollution. The surveyor , again visited it on the 11th July, after the recent rainfall.j when sewage in considerable quantity was flowing on to itl and also effluent water from the outlet in Wilmere-lane.l The latter was almost colourless and apparently free from anything objectionable anal the ditches were quite clean. The Sanitary Authority are quite satisfied that the Widnes Local Board had no grounds for complaint when they thought fit to trouble you CO their letter en the 9th July last. I am, my lords and gentlemen, your obedient servant, S H HARTLEY, elerk."—Mr Allen replied as follows :—"Sir, —I beg to acknowledge yours of the 18th. As the state- ments made by the Rural Sanitcry Authority are-so directly opposed to those made by this authority I am inetructed by the chairman of the Health Committee of this Board to re- peat the request made by this 80ar..1 on the 9th July being, that your Board should send down an inspector to examine take evidence, and report. If this coarse is taken the matter will be very easily settled at a very slight cost, it would also prove to your Board the value of tka statements made by both the local authorities coneerned. To-day the field has been again inspected and I send samples without comment. Complaints were still made by the farmers about the pollu- tion of the stream."—Mr A E Fletcher, alkali inspector, Edge-lane, Liverpool, wrote respecting the nuisance from the waste heaps near the central station. He said a few months ago the waste was deposited in a very unsatisfactory ' manner, but he bad lately insisted upon tho adoptlon of a
method whereby the. bank wae. made more solid and less

pelvious to air. The new method was more expensive to those depositing the waste, but the manufacturers had been willin to incur the extra cost so as to diminish the nuisance. He attributed the smells complained of to the hot weather,
and said he loalieved the smell was now very much dimin- ished.—Mr Ai:fleck, the local inspector, wrote in somewhat similar terms, and added that if it were practic-

• able to take the waste out to sea as done on te Tyne.it would be a great benefit to Widnes egad district. the committee recommended that application be mtde to the Local Governraent Board to sanction Mr Coopsr's ap- . .

_ pointment is medical officer for another ye *r. Instructions had been given to be very strict in collecting toll of hawkers.—Dr O'Keefe said he mast state in the strongest manner possible that the Local Government Board were not treating the Board as they ought to with regard to the Rtinhill sewage farm. All the 'efforts the Board had made to preserve the health of the township had been coldly received. Re wished the Local Governmmt

Board would exercise their autocracy in preserving the health of the people ef Widnes as well as if it were a por- tion of Belgravia. He remarked that there had not bePn the slightesc improve in regard to the waste he ips Toe health of the people was the supreme law, and the .in-

spectors ought to see that the waste heaps were hid in such a manner as not to be injurious to the public.—Mr Gas- kell suggested that the Skeilield and Midland Company should be written to on the subjece—Mr Webster remarked upon the high death rate, and wished to be informed what the committee were doing to lessen it. Referring to the waste heaps, he said Mr Small could son cry out when he was hurt. A short time ago he opposed the drainage , scheme, and he did not cry out ab net the smells from • the sewers while the people had been nearly pokonecl by the smells from the sewers. He did not care if the whole town were poisoned so long as be got none of the poison himself.—Mr Midwood asked whether hawkere could s-11 within a half mile radius of the market —Mr Sadler said he did not think the instructions as to collection of toll from hawkers would meet the nuisance, for nuisance un- doubtedly it was. About Bor 9 o'clock at night, when the officials were off duty, hawkers came from the neighbouring towns, St Helens and Warrington, and stool before the doors of small shopkeepers, and the consequence was that they escaped the payment of toll through entering the to on so late —Dr O'Keeffe, replying to Mr Webster, said the com- mittee wera attempting to keep down disease by depositing chloride of lime in the back passages of thickly populated neighbourhoods. With regard to htwking, a few years ago hawkers could not come within a radius of half a mile from the market, but subsequently the area was extended to the whole township. No doubt the hawkers abused their privi- leges, but it was thought the instructions of the committee would, if carried out, meet the case.—The minutes were passed.—Dr O'Keeffe moved that the Local Government Board inspectors and the Sheffield and Midland Company be communicated with with respect to the nuisance from the waste heaps —Mr Dutton seconded the motion.—Carried. THE PROPOSED INFECTIOUS DISEASES HOSPITAL —The Clerk read a letter dated the 4th September from the Local Government Board with reference to the application of the Board for sanction to borrow Pl7O for the purchase of land as a site for a hosp7tal for infectious diseases. The Board would direct a local inquiry to be held on the subject, but in the meantime they wished to be informed of the assessable value and existing debt of the di3trict. The Board under- stood from Dr Parson's, who visited the site last year, that no sewers are available for the drainage of the intended hospital, and it would therefore be necessary to dell with the sewage on the site. Under these circumstances it would be desirable to obtain a somewhat large area of ground.—Dr O'Keeffe retnarked that the Board's surveyor knew far more about the township of Widnes than either Dr Parsons or any of the clerks Of the Local Government Board or even Sir Charles Dilke himself, and if the Local Boat d could not select a site where they could drain the hospital so as to meet every requirement, they ought not to ba entrusted with the duties imposed upon them by the ratepayers. He I moved a resolution to the effect that the Board were nego- tiating for the purchase of a further half-acre of land.—Mr Midwood seconded the motion.—The Clerk said he had received a letter from Mr Rowclitie, solicitor to the Le,gh estate, who apprehended there would be no difficulty in in- creasing the site from 21- acres to three. FINANCE —The Finance Committee recommended the payment of the following accounts :—Gas £497 53, water £2Ol 93 11,1, hospital £9 153, sewerage £l,lOB 53 61, high- way £1.57 153 7d, health £B6 163 91, finance £9,242 Is 51, total £11,302 103 21. The minutes were adopted on the motion of Mr Wright, seconded by Dr O'Keeffe. ALLEGED STOPPAGE OF TILOROUGHFARES.—Mr Webster moved that in accordance with the laws of the Board notice be given for the removal of the obstruction in Oakland-st. He also asked what the surveyor Was doing with his men. He went up and down the road very often and he saw none of them. The roads were in a fearful state, and he could not think what he was doing. The winter was approaching and be thought the roods ought to be put in proper order They would be over the shoe tops in mud directly. Mr. Sadler saggested that they should bring Mr Webster a pair of shoes —The Chairman supposed Mr Webster wished the Highway Committee to take these matters in hand.— Mr Midwood said he did not know what Mr Webster Was referring to. He had not heard of Oakland-street being stopped up, but if such was the case the Highway Com- mittee would take action.—Mr Webster : It his been stopped up three weeks.—Mr Dutton: Shoot away, I am ready for you.—Dr O'Keeffe said the footpath leading from Widnes to Dittos Hall, which had been in existence over 20 years, had been stopped.—The Chairman explained that the footpath had been diverted to allow the Cheshire Lines to be made.— Dr O'Keeffe said legal action had never been t %ken for the purpose of stopping up the footpath —Mr Midwood thanked Dr O'Keeffe for mentioning, the subject, which, he said, ah.uld have the immediate attention of the cenanitte.e— Mr Sadler thought Mr Webster Ought to mention the note of the person causing the stoppage in Oakland-street. —Mr Dutton said he was a large owner in o.lkland-streat, and neither he nor any occupier had complaine I of any stoppage of the street. He thought it was out of order f a any mem- ber to make such stateme.nts as Mr Webster had done.—The meeting then concluded.

LATEST NEWS Further foreign quarantine notices received at the Foreign Office are gazetted. Mr Gladstone will arrive at Brechin on Wednesday, where several addresses will be presented to him. Carcanr.—ln the' moon, yesterday, Australians v. South of England, the Australian innings ended for 163. Earl Spencer passed through Drimoleague on Friday afternoon on his way to Cork, and was corditily received by a large concoursi of people assembled at the railway station.

A man. named Car..hman, herd of Mr D M'Cartlav, Fart Grady, Mill-street, near Cork, was found near a fence with his throat cut. It is stated that the outrage was committed while the man was asleep. THE MEELING OF PARLIAMENT. Friday night's Gazette publishes the Queen's proclamation further pro- roguing Parliament to Thursday, October 23,d, upon which date both Houses are r(quired and commanded to assemble for the despatch of divers urgent and important affairs. LONG FIRM SWINt/LING —A men who has been trading in several places in Leeds, under various aliases, was arres- ted on Fi idly, at Nottingham, on a charge of being engaged in extensive long firm transactions. He is specially char- ged with swindling Messrs Hayes and Co, of Waterfold, out of butter to the value of £520.

HORRIBLE DEATH OF A FAR-MER.—A shocking occur- rence was on Friday reported from Curryglass, in county Waterford. A farmer named Ahern had bathed his leg and bound it with a bandage saturated with paraffin oil, when it caught fire and blazed furiously, setting his clothes aflame and so horribly burning him that death resulted shortly afterwards. EXCITING FATALITY AT ChksGow.—A plank communica- tion between the quay at Glasgow and the steamer Canadian broke on Friday morning, and three men who were on it were precipitated into the water. Two were rescued, but the third, a labourer, named Joseph Wenney, disap- peared below the vessel and was drowned. The body was recovered half an hour after the accident. is belonged to Dundee. _ .

CAPTAIN DUDLEY IN LoNDON.—Captain Dudley, of the : ill-fated yacht Mignonette, arrived in London on Friday morning from Falmouth, and was met by his wife. The meeting between them was of a most affecting nature. Mrs Dudley had been prostrated for some days, but travelled to London to receive her husband. Beth proceeded by cab to Victoria wation, and left for Captain Dudley's house at Sutton, where a doctor was procured to dress the wounds from which Captain Du Iley still suffers. A VINDICATION BY Mae. BRADLAUGII The correspon- dent of a morning paper having written that Mr Bradlaugh received a consideration of £2,5 for attending the Liberal demonstration at Crewe on the Franchise Bill, the hon member for Northampton writes declaring that except from the annual miners meeting, he never in his life re- ceived one farthing for travelling or hotel bills in connec• tion with out-do3r meetings on political questions. "It is true," he adds, "that my tongue often earns large sums. If it did not, I should starve." A MERCHANT KILLED WHILE PARTRIDGE SHOOTING. Mr Angus ill'lntyre, a well known merchant in Dundee, was accidentally killed while partridge shooting on Thursday, on Sidlaw Hills, with a party of gentlemen. The game- keeper accompanying the party was laying down a gun ' when the trigger was caught by potato tops, and a charge of small shot lodged is Mr M'lntyre's left leg. The limb was amputated, but Mr M'lntyre never recovered the shock, and died this morning. The deceased was 45 years of age, and has left a widow and family.

A LOCAL ROMANCE: "TRUTH STRANGER THAN FICTION." The incidents of a rather romantic Wary have 1 within the last few days been brought to light in Warring,to.n. The principal dramatis personae are a West Indian sugar planter named L averens and a Warrington fustian cutter, whose maiden name was Higgins. Some five•and-twenty years ago the gentle- man, who is said to be of so dark a complexion as to i be described as a mulatto, was sent over to Eneland by his father, a sugar planter and rum merchant of considerable wealth and repute, to receive the benefit of an English education and accomplishments. He was then only eleven years of age, so that he will now have arrived at the age of thirty-six. He was i placed in the hands of the preceptors of what is now called the Liverpool College, but was then simply described as "The Collegiate." Here he remained some , time and acquired a sound Eaglish education. Whilst I thus pursuing his studies, he made the acquaintance , and secured the friendship of a young gentleman of good pesition, who Came from Warrington, and who I , was also being educated at " The Collegiate." On 1 the completion of his education, he came to Warring- ton and was at the instance of his father apprenticed , to Mr. Needham, a civil engineer, then occupying a I place of business in Scotland•roal, it being thought that the knowledge of that profession would be fouerl 1 of considerable advantage to him on his return to St. I 1 Lucia, the island in the West Indies, where his [family are in possession of estates. Before the term of his apprenticeship had expired, he was, however, I badly burnt on sue of his hands, and was in con- I 1 sequence incapacitated from following the avocation he we, learning. He still remained in Warrington, and was m untamed by his father. At the ay,-e of nineteen the youth, who is said by tiaat time to have acquired a taste for British sports, appears to have succumbed to the charms of a fustian cutter, wile was them little more than " sweet six- teen," and who is described by those who knew her at the time as baying been an unusually pretty and at- tractive girl. The tender youth was successful in his love-making, his advances were favourably received, and before long the two were made happy by mar- j riage and became known as a steady and respectable couple. They appear to have lived happily together for about three years, three children being the result of the union. About this time the father of the young man sent for hie son to come home to occupy the position on his native island which he had been educated .to maintain, and the summons was obeyed. The young wife and family were meanwhile left in Warrington, both, it is said, indulging in fervent hopes that the son would induce the father to over- look what would be by him considered a sad mesal- Nance, and allow him to send for his loved ones to join him. The husband for some time sent remittances of money to his wife, but it is not ascertainable how long they were continued. That they ceased within the course of two or three years, if not earlier, seems, however, to be certain, and this appears to have given rise to the idea in the mind of the wife that her husb and was dead. She continued to work at her old occupation as a fustian cutter, and some three or four years ago entered into the bonds of marriage with a man named Molyneaux,one in her own position in life, by whom she has had children. Those who knew the parties and the circumstances of their lives say that the second husband was a soldier who was invalided from Zaluland, and that on his return he became enamoured of the neglected wife, whom he almost persecuted with attentions that were for a time repulsed. Finally he pressed his suit with more success, she consented, and they were du'y mar- ried, she, it is supposed, being thee fully confirmed in the conviction that her first husband was dead. The more curious part of the story is yet to follow. A daughter by the first marriage, who had no doubt heard some talk of her parentage, was not long ago rummaging some papers belonging to her mother, when she discovered a letter that had been written to her mother by the distant husband and father. This girl, who is a little ()e'er fifteen years of age, made no meation to her mother of the discovery, but procured the assistance of a friend to write a letter to her father, informing him of the second marriage. This letter was received in due course, and as the old gentleman had died some short time previously to that date, the son, who had come into poss ;ssion of a considerable portion of the property, determined on visiting England. Two days afterwards he took passaae in a trading vessel that was pass:ng the island, and arrived in London on Friday last. He at once took train to Warrington, and reached his old home in Fenn ell-street at about nine o'clock in the evening. What adds a melancholy interest to the efftir is that the father of the wife was at the time lying dead in the house, which was the same in which the wedding breakfast was served whoa the I first marriage was celebrated. On the arrival be- coming known, word was passed round to the neigh- bours that " Lawrens had come bank," and some stir ensued. A crowd collected rouad the somewhat embarrassed foreigner, and many old acquaintances shook him by the hand. The woman whom be left the inother of three children when she w•s but twenty- one was again brought face to face with him, but, as he had previously received the intimation from his daughter of the second marriage, he was not taken by surprise. Notwithstanding, the meeting may be described as having been an affecting and painful, if not an affectionate' one. The daughter whose action broueht her father again to the shores of England seems at once to have found favour in his sight. She is described as being dark, good-looking, genteel and tasteful in her dress, and, moreover, as bearing a groat resem- blance o her father. She was the second child of the first marriage, the eldest and youngest of the offspring having died, and she was, of course, a child only when her father re-visited the place of his nativity. The meeting between the father and daughter is said to have been exceedingly touching. lie evinced great affection, warmly embracing her, and scarcely seemed happy out of her company. With very little persuasion, if indeed any were re- quired, she consented to accompany her father back to St. Lucia, and on Wednesday the two left War • Huston for Liverpool, and it is expected that they will sail this day (S atarday) in the same vessel that brought the father to Eagland. It is thOtlght to be the intention of Mr. Lawrens to take his daughter to see her grandmother, and thee place her at some suitable school to be educated. Before leaving home finelly she was provided with a more extensive and c astly wardrobe than, probably, she ever dreamt of possessing. The daughter had been apprenticed to Mr. Platt as a fustian cutter, and had yet four years to serve. She appears to have been of rather a flighty dispo- sition, and SOOl5 short time ago she left work and ran away to Salford, Manchester, whence she was brought back by an Inspector of the Borough Police force, and subsequently summoaed, in company With others, before the magistrates, to answer a charge of neglec- ting her work. The occurrences of the last few days have created intense interest in the cutting rooms, and have been the chief topic of conversation. It is asserted that the letters written between husband and wife were intercepted by the watchful father, and, if so, that will go a long way to explain the estrangee ment, and the conviction of the wife that the lover of her youth was lost to her for ever. It is also said that the youth had been somewhat harshly treated in consequence of his contracting a marriage with a humble English girl ; but that statement appears to be a matter more of conjecture than ascertained fact.

The mother of the hero of the romance is of French birth, and the father is said to have been of Spanish extraction, but a native of St. Lucia. It is not yet known what aspect affairs will assume as regards the anomalous positions of the twice married Eden Hig- gins, and the man with whom she contracted a second alliance, but it is stated that•sho expresses her determination not to live, with him again. The second husband, who is an Irishman, was considerably agitated on the appearance of his sup- posed wife's first husband, and during the interview that took place in private between La,wrons and his wife, appeared very uneasy. The neighbourhood in which the parties reside has been thrown into quite a state of excitement by the romantic occurrence, which seems likely to prove more than a "nine days' wonder." The story is another illustration of the adage, that " Truth is stranger than fiction."

The inquest on the body of Ann Eliz kbeth Brown, who Wig fatally struck on the head with a poker by her son, Henry Brown, at California, near Yarmouth, terminated on Thursday night in a verdict of wilful murder against the latter.

It haying been stated that on his release "the Claimant " will be eng)ged by the Church of England Temperance Society "to give his experience of total abstinence," the general secretary to the society writes that "there is not a word of truth in it."

In a telegram from Naples of Thursday's date as to the ravages of the cholera, it is stated that the condition of affairs there remains as distressing as ever. The King was prevented from visiting the poorer quarter of the city on Thursday, as he intended. SUDDEN DEant.—On Monday a child named John Law- ton, three years of age, eon of John Lawton, weaver, Lvthgoes-lare, died suddenly in convulsions. Ile had been delieato from birth, and an inquest was not deemed neces- sary,

div.head: TRADES CONGRESS.
div.p: THE TRADES CONGRESS.

At Friday's meeting of the Trades' Congress a question arose as to the Standing Orders Committee having rejected a proposed resolution concerning Sunday opening of muse- ums and libraries, and it was resolved by a majority that the subject should be discussed on Saturday. A resolution was passel, calling attention to the necessity of the Parliamen- tary Committee obtaining 931110 direct and easy method of prosecution against falsely marking spurious good 3. There was again a large attendance of delegates. Resolutions were passed in favour of the Railway Regula- tions Bill, especially viewing the necessity for reducing the working hours of railway servants, also urging the appoint- ment of practical inspectors for shipbuilding yards. A long and interesting discussion followed upon a motion against the employment of female children under 14 years of age at forging nail, chain, or bolts. The women delegates moved the omission of the word "female," but, upon a division, the original resolution was carried by a large majority.

div.p: THE CASE OF THE NISERO,

SINGAPORE. FRIDAY.—The Italian sailors of the captive Crew of the Nisero were released on the 3rd instant by the Rajah of Tenorn, who has also promised to give up the remaining prisoners. THE NILE EXPEDITION.

MALTA, FRIDAY =The hired transport Rewa has arrived here, and will sail to-day for Calcutta. She has on board 412 officers and men, being drafts for various regiments in Egypt, who will be disembarked at Alexandria. THE CROLERA EPIDEMIC.

ROME, FRIDAY.—The health of the capital continues excellent. NAPLES, FRIDAY.—The improvement in the public health noticed here yesterday evening continued through the night. Wooden huts are being constructed to shelter the poor and for hospital purposes. The difficulty in the meat supply, owine to the strike among the butchers, has been settled. The King still declines to leave Naples. MADRID, FRIDAY.—The official bulletin issued this morning reports that during the last 21 hours there have been eight cases of cholera and four deaths at Elche, five ctses at Novelda, and two cases at Oadon Da Las Nieves, a village near Novelda. THE 14'ttANCO-CHINESE WAR. THE BLOCKING OF WOOSING BAR. _ .

The Press Association has been informed that the Penin- sular and Oriental Steamship Company this morning re- ceived a telegram from Shanghai confirming the statement already published that the Chinese were hastening their preparations for blocking Woosing B tr. The foreign con- suls at Shangh ti are making strong and earnest protests against this measure as being productive of permanent in- jury to the only passage to the river.
A Central News Pads telegram says : An official despatch states that Admiral Courbot is at Mat?ou, esaling and re- victualling. The squadron is not yet completed.

GRAPPENKAUL PARISH CHURCH.—This church is abmt to be provided with a handsome stained glass window, which it is intended shall be plac9d in the east end of the building. The subject of the window will be the five chief events in the history of our Saviour—the Nativity, Baptism, Cruci- fixion, R-surrection. and Ascension. There will also at t
same time be introduced into the church a new reredos, he which the subject will be "The List Supper,'bth being by Meegrs Mayerl; Co., of London and Munich.

CRUELTY TO ANtmats —At the Warrington Borough Police Court, yesterday, James Whitley, of Stockton Heath, was charged with causing a horse to b 3 illtreate.d on the 3rd September.—Mr R Davies, solicitor, Warrington, defended, and pleaded not guilty. Inspector Nicholls, of the R S.P.C.A., said that on the afternoon of the day in ques- tion he was in Sankey-street. Warrington, when he saw the son of the defend mt driving a brown pony attached to a cart. The pony WAS very lame on the off hind leg, and was sufforing from a diseased hock.—Mr Davies called a wit- ness to prove that the horse was nq suffering as described by the Inspector and Mr Robinson, V.S , who gave evidence as to its condition. Mr Davies also mentioned that he had noticed what he thought great cruelty to horses that were driven on Sundays, often with very heavy leads.—The Bench fined the defendant 103 and costs.— InspecOr Nicholls said that with regard to cruelty to animals on Sun- days, the officers of the society were paid by voluntary sub- scriptions, and he believed none were received from War- rington, so that the officers could not be expected to be on duty there.—James Swindle, Edon-street, and Thomas Parker were charged, the former with ill-treating, and the latter with causing to be ill-treated, a horse, on the 3rd instant.—The case was proved by P.C. Johnstone, In- spector Nicholls, and the veterinary surgeon—Parker was fined Ws and costs, and fwindle 53 and costs.

FACTORS ACT PROSECTJTIONS.—At the Warrington Borough Court yesterday morning, Messra Armitage and Rigby, cotton manufacturers, Warrington, were summoned for employing in, or allowing to remain in, a room in which a manufacturing process was carried on, a member of hands in their employ.—Mr Mead-King, factory inspector, said that proceedings were taken under the 17th section of the Act, which provided that no young persons or women should be allowed during meal hours to remain in, or be employed in, a room where a manufacturing process was being carried on. Eight minutes before the expiration of the half hour allowed for breakfast, a certain number of females were found at work.—Mr S R Armitage appeared for the firm, and pleaded guilty, but stid that the offence was not intentional. They were not aware that the engines had been started -so numb before time, but they .knew they were started say about two minutes before time, which was consequent on the largeness of the place and the difficulty of the hands getting to their several rooms by the time the hour was up. It was sometimes nearly impossible to keep the whole of the bands out of the shed, bat they did all that was possible. Since the inspector had called upon them, they had had fired an electric bell which would en- able the firm itself to superintend the starting of the engines. The offence was not committed with their know- ledge.—The Inspector said that the works in question had been very well conducted indeed since he had had charge of the district, a d he was glad to see that steps bad •been taken to prevent any repetition of the offence. He did not press for a heavy penalty.—The Bench inflicted a penalty I of £1 in the first case mentioned in the charge, and Is in respect of each other person named, and the costs.-- Niessrs James Platt and Son were similarly summoned in respect to several girls employed by them.—Mr R Davies, solicitor,Warrington, defended, and pleaded not guilty.—An inspector proved seeing some of the females employed by the defendant at work during the breakfast hour.—At the• request of Mr Davies, Mr Mead-King read a section of the Act, showing that if an occupier had paid all due attention to preventing such an offence, and others had committed the offence against his will and without his cognisance, such persona could be summoned and made answerable.— Mr Davies wished that point to be made public for the benefit of tbeamployers. His object in raising the question was that those who actually broke the law should be made responsible, and Mr Platt wished it to be understood that he had not wilfully broken the law. For 16 years Mr Platt had carried on the businees in the most creditable manner, which was no easy task whoa it was considered that he had over 1,200 people in his employ. He thought it might be understood that if another case of that kind occurred those workpeople who offended would also be summoned.—The Magistrates inflicted a penalty of 103 and costs in the first case, and Is in each of the manias ones mentioned in the anunnocs, sorl oasts..

At the Liverpool City Police Court, on Thursday, Ernest Heymans, provision merchant, was brought up on various charges of fraud under the Debtors' Act, and remanded for seven days. The first denominational hall in connection with Queen's College, Ireland, was opened at Cork, on Wednesday, by the Right Rev Dr Gregg. The hall has cost £9,000, and is in- tended for resident Protestant studente. AN EARLESTOWN AFFILIATION CASE AT ST. HELENS. —Several persons from Earlestown attended the St Helens Police Court, on Monday, when James David Edwards, a striker at the Viaduct Works, Earlestewn, was summoned to show cause why he should not contribute te the support of the illegitimate child of Elizabeth Chisnall, of which he was alleged to be the father.—The defendant, who was re- presented by Mr W Swift, denied the alleged paternity.— Mr H L Riley appeared for the complainant—it was stated that the complainant was a single young woman, and resided with her father and mother at Broad Oak, Parr. Some years ago she was in service at E arlestown, and had a sweetheart named Edwards (the defendant), but for some reason she gave him up. At the last Newton races but one the defen- dant sent a message to her, and she ultimately saw him, with the result that they made up their difference, and they courted again. They went courting along the canal bank, and they were also seen in a wood. They were seen stand- ing in the garden of the complainant's home for about an hour, and during that time defendant said, " Lizzie, we shall not have long to stand here; we shall be married before Christmas." The defendant ultimately stopped coining to her house, and on being asked why he did so, he said it was very dark at nights, but he would come as usual en the Saturday nights. She wrote to him on two occasions, but he refused to answer the letters. She was delivered of a female child on the 27th June last, and the defendant was the father of it. The complainant added that the child was a " speakieg likeness " of the defendant.—Margaret Chis- nail said she had seen the defendant and her daughter in the 1 garden. The defendant had his arm round her waist.— Other witnesses were called, who stated that they bad s•en the parties together.—For the defence Mr Swift said that ' proof of mere courtship was not sufficient testimony of the paternity of a child. Merely putting one's arm round a girl's waist did not make a man the father of a child she might bear.—A young man was called as a witness, aud said he had seen the complainant on the canal bank, and she then informed him that she had given over going with the de- fendant.—The Eench made an order for the payment of 3s per week with the usual expenses HOLLOWAY'S PlLLS.—There is nothing in the whole " lelateria fitedie,a" like these Medicaments for the certainty of their action In lumbago, sciatica, tic doloreux, and all flying or settled pains in the nerves and muscle.. • WARRINGTON -(ASSOCIATION) FOOTBALL CUB, Oe Tuesday evening a meeting of the members of this newly' formed club Wan held in the Temperance rooms, Sankey- street, for the purpose of electing a committee and range to act provisionally. It was stated that a field to play ill had been procured in Latchford at a reasonable rent, ana also that efforts were being made to arrange matches with neighbouring clubs. It was agreed after some convertia- tion that the subscription for the season should be fixed at four shillings, one shilling to be paid on entrance and the alit' three before the 4th October. The following commit- tee and officers were then appointed, Viz :—Cmonalittee Messrs Savage, Pearson, Matthews, Walton, Royston, and You-ge; hon sec, Mr Philips ; and hon treasurer, Mr Adam- son. The s!cretary ' was also instructed to make arrangements for play to c nntnence to-day (Saturday), if pocsible. - CHILDREN'S TREAT AT CROFF.—The Custom Of giving the children of this parish a treat in the early par; of Sep' tembsr was observed on &stud ty. The weather was very unfavoarable, and from the time the children assembled at the Board School (one o'clock) until after darkness had set in, it rained without the least Case ation. However, it W3B decided that the procession should take place as usual, but those only took part in it who were provided with urnbrellae or cloaks. Two binds, the Lawton Brass and the Croft Drum and Fife, were in attendance. There being no avail- able room in which the children could be entertained, the schoolmaster (Mr. Ball) decided, after MI, on distributing nuts and sweets to all, to dismiss them with the promise that the usual sports should be held in a few days. A large number of adults partook of t-a, and spent a very enjoyable evening in the school, the Lo anon Band (under the endue- torshp of Mr. Charles Wood) bsing present.' _ MARRIAGE OF MR EDWARD GREENALL, JUN.—The mar riage of Mr Edward Greenall, pin. (eAest son of Mr Edward Greenall, J.P.), of Grappenhall Hill, Cheshire, to Miss A 14 Dunn (loath daughter of Mr Nicholas J Dunn, Of Manor House, Clifton), tosk place on Tuesday morning, at St. Paul's Church, Clifton, a large number of persons being present. The ceremony was pet f armed by the Rev Canon Mather, assisted by the Roe Canon Greenall, f Grappen• hall. Mr J U Dunn, brother of the bride, was best man ; and the bridesmaids were Miss Dunn, Miss Imogene Dunne Miss Johanna Dunn, Mies Frances Dunn, Miss Florence Dunn, Miss Ecriersley, Miss Bennett, and Miss Harriette.
